📋 The DevOps Lifecycle — 6 Phases
📌PlanJira
Track features, bugs, and sprints. Teams align on what to build before any code is written. Jira tickets define scope and ownership.
💡 Agile sprints, epics, user stories — know the vocabulary.
💻CodeGit / GitHub
Write modular, readable code so teammates can understand it. Use feature branches, meaningful commits, and pull requests with code reviews.
💡 Modularity = maintainability. PRs are the gate before code merges.
🔨BuildDocker / Makefile
Prepare code for deployment — build Docker images, run containers. A Makefile automates this so every commit triggers a clean, repeatable build.
💡 make build → docker build → image pushed. Reproducible every time.
🧪TestJest / Pytest
Automated tests run in CI. If anything breaks, the pipeline stops. Broken code never reaches production.
💡 Fail fast. Unit → Integration → E2E. Each layer catches different bugs.
🚀DeployJenkins / Kubernetes
Pipelines handle the entire deployment process automatically. Kubernetes orchestrates deployment at scale — deciding where containers run, how many copies, and recovering crashes.
💡 Your job as a DevOps engineer: build these pipelines.
📊Operate + MonitorPrometheus / Grafana
Monitor server health, scale resources when traffic spikes, apply security patches. Collect latencies, error logs, CPU/memory. Dashboards + alerts close the feedback loop.
💡 Operate = keep the lights on. Monitor = know when lights flicker.
🌉
The DevOps Role in One Sentence
Bridge the gap between dev and ops teams by automating the boring, manual work.
Plan → Code → Build → Test → Deploy → Operate → Monitor → Plan again.
🗺️ The Right Order to Learn This — And Why Nothing Here Is Redundant
The most common point of confusion: "Kubernetes already restarts my containers — why do I need AWS too? If Kubernetes schedules everything, what's Terraform even for?"

Here's the actual answer: none of these tools do the same job. Each one is responsible for one layer of the stack, and hands off to the next. They feel redundant only because you're seeing the end result (an app running in production) without seeing which tool did which part to get it there. Once you learn them in the right order, each new tool doesn't feel like a brand-new unrelated thing — it feels like the exact same idea you just learned, applied one layer up.
🧱 Who's Actually Responsible for What
LayerToolActually responsible forNOT responsible for
CodeGit / GitHubTracking every change, letting people collaborate without overwriting each other, reviewing before merging.Doesn't run or package anything.
PackagingDockerBundling your app + everything it needs into one portable image that behaves the same everywhere.Doesn't decide where that image runs, or how many copies.
AutomationCI/CD (GitHub Actions / Jenkins)Reacting to an event (a push) and running a checklist — test, build, push — with zero human involved.Doesn't manage containers long-term, doesn't provision servers.
OrchestrationKubernetesDeciding how many copies of a container run, restarting crashed ones, load-balancing between them, scaling with traffic.Doesn't create the underlying machines it schedules pods onto — it needs somewhere to run first.
InfrastructureAWS (or any cloud)Providing the actual rented servers, networks, and storage that everything above physically runs on.Knows nothing about your app's code, containers, or pipelines — it just rents you machines.
ProvisioningTerraformThe code that requests and configures that AWS infrastructure repeatably, instead of clicking through a console by hand.Doesn't run your app — it just builds the ground your app stands on.
FeedbackPrometheus / GrafanaReporting what's actually happening once everything above is live — CPU, errors, latency.Doesn't deploy or fix anything itself — it just tells you something needs fixing.
The punchline: Kubernetes needs a machine to schedule containers onto. AWS is where that machine comes from. Terraform is how you asked AWS for that machine as code instead of clicking a console 40 times. Nothing here overlaps — it's one continuous handoff, top to bottom, not six tools competing to do the same job.
📚 Learn Them in This Order — Each One Becomes the Vocabulary for the Next
1
Gitversion everything
The big idea: a change is tracked, reviewable, and reversible. Carries forward: every tool below also stores its config in Git — Dockerfiles, Kubernetes YAML, Terraform files. Same discipline, just a new file type each time.
2
Linux / Shellthe CLI is the interface
The big idea: a real server has no GUI — the command line is the only way in. Carries forward: docker, kubectl, terraform, aws — every tool after this is "type a command, read the output." Same muscle memory, reused everywhere.
3
Dockerdescribe the end result, not the steps
The big idea: write one file (a Dockerfile) describing what the finished thing should contain, and package it once so it runs identically anywhere. Carries forward: this exact pattern — a file describing a desired end-state — is precisely what Kubernetes YAML does next, one layer up.
4
CI/CD — GitHub Actions or Jenkinsevents trigger automatic reactions
The big idea: something happens (a push) and a system reacts automatically, unattended, the same way every time. Carries forward: that "event happens → system reacts" pattern is the same mental model behind Kubernetes self-healing (a pod dies → it reacts) and cloud auto-scaling (traffic rises → it reacts).
5
Kubernetesdeclare the state, let a controller enforce it
The big idea: don't run containers directly — describe the desired state ("3 replicas of this image") and a controller continuously makes reality match that description. Carries forward: that is exactly how Terraform works in the next stage — same discipline, aimed at servers instead of containers.
6
Cloud (AWS) + Terraformthe ground everything else stands on
The big idea: none of the above runs on nothing — Docker images, Kubernetes clusters, and CI runners all execute on real (rented) machines somewhere, and that's what AWS provides. Terraform then applies stage 5's exact idea — describe the desired state as code — to the machines themselves, instead of what runs on them.
🧩
Learn it top to bottom, and monitoring closes the loop
Git → Linux → Docker → CI/CD → Kubernetes → AWS + Terraform. | Then Prometheus/Grafana watches the result and feeds problems back into Git as new commits — the same loop from the top of this tab, now automated end to end.

⚙️ Pipeline — Stage by Stage
📝
STAGE 01Code & PushGit / GitHub
Write code locally, commit and push to remote repo. Starting gun for everything else.
git commit -m "feat: ..."git push origin main
💡 Every push triggers the belt. Feature branches keep main stable.
⚡
STAGE 02CI TriggeredJenkins / GitHub Actions
Webhook fires the moment code lands on GitHub. Jenkins kicks off the automated pipeline instantly — no manual clicking.
💡 Webhook = push notification. Polling = asking every few mins. Webhooks win.
🧪
STAGE 03Build & TestDocker / Makefile / Jest
Makefile builds Docker image. Tests run automatically. Any failure stops the pipeline. Safety net — nothing broken escapes.
make buildnpm test
💡 CI = every push tests automatically. CD = tests pass → app deploys automatically.
🐳
STAGE 04DockerizeDocker / ECR / Docker Hub
App + all dependencies packaged into a portable image. Pushed to a registry. Same image, every environment.
docker build -t myapp .docker push registry/myapp:v2
🚀
STAGE 05DeployKubernetes / ECS
Pipeline deploys to staging first, then production. Kubernetes manages all containers at scale.
kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml
📊
STAGE 06MonitorPrometheus / Grafana
Prometheus scrapes metrics. Grafana dashboards show CPU, memory, error rates, latency. Alerts fire, loop restarts.
metrics: cpu, mem, rps, p99, errors
🔁
The Core DevOps Loop
Bug found → fix committed → webhook fires → tests run → image built → deployed → monitored. This loop running fast and automatically IS DevOps.
☸️Kubernetes (K8s)Container Orchestrator
In a real app you don't have one container — you have many. A microservice container, a background job container, a database container, a cache container.

Problem: Someone needs to decide where each container runs, how many copies to spin up, and what happens when one crashes.

Solution → Kubernetes. It schedules containers across your servers, automatically restarts crashed pods, scales replicas on traffic spikes, and scales down when load drops.

Think of K8s as the hotel manager: assigns rooms (servers) to guests (containers), handles complaints (crashes), calls for extra staff (scaling) when the hotel is full.
Pod = smallest unitDeployment = manages replicasService = exposes podsAuto-scalingSelf-healing
📋Infrastructure as Code (IaC)Terraform / CloudFormation
Your entire infrastructure — servers, networks, databases, load balancers — described in code files, stored in Git, reviewed like any other code change.

Why? Without IaC, someone manually clicks around in the AWS console. That's slow, error-prone, impossible to reproduce. With IaC, run one command and your entire environment spins up identically — dev, staging, production.

No company owns physical servers. They rent compute from AWS, Azure, or GCP. IaC manages that rented infrastructure in a repeatable, auditable, version-controlled way.
describe in codestore in gitrepeatable environmentsno manual clickingAWS / Azure / GCP
📊Monitoring & ObservabilityPrometheus + Grafana
The team continuously gathers data: latencies, error logs, CPU, memory, request rates.

Prometheus — scrapes metrics from your app on a schedule. Stores time-series data.

Grafana — connects to Prometheus and turns raw numbers into dashboards. Alert rules: "if error rate > 1%, page the on-call engineer."

Operate phase: Scale resources when traffic spikes, apply security patches, respond to incidents before users notice.
latency (p50/p95/p99)error rateCPU / memoryRPSalertsdashboards
🎯What is the DevOps Role?The Bridge
DevOps engineers bridge the gap between development teams (who write features) and operations teams (who keep systems running).

Core job: automate the boring, manual, repetitive work — so developers focus on features and ops engineers focus on reliability, not clicking buttons.

Concretely: building CI/CD pipelines, managing Kubernetes clusters, writing Terraform for infra, setting up monitoring, and making sure deployments happen safely and automatically.
bridge dev ↔ opsautomate everythingbuild pipelinesreliability
📖 Quick Reference — All Key Terms
CI
Auto-build + test on every push. Catch bugs early.
CD (Delivery)
Every passing build is deployable. Human approves final push.
CD (Deployment)
Every passing build auto-deploys. Fully automated.
Webhook
HTTP push notification when an event fires (e.g. git push).
Docker Image
Portable snapshot: app + all dependencies. Immutable.
Container
A running instance of a Docker image. Isolated, lightweight.
Registry
Storage for Docker images. Docker Hub, AWS ECR, GCR.
Kubernetes (K8s)
Orchestrates containers — scheduling, scaling, self-healing.
Pod
Smallest K8s unit. Wraps one or more containers.
Deployment (K8s)
Manages replicas of a pod. Handles rolling updates.
Rolling Update
Replace containers gradually. Zero downtime.
Blue-Green
Two identical envs. Flip traffic switch. Instant rollback.
Canary Deploy
Route X% of traffic to new version. Validate before full rollout.
IaC
Infrastructure described in code. Stored in Git. Repeatable.
Terraform
IaC tool. Declare infra in HCL files. Works across clouds.
Makefile
Automates build commands. make build → docker build + run.
Prometheus
Scrapes and stores time-series metrics from your app.
Grafana
Visualizes Prometheus data into dashboards + alerts.
Microservices
App split into small independent services, each in its own container.
Staging
Pre-production environment. Mirrors prod. Where CD deploys first.
Jira
Project planning tool. Tracks sprints, tickets, epics.
4 Golden Signals
Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation — Google SRE monitoring framework.

📁 Navigation & File Management
pwdlocation
Print working directory — shows where you are right now.
$ pwd
/home/ibrahiem
ls -lalist
ls lists files. -l = long format (permissions, size, date). -a = show hidden files (starting with .).
$ ls -la /var/log
cd /var/lognavigate
Change directory. cd .. = go up one level. cd ~ = go home. cd - = go back to previous dir.
$ cd /var/log
$ cd ..
touch / mkdircreate
touch app.log creates an empty file. mkdir logs creates a folder. mkdir -p app/config creates nested dirs in one shot.
$ touch app.log
$ mkdir -p app/config
cp / mv / rmmanage
cp file.txt backup.txt copies. cp -r dir1 dir2 copies directories. mv old.txt new.txt renames or moves. rm -rf folder deletes folder recursively — no confirmation, no undo.
$ cp -r dir1 dir2
$ rm -rf folder ⚠️
📄 Reading Files
cat file.txtread all
Dump entire file to terminal. Good for small files. Avoid on huge log files.
head / tailpartial read
head -n 10 file.txt = first 10 lines. tail -n 10 file.txt = last 10 lines. tail -f app.log = follow live — watches the file as new lines are written. 🔥 Essential for watching logs in real time.
$ tail -f app.log  # live stream
grepsearch
grep "error" app.log — find lines with "error". -i = case insensitive. -r = search recursively through all files in a directory.
$ grep -i "error" app.log
$ grep -r "error" .
findlocate files
Search the filesystem by name or type. find . -name "*.log" = all .log files in current dir. find / -type f -name "config.yaml" = search entire filesystem.
$ find . -name "*.log"
$ find / -type f -name "config.yaml"
🔗 Pipes & Redirects — The Power Combo
Pipe ( | ) = take the output of one command and feed it as input to the next.
Redirect ( > ) = send output to a file (overwrites). ( >> ) = append to file.
ls | grep ".txt"pipe
List files, then filter to only show .txt files. Output of ls is piped into grep.
grep "error" app.log | wc -lcount
Count how many lines contain "error". wc -l counts lines. Useful for quick error counts.
$ grep "error" app.log | wc -l
42
> and >>redirect
echo "hello" > file.txt — overwrites the file with "hello". echo "world" >> file.txt — appends "world" as a new line. > destroys existing content. >> is safe.
$ echo "hello" > file.txt
$ echo "world" >> file.txt
🔐 Permissions
Reading permission strings:
-rwxr-xr--

- = file type (-=file, d=dir, l=symlink)
rwx = owner can Read, Write, Execute
r-x = group can Read, Execute (no write)
r-- = others can only Read

Numeric mode: r=4, w=2, x=1. Add them up per group.
755 = owner:rwx(7) group:r-x(5) others:r-x(5)
644 = owner:rw-(6) group:r--(4) others:r--(4)
chmodchange perms
chmod 755 script.sh = set numeric permissions. chmod +x script.sh = add execute permission for everyone. Scripts need +x to run.
$ chmod +x deploy.sh
$ ./deploy.sh
chownchange owner
chown user file.txt = change owner. chown user:group file.txt = change both owner and group. Used when files are created by root but need to be accessed by app user.
$ chown deploy:www-data /var/app
⚙️ Processes & System Health
ps auxprocesses
List all running processes with PID, CPU%, MEM%, and command. Pipe to grep to find a specific process: ps aux | grep nginx.
$ ps aux | grep nginx
top / htoplive monitor
Live CPU/memory monitor. Updates in real time. Press q to quit. htop is the prettier version (if installed). Essential for spotting runaway processes.
kill / kill -9stop process
kill PID = graceful stop (lets process clean up). kill -9 PID = force kill instantly — no cleanup. Use graceful first, -9 as last resort.
$ kill 1234
$ kill -9 1234  # nuclear option
df -hdisk space
Show disk space on all filesystems. -h = human readable (GB/MB). Critical for catching "disk full" issues before they crash your app.
$ df -h
Filesystem Size Used Avail Use%
du -sh *folder sizes
Show size of each file/folder in current directory. du -sh /var/log/* = see which log files are eating your disk.
$ du -sh /var/log/*
free -hRAM
Show total, used, and free RAM. -h = human readable. Critical metric — if RAM is full, apps start crashing or swapping to disk (very slow).
$ free -h
Mem: 7.7G 4.2G 1.2G
uptimesystem age
Shows how long the system has been running + load average (1m, 5m, 15m). Load avg > number of CPU cores = system is overloaded.
$ uptime
up 14 days, load avg: 0.5 0.4 0.3
🌐 Networking
pingreachability
Check if a host is reachable. ping google.com sends ICMP packets and measures round-trip time. Ctrl+C to stop.
curlHTTP requests
Make HTTP requests from the terminal. Essential for testing APIs. curl http://api.com = GET request. Add -v for verbose output, -X POST for POST.
$ curl -v http://localhost:8080/health
wgetdownload
Download files from URLs. wget file_url saves to current directory. Good for downloading configs, binaries, or scripts onto a server.
🔧 Services (systemctl)
systemctl statuscheck
systemctl status nginx — shows if the service is running, failed, or stopped. Also shows last few log lines. First thing to run when something seems broken.
$ systemctl status nginx
● nginx.service - Active: active (running)
systemctl restartrestart
systemctl restart nginx — stops and restarts the service. systemctl stop / start available too. systemctl enable nginx = auto-start on boot.
$ systemctl restart nginx
$ systemctl enable nginx
🧠
The DevOps Linux Survival Kit
Investigate: ps aux | grep app → tail -f app.log → grep -i error app.log | wc -l
Health check: df -h → free -h → uptime → top
Service down: systemctl status nginx → systemctl restart nginx
🔣 Symbols & Flags Cheat Card
🧠 VERY important trick: Don't memorize -h, -a, -f, etc. as having one universal meaning — the meaning depends on the command. For example: df -h → -h = human-readable. But tail -f → -f = follow. So think: command + option = meaning, not "this flag always means X."
SymbolMeaningExample
-hHuman-readabledf -h
-R / -rRecursive / related behavior depending on commandchmod -R 755 folder
-fFollow / force / other meaning depending on commandtail -f file
-aAllps -a
-lLong formatls -l
-vVerbose / version depending on commandsomecommand -v
-nNumber / no / other meaning depending on commandhead -n 5 file
-pPort/path/parents/etc. depending on commandmkdir -p folder/a/b
-qQuietsomecommand -q
-iInteractive / ignore-case depending on commandrm -i file
-xExecute / exclude / other meaning depending on commandchmod +x script.sh
--helpShow helpls --help
--versionShow versionnode --version
&Run in backgroundnode app.js &
|Send output to next commandps aux | grep node
>Redirect output, overwrite fileecho hi > file.txt
>>Redirect output, appendecho hi >> file.txt
<Take input from a filecommand < file.txt
&&Run next command only if previous succeedsmkdir app && cd app
;Run commands one after anotherpwd; ls
*Wildcard — anythingrm *.log
.Current directory./script.sh
..Parent directorycd ..
🧠 Remember the main symbols — think of these as special operators:
&→ background||→ pipe/send|>→ overwrite|>>→ append
&&→ if successful, continue|;→ just continue|*→ anything|.→ here

🗺️ Where This Connects — The Whole Point
None of the above lives in isolation. chmod +x is why a CI script fails with "Permission denied." df -h is why a Docker build fails with "no space left on device." grep and tail -f are exactly what kubectl logs does under the hood, just for a container instead of a raw process. systemctl is what keeps a service alive the same way Kubernetes keeps a pod alive, just one layer down. ssh + scp are literally how GitHub Actions deploys code onto a real server in Example 3. This isn't a separate skill from the rest of this cheat sheet — it's the layer every other tab is quietly standing on.
🎯 Real Interview Q&A — 15 Questions, Straight From the Interviewer's Mouth
These are asked, word for word, in real DevOps interviews. Click any question to reveal the full answer — quick version first, then the deep version, a real story, the follow-up trap they'll spring next, and the mistake that gives away a shallow answer.
L1Walk me through what happens when you type >, >>, and 2> at the end of a command.▼
ANSWER
Quick answer: > overwrites a file with stdout, >> appends to it, and 2> redirects stderr instead of stdout.

Detailed answer: Every command in Linux talks through three streams — stdin (0), stdout (1), and stderr (2). When I run ls > files.txt, the shell sends stdout into the file, replacing whatever was there. >> appends — I use this for cron logs so I don't lose history. 2> catches errors specifically. To silently ignore errors I do command 2> /dev/null. To capture both, I use > file 2>&1 or &>.

💬 Quick story: I once had a script writing to /var/log/myapp.log using > instead of >> — every cron run was overwriting the previous log. Lost three days of debugging data before I caught it. Since then, >> is muscle memory.

⚠️ Follow-up trap: If they ask "what does 2>&1 mean and why is the order important?" — explain it redirects stderr to wherever stdout is currently going. Order matters: > file 2>&1 works, but 2>&1 > file doesn't.

🚫 Common mistake: Saying "> is for output and 2> is for errors." Surface-level. Mention file descriptors (0, 1, 2) — that's what separates memorization from understanding.
L2Disk is at 95% on a production server. Your senior just pinged you on Slack. What do you actually run?▼
ANSWER
Quick answer: df -h to confirm the mount, du -sh /* to find the heavy directory, then find to spot huge or old files for rotation.

Detailed answer: First — df -h to confirm which filesystem is full. Then I cd into the suspect path and run du -sh * | sort -hr | head -10 to see top offenders. Nine times out of ten it's /var/log with unrotated logs. I run find . -type f -size +500M for huge files, or find /var/log -type f -mtime +30 for old ones. For logs, I truncate with > /var/log/bigfile.log — never rm an open log file. Then I set up logrotate so it doesn't repeat.

💬 Quick story: The first time I dealt with this, I rm'd a 40 GB log file and watched df -h still show 95%. The application had the file open. I had to restart the service to release the descriptor.

⚠️ Follow-up trap: "What if du shows everything is small but df says full?" — deleted-but-open files. Use lsof | grep deleted to find processes holding deleted file descriptors, then restart that service.

🚫 Common mistake: Don't jump straight to rm -rf. Senior engineers want to hear that you investigate first, fix the root cause (set up rotation), and never delete anything you can't recover.
L3What's the difference between a hard link and a soft link? And when have you actually used either one?▼
ANSWER
Quick answer: A hard link is a second name for the same inode; a soft link is a separate file pointing to a path. Delete the original — hard link still works, soft link breaks.

Detailed answer: Every file in Linux is an inode (the actual data) plus a name pointing to it. A hard link gives you a second name for the exact same inode — both equal, no "original." Delete one, the data stays until the last name is gone. A soft link is its own tiny file containing a path — if the target moves or gets deleted, it dangles. I use soft links daily — pointing /usr/bin/python to python3.11, symlinking config into /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/. Hard links I've used for backup scripts where I want multiple snapshots without duplicating disk.

💬 Quick story: We had a deploy script that created a symlink current → release-v23. To roll back, we just repointed the symlink to v22 — instant rollback, no file copy. Symlinks make tricks like this possible.

⚠️ Follow-up trap: "Can you hard-link across filesystems?" — No. Hard links share inodes, and inodes are filesystem-specific. Soft links can cross filesystems because they just store a path.

🚫 Common mistake: Don't say "a hard link is a copy." It's not — same data, two names. Saying "copy" loses the interviewer instantly.
L4Some service is using port 8080 and you don't know who. How do you find the process?▼
ANSWER
Quick answer: sudo lsof -i :8080 or sudo ss -tulnp | grep 8080 — both give you the PID and process name.

Detailed answer: On modern systems I prefer ss over netstat — faster, pre-installed. Flags: -t TCP, -u UDP, -l listening, -n numeric, -p process. So sudo ss -tulnp | grep 8080 gives me everything. If ss isn't there, sudo lsof -i :8080 works and shows the user. Once I have the PID, ps -p <pid> -f shows the full command line.

💬 Quick story: I once spent 20 minutes trying to start a Docker container on port 8080 before realizing a leftover python http.server from a previous test was still running in a detached tmux session. lsof -i :8080 solved in 2 seconds what 20 minutes of docker logs couldn't.

⚠️ Follow-up trap: "Can you find it without sudo?" — You can't see other users' processes without sudo. The PID column will be blank. That's a Linux security feature, not a bug.

🚫 Common mistake: Don't say netstat -anp. Deprecated on most modern distros. ss kept up.
L5Tell me the difference between ps, top, and htop — and which one you reach for in production.▼
ANSWER
Quick answer: ps is a snapshot, top is a live view that ships with every Linux box, htop is the prettier interactive version — but not always installed.

Detailed answer: ps gives a one-time snapshot — I use it for scripting because output is parseable: ps -ef | grep nginx. top is what I reach for first on any production box because it's always there. Updates every few seconds, shows CPU, memory, load average. htop I install on dev boxes — colored, tree view, click-to-kill, scrollable. Same data, friendlier UI. In an incident, I start with top, hit M to sort by memory or P by CPU, and find the offender in seconds. Press H for threads.

💬 Quick story: A Java service slowly ate memory in staging. top showed the JVM at 8 GB and climbing. Sorted by memory with M, confirmed a leak, dug into GC logs. Without top, I'd have stared at Grafana for an hour.

⚠️ Follow-up trap: "What does load average actually mean?" — the average number of processes in a runnable or uninterruptible state over 1, 5, 15 minutes. Load 4 on a 4-core box = 100% utilization. Load 8 on the same box = processes queuing.

🚫 Common mistake: Don't say load average is "CPU usage." It includes processes waiting on disk I/O. Mixing them up tells the interviewer you've never debugged a real I/O bottleneck.
L6What does chmod 755 file.sh actually mean? Break the numbers down for me.▼
ANSWER
Quick answer: Owner gets read-write-execute (7), group gets read-execute (5), others get read-execute (5). Standard for executable scripts.

Detailed answer: Three permission groups (owner, group, others) and three permissions (read=4, write=2, execute=1). Add them: 7 = 4+2+1 (full), 5 = 4+1 (read+execute), 4 (read-only). For a script anyone should run, 755 is right. For a private SSH key, 600. For a config with secrets, 640 or 600.

💬 Quick story: I once chmod 777'd a directory because I was tired of fighting permissions on a shared dev box. Two days later, our security scanner flagged it and I had to write up an incident report. 777 is almost always the wrong answer.

⚠️ Follow-up trap: "Difference between chmod and chown?" — chmod changes permissions (what), chown changes ownership (who). Used together: chown to assign the right user, then chmod to set permissions.

🚫 Common mistake: Don't memorize "755 means executable." Understand the math. If they ask about 2755, you should derive it on the spot — the leading 2 introduces setgid, which trips up most candidates.
L7Walk me through scheduling a job to run every 5 minutes. And how would you debug it if it doesn't run?▼
ANSWER
Quick answer: crontab -e, add */5 * * * * /path/to/script.sh, and if it doesn't run I check journalctl -u cron plus the script's output redirection.

Detailed answer: Cron format: minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week. */5 * * * * means every 5th minute. I always redirect both stdout and stderr: */5 * * * * /path/to/script.sh >> /var/log/myscript.log 2>&1 — cron has a stripped-down environment with almost no PATH and silent failures. If it's still not running, check journalctl -u cron. Nine times out of ten it's PATH — the script works in my shell, cron doesn't know where kubectl or python live. Fix: absolute paths, or source /etc/profile at the top.

💬 Quick story: Wrote a backup cron, tested manually, forgot output redirection. Silently failed for two weeks because cron emailed output to root@localhost and there was no mail daemon. Two weeks of zero backups. >> file 2>&1 is now mandatory in every cron line I write.

⚠️ Follow-up trap: "Run every 5 minutes during business hours only?" — */5 9-17 * * 1-5 /path/to/script.sh.

🚫 Common mistake: Don't forget cron's environment is not your shell's. Test with env -i bash -c "/path/to/script.sh" to simulate cron's empty environment before trusting it.
L8kill, kill -9, kill -15 — what's the difference and which should you use first?▼
ANSWER
Quick answer: kill defaults to -15 (SIGTERM, polite), -9 is SIGKILL (forced, no cleanup). Always start with -15; only escalate to -9 if it refuses.

Detailed answer: SIGTERM is "please shut down." The process catches it, finishes current work, closes DB connections, flushes logs, exits cleanly. SIGKILL bypasses the process — the kernel kills it instantly. No cleanup means open files might corrupt, transactions left half-done, child processes orphaned. My rule: -15 first, wait 10–15 seconds, only -9 if genuinely stuck.

💬 Quick story: A teammate kill -9'd a stuck PostgreSQL during an incident. The DB came back up, but one table was inconsistent — four hours of recovery. I treat -9 as last resort, not first move.

⚠️ Follow-up trap: "What if a process ignores SIGTERM?" — Some catch it and refuse to die because they're waiting on something (like a stuck NFS mount). At that point, SIGKILL is the only option because the kernel handles it directly.

🚫 Common mistake: Saying "-9 is the safe option because it always works." It "works" in that it terminates — but at the cost of data integrity. Red flag in any production-minded interview.
L9What is journalctl and how do you use it to debug a service that's failing to start?▼
ANSWER
Quick answer: The systemd log query tool. For a failing service: journalctl -u <service> -n 100 --no-pager for the last 100 lines, or -f to tail live.

Detailed answer: On any modern Linux, systemd manages services and journalctl reads its logs. Flags I use most: -n 200 last 200 lines, -u nginx filter by service, -f follow live, --since "10 min ago", -p err errors only. My flow: systemctl status <service> first — gives recent log lines and the exit code. If I need more, journalctl -u <service> -n 500. I look for the first error, not the last — cascading failures hide the real cause.

💬 Quick story: Jenkins refused to start. systemctl status said "failed." journalctl -u jenkins showed "Java not found in PATH." Root cause: someone had uninstalled Java for a "cleanup." Two minutes saved a full rebuild.

⚠️ Follow-up trap: "How do you keep journal logs from growing forever?" — Edit /etc/systemd/journald.conf: SystemMaxUse=2G or MaxRetentionSec=1month.

🚫 Common mistake: Saying "I'd tail /var/log/syslog." On systemd distros, services log to journal first — syslog may have something or nothing. journalctl is authoritative.
L10grep, awk, sed — explain when you'd reach for each one. Make it real.▼
ANSWER
Quick answer: grep finds lines, awk extracts and processes columns, sed edits text in place. I use them together in pipelines where each does what it's best at.

Detailed answer: grep: searching — "does this line contain X?" Use -i case-insensitive, -v invert, -E extended regex. awk: column-aware, a mini language. Logs and CSVs are home turf. awk '{print $1, $7}' on access.log gives column 1 and 7. awk '$9 == 500' filters where column 9 equals 500. sed: in-place editing. sed -i 's/old/new/g' file.txt replaces every "old" with "new" — I use it for find-and-replace across config files during deploys. A pipeline I run all the time: cat access.log | grep " 500 " | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10 — top 10 IPs hitting my server with 500 errors, in one line.

💬 Quick story: During an incident, the app was returning 500s. I had load balancer logs but no fancy dashboard. That one-liner identified a single IP making 90% of bad requests in seconds. Blocked it, traffic normalized.

⚠️ Follow-up trap: "Could you do all this in awk alone?" — Technically yes: awk '/pattern/ && $9==500 {print $1}'. But mixing tools in a pipeline is more readable than a 200-character awk script. Readability matters at 3 AM.

🚫 Common mistake: Saying awk is "for printing columns." That's 1% of what it does — it has variables, conditionals, loops, regex, a full language. Underselling it tells the interviewer you've used it once.
L11How do you find files modified in the last 24 hours?▼
ANSWER
Quick answer: find /path -type f -mtime -1 — modified less than 1 day ago. Or -mmin -60 for the last 60 minutes.

Detailed answer: find uses three time flags: -mtime modification time in days, -atime access time, -ctime inode-change time. Negative means "less than" — -mtime -1 is "modified less than 24 hours ago." Positive means "more than." Add -type f for files only, -type d for directories. For sub-day precision, use -mmin in minutes. To run a command on each result: -exec ls -lh {} \;.

💬 Quick story: Production was acting weird after a deployment. I ran find /etc -type f -mtime -1 and found two config files someone had hot-patched manually. They never told the team. Diff against Git answered the rest.

⚠️ Follow-up trap: "Difference between mtime, atime, ctime?" — mtime = content changed, atime = file was read, ctime = inode changed (permissions, ownership). ctime is the one most candidates miss.

🚫 Common mistake: Confusing -mtime 1 (exactly 1 day) with -mtime -1 (less than 1 day). The sign matters.
L12What is a zombie process and how do you handle it?▼
ANSWER
Quick answer: A zombie is a child process that's finished but its parent hasn't called wait() to read its exit status. It holds a PID slot until the parent reaps it.

Detailed answer: When a process exits, the kernel keeps minimal info (PID, exit code) until the parent reads it via wait(). If the parent doesn't, the child sits in <defunct> state — a zombie. It uses no CPU or memory, but it holds a PID. If a buggy parent never reaps and keeps spawning, you eventually exhaust the PID table and can't fork new processes. To check: ps aux | grep defunct. You can't kill a zombie directly — it's already dead. You kill the parent, and init (PID 1) adopts and reaps the orphans.

💬 Quick story: A Python app on a customer's server stopped accepting new connections. ps aux showed 30,000 zombies. The parent process was spawning workers but never calling wait(). We killed the parent, init reaped them, and the server breathed again.

⚠️ Follow-up trap: "What's the difference between a zombie and an orphan?" — Orphan: parent died, init adopts. Zombie: child died, parent didn't reap. Different problems.

🚫 Common mistake: Saying "I'd kill -9 the zombie." You can't — it's already dead. Killing the parent is the fix.
L13Explain the Linux boot process in brief.▼
ANSWER
Quick answer: BIOS/UEFI → bootloader (GRUB) → kernel + initramfs → init system (systemd) → target/runlevel → user login.

Detailed answer: Power on: BIOS or UEFI runs hardware checks (POST), finds the bootloader on disk. GRUB loads, shows the boot menu, hands control to the kernel. The kernel decompresses, mounts initramfs (a tiny RAM filesystem with just enough drivers to mount the real root). Once root is mounted, the kernel hands off to PID 1 — usually systemd. Systemd reads its target (like multi-user.target or graphical.target), starts services in dependency order, and finally launches getty for login. The whole thing takes seconds on modern hardware.

💬 Quick story: A box wouldn't boot after a kernel update. Got the GRUB screen, but the kernel kicked into an emergency shell. journalctl from the rescue shell showed initramfs was missing the SCSI driver. Booted the previous kernel, rebuilt initramfs with dracut, problem solved.

⚠️ Follow-up trap: "What's the difference between BIOS and UEFI?" — UEFI is the modern replacement: faster boot, supports drives >2TB, secure boot, GUI-friendly. BIOS is legacy 16-bit firmware.

🚫 Common mistake: Skipping initramfs entirely. It's the bridge between the kernel and the real root filesystem — interviewers love asking why it exists.
L14How do you write an idempotent shell script?▼
ANSWER
Quick answer: Make every operation safe to run multiple times — check before acting. Use if [ ! -f file ]; then create file; fi instead of blind creation.

Detailed answer: Idempotent means: run it 10 times, the result is the same as running it once. For file creation: [ -f /etc/myconfig ] || cp template /etc/myconfig. For directories: mkdir -p instead of mkdir. For users: check id user >/dev/null 2>&1 || useradd user. For packages: most package managers are already idempotent — apt install -y nginx is safe to re-run. For lines in config files: use grep -q "pattern" file || echo "pattern" >> file. The principle: never blindly append, overwrite, or create — always check state first.

💬 Quick story: Wrote a non-idempotent setup script that appended a line to /etc/hosts. Re-ran it three times during testing. Ended up with three duplicate entries breaking DNS resolution. Now every config-modifying script I write starts with a state check.

⚠️ Follow-up trap: "How is this different from Ansible?" — Ansible's modules are idempotent by design. Same logic, just wrapped in a higher-level abstraction. Ansible is essentially industrial-strength idempotent shell.

🚫 Common mistake: Saying "I use set -e for idempotency." set -e makes scripts exit on error — that's safety, not idempotency. Different concepts.
L15What's the difference between &, &&, |, and ||?▼
ANSWER
Quick answer: & runs in background, && runs the next command only if the previous succeeded, | pipes output between commands, || runs the next command only if the previous failed.

Detailed answer: &: long-script.sh & backgrounds it, frees the shell. &&: make && make install — install only runs if make succeeded. |: cat file | grep error — stdout of the left becomes stdin of the right. ||: cmd || echo "failed" — fallback if cmd fails. You can chain: backup.sh && echo "ok" || echo "failed". Common pattern: command || exit 1 in scripts to bail early on failure.

💬 Quick story: A teammate's deploy script had build & deploy instead of build && deploy. Build was running in the background while deploy started immediately on stale artifacts. Looked random in CI. One character, one production rollback.

⚠️ Follow-up trap: "What does $? hold?" — The exit code of the last command. 0 = success, anything else = failure. && and || both check this.

🚫 Common mistake: Confusing | and ||. A single pipe is data flow, a double pipe is a logical OR. Completely different worlds.
🧱
This is the actual foundation — everything else is built on top of it
Files & permissions → processes & services → networking → text tools → remote access. | Docker, Kubernetes, and CI/CD don't replace any of this — they're automation built on top of exactly these commands.
🎭 Real Scenarios — Learn Commands by Solving the Problem First
Every card below starts with a real situation, not a command name. Read it, think about what you'd actually type, then click ▶ Run to reveal the command and its real output.
This is the opposite direction from the simulator above. Up there, you already know the command's name and want to see what it does. Down here, you only know the problem — the way it actually happens on the job — and have to work out which command solves it. That's the real skill interviews (and real incidents) actually test.
1
The situation: You SSH into a server you've never touched before. Before you install anything or change a single setting, you want to know exactly what you're working with.
What would you run?
uname -a
Linux web01 5.15.0-91-generic #101-Ubuntu SMP x86_64 GNU/Linux
Why this command: One line tells you the OS, kernel version, and CPU architecture — all three matter before you install anything architecture-specific or run a script written for a different distro.
2
The situation: A teammate messages you: "the server feels slow." That's the entire report — no error, no logs, nothing else. Where do you actually start?
What would you run?
top
PID USER %CPU %MEM COMMAND 4821 devops 94.2 12.0 node 112 root 1.1 0.4 systemd 980 root 0.8 1.2 dockerd ↳ node is at 94% CPU — that's your suspect
Why this command: A live, constantly-refreshing view of every process's CPU and memory — the fastest way to turn a vague "it's slow" into a specific PID to investigate.
3
The situation: df -h shows the disk is at 97% full. You need to know exactly what's eating all that space before you can do anything about it.
What would you run?
du -sh /var/log/* | sort -rh | head -5
2.1G /var/log/app.log 340M /var/log/nginx 88M /var/log/apt ↳ app.log is the culprit — probably needs log rotation
Why this command: df -h only tells you the disk is full — du -sh is how you find out WHAT is filling it. Sorted largest-first, the answer is usually the very first line.
4
The situation: You just deployed your app on port 3000, but nobody can reach it. Before blaming the network or a firewall, you need to confirm the app is even listening at all.
What would you run?
ss -tulpn | grep 3000
(no output — nothing is listening on port 3000)
Why this command: Empty output here is itself the answer — the app never actually started, or it's listening on a different port than you think. Confirm this BEFORE spending an hour debugging firewalls for a problem that isn't there.
5
The situation: Your CI pipeline fails with Permission denied trying to run ./deploy.sh — the exact same script that works fine when you run it locally.
What would you run?
chmod +x deploy.sh git add deploy.sh git commit -m "fix: make deploy.sh executable"
before: -rw-r--r-- deploy.sh after: -rwxr-xr-x deploy.sh
Why this command: Git tracks the execute bit. If the file was ever committed without it, every fresh checkout — including your CI runner — loses execute permission, even though your own local copy still has it set.
6
The situation: You're migrating to a new API domain. Before you change anything, you need to find every single config file that still mentions the old one.
What would you run?
grep -rl "old-api.example.com" /etc/
/etc/nginx/sites-enabled/app.conf /etc/myapp/config.yml 2 files found
Why this command: -r searches every subfolder, -l prints just the filenames (not every matching line) — exactly the checklist you need before a domain migration, in one command.
7
The situation: A stuck process refuses to shut down. You already tried asking it nicely — it ignored you.
What would you run?
first, the polite request (already tried, ignored): kill 4821 it's still running 15 seconds later — now force it: kill -9 4821
process 4821 terminated
Why this order matters: plain kill sends SIGTERM — a clean shutdown request the process can catch and finish up gracefully. -9 is SIGKILL, enforced instantly by the kernel with zero cleanup. Always try the polite version first.
8
The situation: You just edited nginx's config file to fix a routing bug. You reload the site — nothing changed. The bug is still there.
What would you run?
sudo systemctl restart nginx
nginx.service restarted
Why this command: Editing a config file only changes the file on disk — the running process keeps using whatever it loaded into memory at startup. Nothing takes effect until the service actually restarts and re-reads it.
9
The situation: systemctl status myapp just shows "failed" — no explanation. You need the actual error, not just the word "failed."
What would you run?
journalctl -u myapp -n 50 --no-pager
10:14:02 myapp Started myapp.service 10:14:03 myapp Error: connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432 10:14:03 myapp Process exited with code 1
Why this command: "failed" is systemd's one-word summary — journalctl -u shows the actual log lines that service printed right before it died. The real cause is almost always in the last few lines before the exit.
10
The situation: Your backup script runs perfectly every time you test it by hand. Every night at 2am via cron, it silently does nothing.
What would you run?
crontab -l # then simulate cron's actual (near-empty) environment: env -i bash -c "/home/deploy/backup.sh"
*/5 2 * * * /home/deploy/backup.sh ... backup.sh: line 4: kubectl: command not found
Why this command: Cron runs with almost no $PATH and none of your shell's usual setup — a script that "just works" in your terminal can silently fail under cron because it can't find a tool by name. Testing with env -i reproduces that stripped-down environment on demand.

If you can already run commands in the 🐧 Linux for DevOps tab, you already know 90% of what a shell script needs — a script is just those exact same commands, saved in a file, run together. This tab teaches everything on top of that: variables, decisions, loops, functions — building from an absolute "hello world" up to three real scripts a DevOps engineer would actually use on the job. Every lesson below now teaches the individual pieces first, then shows how they combine — and there's a real methodology below for how to approach writing a script from a blank file.
🧠 How to Actually Think About Writing a Script
This is the part tutorials usually skip — not "here's the syntax," but "here's the actual thought process," start to finish.
1
Do it by hand firstbefore writing anything
Before you write a single line of a script, run the actual commands yourself, one at a time, in your real terminal, until they do what you want. A script isn't where you invent the steps — it's where you write down steps you already proved work.
2
Find what changes each time→ variables & arguments
Look at the commands you just ran by hand. Which words would be different the next time you run this — a filename, a server name, an environment? Those become variables, or better, arguments ($1, $2) so the script stays reusable instead of hardcoded.
3
Find what could go wrong→ conditionals & exit codes
For every command, ask: "what does it look like when this fails?" A missing file, a failed network call, an empty variable. Each answer becomes a check — an if, a test like [ -f file ], or an exit 1 that stops things before they get worse.
4
Find what repeats→ loops & functions
Doing the same thing to multiple items — servers, files, environments? That's a for loop. Doing the same few steps in more than one place in the script? Pull them into a function instead of copy-pasting.
5
Test each piece alonebefore gluing it together
Run the variable line by itself. Run the loop by itself with an echo instead of the real command inside it. A script that's assembled from pieces you already know work is infinitely easier to debug than one written all at once and tested for the first time as a whole.
6
Add safety last→ set -euo pipefail
Once the logic actually works, put set -euo pipefail on line 2. Not before — while you're still figuring out the logic, you want to see things fail loudly and understand why. Once it's correct, this line makes sure it stays correct by refusing to continue after anything unexpected.
🧠
This is genuinely how every lesson below was built
What would I type by hand → what changes → what could fail → what repeats → test the pieces → add safety. | Each lesson below layers on exactly one new idea from this list — by Lesson 15 you're combining all six at once, without noticing.

🎭 Real Scenarios — Learn Shell Scripting by Solving the Problem First
Read the situation, think about what you'd actually write, then click ▶ Run to reveal the command and its real output.
1
The situation: You need a backup script to run automatically every night at 2 AM, with no one around to trigger it manually.
What would you run?
crontab -e
# then add:
0 2 * * * /scripts/backup.sh
(saved — cron now runs backup.sh at 2:00 AM every day)
Why this command: Cron is the standard Linux scheduler for exactly this — "run this command at this time, every day, forever," with zero human involvement needed.
2
The situation: A deploy script creates a lockfile, but if it crashes partway through, the lockfile is left behind and blocks every future run.
What would you run?
trap 'rm -f /tmp/deploy.lock' EXIT
(lockfile is removed no matter how the script ends — success, failure, or interruption)
Why this command: An EXIT trap runs on every possible way the script can end, guaranteeing cleanup even when the script crashes or is killed midway through.
3
The situation: Your deploy script is always called like "./deploy.sh -e production -v" and needs to actually parse those real flags.
What would you run?
while getopts "e:v" opt; do
case $opt in
e) env="$OPTARG";;
v) verbose=true;;
esac
done
env=production, verbose=true
Why this command: getopts is built specifically for parsing real -flag style arguments, instead of hoping $1 and $2 always show up in the exact right order.
4
The situation: A deploy script needs to wait until a freshly started app is actually responding before it declares the deploy successful.
What would you run?
until curl -sf http://localhost:3000/health; do
sleep 2
done
Waiting...
Waiting...
(loop exits the moment curl succeeds)
Why this command: "until" keeps polling until the health check actually succeeds — far more reliable than a fixed sleep that guesses how long startup will take.
5
The situation: A script kicks off three independent tasks that could run at the same time, and needs to wait for all three before continuing.
What would you run?
./task1.sh &
./task2.sh &
./task3.sh &
wait
echo "All three finished"
All three finished
Why this command: Backgrounding all three with "&" lets them run in parallel, and "wait" with no argument pauses until every backgrounded job has completed.
6
The situation: You need to watch a long deploy script's output live in the terminal, but also keep a saved copy of the full log afterward.
What would you run?
./deploy.sh | tee deploy.log
Deploying v2.0...
Deploy finished
# shown live AND saved to deploy.log
Why this command: tee splits the output two ways at once — to your screen for live viewing and to a file for a permanent record — instead of forcing a choice between the two.
7
The situation: A script isn't behaving as expected, and you need to see exactly what it's actually executing, line by line.
What would you run?
set -x
# rest of the script runs as normal below this line
+ count=3
+ echo 3
Why this command: Debug tracing prints every command as it actually runs, with variables already expanded — far faster than sprinkling echo statements everywhere to guess what's happening.
8
The situation: A Docker entrypoint script starts the real app as its last step, and needs signals like SIGTERM to reach that app directly.
What would you run?
exec node server.js
(node server.js replaces the script's own process — signals now reach it directly)
Why this command: Without exec, the app runs as a child process and a "docker stop" signal can get stuck waiting on the wrapper script instead of reaching the app that needs to actually handle it.

📦 The Daily Git Workflow
git statusinspect
Shows what changed, what's staged, what's untracked. Run this constantly — it's your orientation command.
git status -s = short format: M=modified, A=added (staged), ??=untracked.
$ git status -s M src/auth.js ?? notes.txt
git addstage
Staging = choosing what goes into the next commit snapshot.
git add . — stage everything (. = all files in current dir)
git add src/auth.js — stage one specific file
git add -p — stage chunks interactively, not whole files. Great for clean commits.
$ git add -p  # review each chunk
git commitsnapshot
Creates the snapshot. Each commit gets a unique hash (e.g. a3f9d2c). The message should describe WHAT changed and WHY.
Convention: feat:, fix:, chore:, docs: prefix (Conventional Commits).
$ git commit -m "feat: add JWT auth"
git pushupload
Upload your local commits to the remote (GitHub). Always specify branch.
git push origin feature/auth — push to your feature branch, not main directly.
$ git push origin feature/auth
git loghistory
See the full commit history with hashes, authors, dates, messages.
git log --oneline = compact view, one line per commit. Use the hash to reference specific commits.
$ git log --oneline a3f9d2c feat: add JWT auth b1e8c4a fix: null check on login
git checkout <hash>time travel
Travel back to any past commit using its hash. You enter "detached HEAD" state — you can look around but shouldn't commit here. Use git checkout main to return.
$ git checkout a3f9d2c  # go back $ git checkout main    # come back
🔄 fetch vs pull vs merge vs rebase
git fetch
Downloads changes from remote and updates remote-tracking branches (origin/main etc.) but does NOT touch your working files or current branch.

✅ Safe — inspect before integrating.
git pull
Fetch + merge (or fetch + rebase if configured). Immediately integrates remote changes into your current branch.

⚡ Faster but less control than doing fetch + rebase manually.
git merge
Combines one branch into another. Creates a merge commit that preserves full history. Non-destructive.

Use when combining finished features into main.
git rebase
Replays your commits on top of another branch. Creates a linear history — cleaner but rewrites commits.

⚠️ Never rebase shared/public branches.
🛠️ Fixing & Undoing Things
git stashshelve work
Shelves your uncommitted work-in-progress to a temporary stack, giving you a clean working directory without committing. Useful when you need to urgently switch branches.
git stash pop brings it back.
$ git stash    # save WIP $ git stash pop  # restore it
git reset --soft HEAD~1undo commit
Undoes the last commit but keeps your changes staged. --soft = undo commit only. --mixed = undo commit + unstage. --hard = undo commit + delete changes (dangerous ⚠️).
$ git reset --soft HEAD~1  # safe undo
git revert <hash>safe undo
Creates a new commit that reverses the changes of a previous commit. Safe for shared branches — it doesn't rewrite history, just adds an "undo" commit on top.
$ git revert a3f9d2c  # adds undo commit
git restore <file>discard changes
Discards unstaged changes in a file, restoring it to the last committed state. Cannot be undone — the changes are gone. Different from reset which operates on commits.
$ git restore src/auth.js  ⚠️
git remoteremotes
Manage remote connections. git remote -v shows all remotes and their URLs. origin is the default name for the remote you cloned from (usually GitHub).
$ git remote -v origin https://github.com/you/repo.git
⚔️ Merge Conflicts
A conflict happens when two people edited the same part of the same file. Git can't auto-decide whose version wins.

Step-by-step resolution:
1. git log — understand which commits introduced the conflict
2. Open the conflicting file — Git marks it:
<<<<<<< HEAD
your changes here
=======
their changes here
>>>>>>> feature/their-branch
3. Manually edit to the correct final state, remove all markers
4. git add conflicting-file.js
5. git merge --continue or git rebase --continue

💬 Communicate with the person whose change conflicts with yours — conflicts often reveal an integration problem worth discussing.
🔀 Pull Requests (PRs)
A Pull Request (PR) is a request to merge a feature branch into main. It's not a Git command — it's a GitHub/GitLab feature.

A PR gives teammates a chance to review your code before it merges. They can leave comments, request changes, or approve. CI/CD pipelines also run automatically on the PR — if tests fail, the PR can't merge.

Flow: feature branch → push → open PR → code review → CI passes → merge into main → pipeline deploys
🌿
The Git DevOps Workflow
git status → git add . → git commit -m "feat: ..." → git push origin feature/x → open PR → CI runs → review → merge → deploy
🔍 Advanced Git
git reflogHEAD history
Records every single movement of HEAD — commits, merges, rebases, resets, branch switches. Unlike git log which only shows commit history, reflog is your safety net. Accidentally deleted a branch or did a bad reset? Find the lost hash here and recover.
$ git reflog a3f9d2c HEAD@{0}: commit: feat: auth b1e8c4a HEAD@{1}: reset: moving to HEAD~1 c9d7f3a HEAD@{2}: checkout: moved to main
clone vs forkcopy a repo
git clone — creates a local copy on your machine. You're working with the original repo's remote (origin). Used for repos you have direct write access to.

Fork (GitHub) — creates your own personal copy of a repo under your GitHub account. Freely commit to your fork. To contribute back, open a PR from your fork to the original. Used for open-source contributions.
clone = local copy, same origin fork = your GitHub copy → PR back
🪝 Git Hooks
Executable scripts in .git/hooks/ that run automatically at specific Git events. Used to enforce policies, run checks, and automate tasks. Share them via Husky (npm) to ensure the whole team uses the same hooks.
CLIENT-SIDElocal machine
pre-commit — runs before commit is created. Run linters, formatters, quick tests. Exit non-zero = commit rejected.

commit-msg — validates commit message format. Enforce Conventional Commits (feat:, fix:, chore:).

pre-push — runs before git push. Run full test suite. Stops push if tests fail — last local defence.
#!/bin/sh npm run lint && npm test
SERVER-SIDEremote / GitHub
pre-receive — runs on the server before accepting a push. Reject pushes that violate policy (e.g. direct push to main).

post-receive — runs after push is accepted. Trigger CI/CD pipelines, send Slack notifications, update dashboards.

In GitHub/GitLab these are implemented as webhooks — HTTP callbacks that fire on events.
🍒 More Essential Git Commands
git cherry-pickcopy a commit
Apply a specific commit from another branch to your current branch — without merging the whole branch. Useful for hotfixing: apply a bug fix commit to both main and release/1.2.
$ git cherry-pick a3f9d2c  # apply specific commit
git rebase -i HEAD~3squash commits
Interactive rebase — rewrite the last 3 commits. Squash multiple commits into one clean commit before opening a PR. Keeps main branch history clean. Never interactive-rebase shared branches.
$ git rebase -i HEAD~3  # opens editor
git tagreleases
Mark a specific commit as a release version. Annotated tags are best practice. CI/CD pipelines often trigger differently on tag pushes (build + deploy release artifacts).
$ git tag -a v2.0 -m "Release v2.0" $ git push origin v2.0
git commit --amendfix last commit
Fix the last commit — change its message or add forgotten files. Only safe if you haven't pushed yet. After pushing, use git revert instead to avoid rewriting shared history.
$ git commit --amend -m "fixed: better message"
git clean -fdremove untracked
Remove all untracked files and directories from the working tree. -f = force, -d = include directories. Use -n first to dry-run (see what would be deleted without deleting).
$ git clean -n   # dry run first $ git clean -fd  # actually delete
.gitignoreexclude files
File patterns that Git should never track. Always include: node_modules/, .env, *.log, .terraform/, dist/. Committed to the repo so everyone on the team ignores the same files.
# .gitignore node_modules/ .env *.log .terraform/
⚠️ Dangerous Git Situations — What To Do
SITUATIONHOW TO RECOVER
Accidentally committed a secretRotate the secret immediately — assume it's compromised. Then use git filter-branch or BFG Repo Cleaner to remove it from history. Force-push. Notify security team.
Force-pushed and lost commitsgit reflog — find the lost commit hash. git checkout -b recovery <hash> to recover.
git reset --hard (wrong branch)git reflog — find HEAD before reset. git reset --hard <that-hash> to restore.
Monorepo vs PolyrepoMonorepo — all services in one repo. Easier cross-service changes, atomic commits. Used by Google, Meta. Polyrepo — each service in its own repo. More independent but harder to coordinate. Most startups use polyrepo initially.
🍒 git cherry-pick — Steal a Single Commit
Apply a specific commit from one branch onto another, without merging the entire branch. Useful when a hotfix was applied to main and you need that exact fix on a release branch — without pulling in any other changes.
git cherry-pick a3f9d2c          # apply one commit onto current branch
git cherry-pick a3f9d2c..b1e8c4a   # apply a range of commits
git cherry-pick --no-commit a3f9d2c # apply changes but don't commit yet
🏷️ Git Tags — Semantic Versioning
Tags mark specific commits as important — typically release versions. Unlike branches, tags don't move. Semantic Versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH — e.g. v2.1.3. MAJOR = breaking change, MINOR = new feature backward-compatible, PATCH = bug fix. Docker images are tagged the same way.
git tag v2.1.0                     # lightweight tag
git tag -a v2.1.0 -m "Release 2.1.0" # annotated tag (recommended)
git push origin v2.1.0                # push tag to remote
git push origin --tags                # push all tags
git tag                              # list all tags
📝 .gitignore — What to Never Commit
# Dependencies
node_modules/
vendor/

# Build outputs
dist/
*.jar *.class

# SECRETS — NEVER COMMIT THESE
.env
*.pem *.key
terraform.tfstate               # terraform state has secrets
.terraform/

# OS / IDE junk
.DS_Store   .idea/   *.swp
🔀 Squash Commits — Clean History Before Merge
Combine multiple messy "WIP", "fix typo", "oops" commits into a single meaningful commit before merging a PR. Keeps the main branch history clean and readable.

git rebase -i HEAD~5 — interactively rebase last 5 commits. Change pick to squash (or s) on all but the first. Git will merge them into one commit and let you write a clean message.

🎭 Guided Scenarios — Watch a Real Workflow Play Out
Click ▶ Run This Scenario and watch every step execute against the graph above, one at a time.
1
The situation: Start a new feature without touching main until it's ready — the most common branching pattern there is.
git checkout -b feature-login
git add . && git commit -m "Add login form"
git checkout main
git merge feature-login
What to watch for: main never moved while feature-login was being built, so the merge is a fast-forward — main's pointer just slides forward to feature-login's tip, no new merge commit needed.
2
The situation: Two people work in parallel — one on main, one on a feature branch — and both make progress before merging.
git checkout main
git add . && git commit -m "Update README"
git checkout -b feature-payments
git add . && git commit -m "Add payment gateway"
git checkout main
git add . && git commit -m "Fix typo in README"
git merge feature-payments
What to watch for: this time main moved too, so a fast-forward isn't possible — git creates a real merge commit with two parent arrows, one to each line's tip.
3
The situation: A commit already made it into history and turned out to be broken — and it may have already been shared with others.
git add . && git commit -m "Accidentally break the build"
git revert HEAD
What to watch for: revert adds a brand-new commit that undoes the change — the broken commit is still right there in history, just canceled out. Nothing is rewritten, which is why revert is safe on shared branches.
4
The situation: A feature branch is falling behind main, and you want its history to look like it was built on top of main's latest work.
git checkout -b feature-cleanup
git checkout main
git add . && git commit -m "Update dependencies"
git checkout feature-cleanup
git add . && git commit -m "Remove dead code"
git rebase main
What to watch for: feature-cleanup's old commit fades out (unreachable) and a brand-new commit with a new ID appears sitting right on top of main — rebase doesn't move commits, it replays them as new ones.
5
The situation: A one-line fix landed on a hotfix branch, and you need that exact fix on main too — without merging the whole branch.
git checkout main
git checkout -b hotfix-typo
git add . && git commit -m "Fix typo in footer"
git checkout main
git cherry-pick hotfix-typo
What to watch for: a new commit with the same message appears on main's line, separate from hotfix-typo's own copy — cherry-pick duplicates one specific commit instead of merging everything on that branch.
6
The situation: You're mid-change with nothing committed yet, and suddenly need to switch branches for something urgent.
git add .
git stash
git checkout -b urgent-fix
git add . && git commit -m "Urgent fix"
git checkout main
git stash pop
What to watch for: stash shelves your in-progress work with no commit and no graph change at all — it's not part of history, just a saved-aside pile you can restore later with stash pop.
7
The situation: A build is finally stable enough to mark as an official release that should never move.
git add . && git commit -m "Release-ready build"
git tag v1.0.0
What to watch for: the tag lands on that exact commit and stays put forever — unlike a branch label, which keeps sliding forward with every new commit, a tag is a fixed, permanent marker.
8
The situation: Local commits exist only on your machine so far, and it's time for the team to actually see them.
git remote add origin https://github.com/you/project.git
git add . && git commit -m "Ready to share"
git push origin main
What to watch for: a dashed, greyed-out origin/main tag appears once you push — that's your remote-tracking branch, showing exactly what the remote has last seen, separate from your own local main.

📋 All Dockerfile Instructions
INSTRUCTION WHAT IT DOES
FROMFirst line. Sets the base image. FROM node:18-alpine, FROM python:3.11
WORKDIRSet working directory inside image. Subsequent commands run from here.
COPYCopy files from host into image. COPY . /app. Most common instruction.
ADDLike COPY but also supports URLs and auto-extracts tar files. Use COPY unless you need extras.
RUNExecute commands at build time. RUN npm install. Creates a cached layer.
CMDDefault command when container starts. Can be overridden at docker run.
ENTRYPOINTMain executable. Unlike CMD, can't be fully overridden — only arguments change.
ENVSet environment variable available at runtime. ENV NODE_ENV=production
ARGBuild-time variable only. Pass via docker build --build-arg KEY=val. Not in final image.
EXPOSEDocument which port the app listens on. Doesn't actually publish it — -p flag does that.
VOLUMECreate a mount point for persistent storage. Data in volumes survives container restarts.
USERSet user to run as. Security best practice — never run as root in production.
LABELAdd metadata key-value pairs to the image. Good for versioning and documentation.
HEALTHCHECKHealth probe command. Docker marks container unhealthy if it fails. Kubernetes uses this.
🔍 Example Dockerfile — Explained Line by Line
FROM node:14
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["npm", "start"]
Base image: Node.js v14
Working dir: /app inside container
Copy deps first (cache optimization!)
Install deps (cached if package.json unchanged)
Copy app code (changes most often = last)
Document port 3000 (doesn't publish)
Start command when container runs
⚡ Layers & Caching — The Performance Secret
Each Dockerfile instruction creates a layer. Unchanged layers are cached — Docker skips rebuilding them.

The golden rule: Put rarely-changing things first (base image, deps install), frequently-changing things last (app code). If you change your code but not package.json, only the last COPY and CMD layers rebuild. Saves huge time.
🗄️ Docker Concepts
Volumepersistent storage
Containers are ephemeral — when they stop, their filesystem is gone. A Volume is persistent storage mounted into a container. Data in volumes survives restarts, crashes, and container recreation. Essential for databases.
$ docker run -v mydata:/app/data myapp
Networkcontainer comms
Docker networks allow containers to talk to each other or the external world. Containers on the same network can reach each other by container name. By default, containers are isolated — you must connect them.
$ docker network create mynet $ docker run --network mynet myapp
docker-composemulti-container
Orchestrates multiple containers together (app + db + cache) via a single YAML file. One command spins up the entire local dev stack. Great alternative to Kubernetes for local development.
$ docker-compose up -d   # start all $ docker-compose down   # stop all
Architectureclient/host/registry
Docker Client — the UI you interact with (docker build, docker run).
Docker Host (Daemon) — background process that manages containers on the host system.
Docker Registry — centralized store for Docker images (Docker Hub, AWS ECR, GCR).
🎯 Key Docker Commands
docker buildcreate image
$ docker build -t myapp:v1 . $ docker build --no-cache -t myapp .
docker runstart container
$ docker run -d -p 3000:3000 myapp -d = detached, -p = port mapping
docker ps / logsinspect
$ docker ps           # running containers $ docker logs <id>    # container output $ docker exec -it <id> sh  # shell inside
docker push/pullregistry
$ docker push registry/myapp:v1 $ docker pull nginx:latest
🐳
Why Docker? The Core Problem it Solves
Without Docker: "works on my machine" — env differences between dev/staging/prod cause bugs.
With Docker: same image, every environment. Build once, run anywhere. Isolation, portability, reproducibility.
🌐 Docker Networking
TYPEWHAT IT DOES
bridgeDefault network. Containers on the same bridge network can talk to each other by container name. Isolated from host network.
hostContainer shares the host's network stack directly. No isolation. Container's port 3000 IS host's port 3000. Fastest, least secure.
overlaySpans multiple Docker hosts (used in Swarm/K8s). Allows containers on different machines to communicate as if on the same network.
🔥 Multi-Stage Builds — Reduce Image Size
Build with all dev tools, then copy only the final artifact into a tiny production image. Result: images go from ~1GB → ~50MB.
# Stage 1: Build (heavy, has compilers/tools)
FROM node:18 AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm install && npm run build

# Stage 2: Production (tiny, only the artifact)
FROM node:18-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist
CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]
📋 COPY vs ADD
COPY
Copies files/directories from host to image. Simple and explicit.
Use COPY by default.
ADD
COPY + also supports URLs and auto-extracts .tar files. Less predictable.
Only use ADD when you need its extras.
🗂️ docker-compose — Full Stack Example
# docker-compose.yml — app + postgres + redis
services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports: ["3000:3000"]
    depends_on: [db, cache]
  db:
    image: postgres:15
    volumes: ["pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data"]
  cache:
    image: redis:alpine
volumes:
  pgdata: # named volume — data persists
⌨️ Essential Docker Commands
docker build -t myapp:v1 .            # Build image
docker run -d -p 3000:3000 myapp      # Run detached, port mapped
docker ps                           # Running containers
docker logs <id> -f                 # Follow container logs
docker exec -it <id> sh              # Shell inside container
docker stop <id>                    # Graceful stop
docker images                       # List local images
docker rmi myapp:v1                  # Remove image
docker push registry/myapp:v1         # Push to registry
docker pull nginx:latest              # Pull from registry
🔒 Docker Security Best Practices
Never run as rootUSER instruction
By default containers run as root — a container escape could give root access to the host. Always add USER appuser at the end of your Dockerfile.

RUN addgroup -S app && adduser -S app -G app
USER app
Never use :latestpin versions
In production, always pin exact image versions. node:18-alpine not node:latest. Latest can change unexpectedly and break your build. Pin both base images and dependencies.
.dockerignoreexclude files
Like .gitignore but for Docker build context. Exclude node_modules, .git, test files, docs. Prevents accidentally copying secrets into the image and speeds up build.
Scan imagesvulnerabilities
docker scout cves myapp:v1 or trivy image myapp:v1 — scan for known CVEs in your image layers. Run in CI to catch vulnerable base images before pushing to production.
⚙️ Container Resource Limits
# Limit container resources to prevent one container starving others
docker run -d \
  --memory="512m" \                 # max 512MB RAM
  --memory-reservation="256m" \   # soft limit
  --cpus="0.5" \                   # max 0.5 CPU cores
  --restart=unless-stopped \      # auto-restart on crash
  myapp:v1
🏥 HEALTHCHECK in Dockerfile
# Docker can monitor container health natively
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=10s --retries=3 \
  CMD curl -f http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1

# docker ps now shows (healthy) or (unhealthy)
# Kubernetes uses its own livenessProbe instead
🧹 Docker Cleanup Commands
docker system prune -a             # remove ALL unused images, containers, networks
docker image prune                 # remove dangling images only
docker container prune             # remove stopped containers
docker volume prune                # remove unused volumes
docker inspect <container-id>      # full JSON details about container
🛡️ Docker Security Best Practices
Never run as rootcritical
Add USER node (or another non-root user) at the end of your Dockerfile. If an attacker escapes the container, they only have that user's permissions — not root. Always the last instruction before CMD/ENTRYPOINT.
RUN addgroup -S app && adduser -S app -G app USER app
.dockerignoresize + security
Like .gitignore but for Docker. Prevents sensitive files from being copied into the image. Also reduces image size significantly.
.git node_modules .env *.pem tests/ docs/
Scan imagesvulnerability
Scan images for known CVEs before pushing to registry. Integrate into CI pipeline — fail the build if critical vulnerabilities found.
$ docker scout cves myapp:v1 $ trivy image myapp:v1 $ snyk container test myapp:v1
Pin base image versionsreproducible
Never use FROM node:latest — it changes every time and breaks reproducibility. Pin to a specific version: FROM node:18.19.0-alpine3.19. Your build should produce the exact same image 6 months later.
📊 Container Resource Limits
Without limits, one runaway container can consume all CPU/RAM on the host and take down every other container. Always set limits in production.
# docker run resource limits:
docker run --memory="512m" --cpus="0.5" myapp
# 512MB RAM max, 50% of 1 CPU max

# Check live resource usage:
docker stats                          # live CPU/RAM for all containers
docker stats <container-id>           # specific container only
❤️ HEALTHCHECK Instruction
# In Dockerfile — Docker marks container healthy/unhealthy
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --retries=3 \
  CMD curl -f http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1

# Check health status:
docker ps                          # shows (healthy) / (unhealthy) status
docker inspect --format='{{.State.Health.Status}}' <id>

🎭 Real Scenarios — Learn Docker by Solving the Problem First
Read the situation, think about what you'd actually run, then click ▶ Run to reveal the command and its real output.
1
The situation: A container exits immediately after "docker run," with nothing obviously wrong printed to your terminal.
What would you run?
docker logs web
Error: Cannot find module 'express'
at Function.Module._resolveFilename
Why this command: The container's stdout/stderr from before it exited is captured here — the terminal itself shows nothing extra because the container already stopped by the time you'd see it.
2
The situation: Your app container can't reach a database container by hostname, even though "docker ps" shows both running fine.
What would you run?
docker network inspect app-net
"Containers": {
"db-container-id": { "Name": "db" }
// "web" is missing from this list
}
Why this command: The app container was never attached to the same custom network as the database — the default bridge network doesn't support name-based resolution, so "web" simply isn't in this network's container list.
3
The situation: You fixed a bug and rebuilt the image, but the running container still behaves like the old, broken version.
What would you run?
docker ps
CONTAINER ID IMAGE STATUS
a3f9d2c1b8e4 myapp:v1 Up 2 hours
Why this command: Rebuilding an image never touches an already-running container — it's still running the old image entirely. The fix is "docker stop web && docker rm web" followed by a fresh "docker run" from the new tag.
4
The situation: A CI runner's disk is nearly full after months of repeated image builds piling up unused layers.
What would you run?
docker system prune -a
Total reclaimed space: 4.2GB
Why this command: Every build leaves behind untagged intermediate layers and old images that never clean themselves up — this sweeps out everything not currently in use by a container in one shot.
5
The situation: You need to grab one config file out of a running container, without opening a full interactive shell session.
What would you run?
docker cp web:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf ./nginx.conf
(file copied to ./nginx.conf)
Why this command: cp moves a single file straight out of the container's filesystem to the host — faster than exec-ing in, catting the file, and manually copying the output.
6
The situation: "docker ps" shows a container marked (unhealthy), and you need to know exactly why before restarting it.
What would you run?
docker inspect --format='{{json .State.Health}}' web
{"Status":"unhealthy","FailingStreak":3,"Log":[{"Output":"curl: (7) Failed to connect"}]}
Why this command: The Health object logs the actual output of each failed probe — here, the healthcheck's own curl command couldn't connect, telling you exactly what's failing and not just that something is.
7
The situation: You're about to launch a production container and want it to come back up automatically if it ever crashes.
What would you run?
docker run -d --restart unless-stopped --name web nginx
a3f9d2c1b8e4
# container now auto-restarts on crash or host reboot
Why this command: Without a restart policy, a crash or host reboot leaves the app down until someone notices and manually restarts it — this is a near-default setting for anything in production.
8
The situation: You need to spin up an app, a database, and a cache together for local development, without three separate "docker run" commands.
What would you run?
docker compose up -d
[+] Running 3/3
✔ Container myapp-db-1 Started
✔ Container myapp-redis-1 Started
✔ Container myapp-web-1 Started
Why this command: compose reads docker-compose.yml and starts every defined service in the correct dependency order — one command instead of three separate ones, and the services can already reach each other by name.

K8s = Workforce Manager
Manages container workforce

Desired State
