🏛️ Core Architecture
🧠 Control Plane (Master Node)
Controls everything in the cluster:

API Server — entry point for all commands. Every kubectl command hits this.
Scheduler — decides which worker node a new pod should run on.
Controller Manager — watches cluster state, makes sure reality matches desired state.
etcd — the cluster's database. Stores all state. If etcd dies, cluster is blind.
⚙️ Worker Nodes
Runs actual applications:

Kubelet — agent on every worker node. Talks to the control plane, ensures pods are running.
Container Runtime — Docker (or containerd). Actually runs the containers.
Pods — the actual workloads run here. One or more containers per pod.
📦 The 8 Objects You Must Know
OBJECTWHAT IT DOES
PodSmallest deployable unit. Wraps one or more containers sharing network and storage. Usually 1 container per pod. Pods are ephemeral — they die and get new IPs.
DeploymentManages desired state: "I want 3 replicas of this pod." K8s creates/kills pods to match. Handles rolling updates. Use for stateless apps (APIs, web servers).
StatefulSetLike Deployment but for stateful apps. Pods get stable names (pod-0, pod-1). Persistent volume per pod. Use for databases, Kafka, Zookeeper.
ServiceStable network endpoint in front of pods. Pods die and get new IPs — the Service IP never changes. 3 types: ClusterIP (internal), NodePort (node IP), LoadBalancer (external).
IngressExternal HTTP/HTTPS routing into the cluster. Path-based rules: /api → backend, / → frontend. One entry point instead of many LoadBalancers. Needs an Ingress Controller (Nginx).
ConfigMapInject non-sensitive config into pods (env vars, config files). Decouples config from image — change config without rebuilding the image.
SecretLike ConfigMap but for sensitive data (passwords, tokens). Base64-encoded — NOT encrypted by default. Use sealed secrets or external secret managers in prod.
NamespaceLogical isolation within one cluster. Separate dev, staging, prod environments. Set resource quotas per namespace.
HPAHorizontal Pod Autoscaler. Auto-scales replicas based on CPU % or custom metrics. K8s watches load and adds/removes pods automatically.
🔑 Service Types
TYPEUSE CASE
ClusterIPInternal communication only. Default type. Service is only reachable from inside the cluster. Use for internal microservice-to-microservice calls.
NodePortExposes service on a static port on every node's IP. Reachable from outside via NodeIP:port. Simple but not production-grade.
LoadBalancerCreates a cloud provider load balancer (AWS ALB, etc.). Gives you an external IP. Production way to expose services. Use Ingress to avoid one LB per service.
🔧 Deployment vs StatefulSet
Deployment — Stateless Apps
Any replica is identical. Easy rolling updates built-in. Easy scale up/down.

Use for: APIs, web servers, workers, anything where one pod = any other pod.
StatefulSet — Stateful Apps
Pods get stable names: pod-0, pod-1, pod-2. Each pod gets its own Persistent Volume.

Use for: Databases, Kafka, Zookeeper — apps that care about identity and data.
⌨️ Essential kubectl Commands
kubectl get pods -n production   # List pods in a namespace
kubectl describe pod <name>      # Full details — events, errors
kubectl logs <pod> -f          # Follow pod logs (like tail -f)
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml  # Create or update from YAML
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- /bin/bash # Shell into running pod
kubectl scale deploy myapp --replicas=5 # Scale manually
kubectl rollout status deploy/myapp  # Watch rollout progress
kubectl rollout undo deploy/myapp    # Rollback to previous version
🔍 ConfigMap vs Secret
FEATURECONFIGMAPSECRET
Data typeNon-sensitive configSensitive data
ExampleDB_HOST, API_URL, config filesPasswords, tokens, TLS certs
EncodingPlain textBase64 (not encrypted by default!)
📦 Helm — Kubernetes Package Manager
Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes — like npm for Node. Instead of writing raw YAML for every resource, you use a Helm chart — a reusable, parameterized template.

helm install myapp ./chart — deploys everything in one command.
helm upgrade myapp ./chart — rolls out changes.
helm rollback myapp 1 — rollback to revision 1.

Public charts available at Artifact Hub for common tools (nginx, prometheus, postgres, etc.)
🔄 Persistent Volumes (Stateful Apps)
PV (Persistent Volume) — storage resource provisioned in the cluster (an actual disk).
PVC (Persistent Volume Claim) — a pod's request for storage. "I need 10GB." K8s binds it to a matching PV.

This decouples storage from the pod lifecycle. When a pod dies and is recreated, it reattaches to the same PVC — data is still there. Essential for databases in Kubernetes.
🔀 Ingress — Smart HTTP Router
# Instead of 3 separate LoadBalancers:
Internet → Ingress Controller (Nginx) → routes by path/host

/api/*     → backend-service (ClusterIP)
/         → frontend-service (ClusterIP)
api.co     → api-service
app.co     → app-service
☸️
The K8s DevOps Flow
Build Docker image → Push to registry → Deploy using Kubernetes YAML (kubectl apply) → K8s schedules pods on worker nodes → Service exposes them → Ingress routes external traffic → HPA scales on load.
🔄 How a Deploy Actually Works — Step by Step
1
kubectl apply -f app.yaml
You send the request. Goes to the API Server — the single entry point for everything in K8s.
2
Stored in etcd
Desired state saved: "Run 3 pods of this image." etcd is the cluster's source of truth.
3
Scheduler decides
Scheduler looks at available worker nodes and chooses the best one for each pod (resources, taints, affinity rules).
4
Workers execute
Kubelet on the assigned node receives the instruction. Container runtime pulls the image and starts the container. Pods are now running.
5
Continuous monitoring
Controller Manager watches. If a pod crashes, it creates a new one immediately. Desired state = reality at all times. This is self-healing.
⌨️ Complete kubectl Reference
# ── CLUSTER ──────────────────────────────────
kubectl cluster-info                    # Is cluster running?
kubectl get nodes                       # Worker nodes + status

# ── PODS ─────────────────────────────────────
kubectl get pods                        # List pods (default ns)
kubectl get pods -n production            # List pods in namespace
kubectl get pods -o wide                 # + which node each pod is on
kubectl run nginx --image=nginx           # Quick pod for testing
kubectl delete pod <name>                # Delete pod

# ── DEPLOYMENTS ──────────────────────────────
kubectl create deployment app --image=nginx # Create
kubectl get deployments                   # List
kubectl scale deployment app --replicas=3   # Scale
kubectl set image deployment/app nginx=nginx:latest # Update image
kubectl rollout undo deployment app         # Rollback
kubectl rollout status deployment app        # Watch rollout

# ── SERVICES ─────────────────────────────────
kubectl expose deployment app --type=NodePort --port=80
kubectl get svc                         # List services

# ── DEBUG (INTERVIEW GOLD) ───────────────────
kubectl describe pod <name>               # Full details + events
kubectl logs <pod>                      # Pod output
kubectl logs -f <pod>                    # Follow logs live
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- /bin/bash       # Shell into pod
kubectl get events                       # Cluster events
kubectl apply -f app.yaml                # Apply from YAML
kubectl port-forward pod/<name> 8080:80    # Test locally

# ── SHORTCUTS ────────────────────────────────
kubectl get po   kubectl get svc   kubectl get deploy
🔥 Debug a Failing Pod — The Interview Flow
Step 1: kubectl get pods — is the pod Running, Pending, CrashLoopBackOff, or Error?
Step 2: kubectl describe pod <name> — check Events section at the bottom. Most answers are here (image pull fail, OOM killed, liveness probe fail).
Step 3: kubectl logs <pod> — read the application's own error output.
If pod won't start: Image name wrong? Resources exceeded? ConfigMap/Secret missing? Node has space?
If pod keeps crashing: CrashLoopBackOff = app crashes on startup. Check logs immediately after start: kubectl logs <pod> --previous
📦 More K8s Workload Types
TYPEWHAT IT DOES
DaemonSetRuns exactly one pod on every node. When a new node joins the cluster, the pod is automatically added. Use for: log collectors (Fluentd), monitoring agents (Prometheus node-exporter), network plugins. Can't scale — always = number of nodes.
JobRuns a pod to completion (not indefinitely). Pod runs, completes its task, exits with code 0. Use for: database migrations, batch processing, one-off scripts. Retries on failure.
CronJobLike a Kubernetes-native cron job. Creates a Job on a schedule. schedule: "0 2 * * *" = daily at 2 AM. Use for: nightly reports, cleanup tasks, backups.
initContainerRuns before the main container starts. Completes then exits. Use for: run DB migrations before app starts, wait for a dependency to be ready, copy config files.
⚙️ Resource Requests vs Limits
Requests — the amount K8s reserves for the pod. Scheduler uses this to decide which node has enough capacity.
Limits — the maximum the pod can consume. If it exceeds CPU limit, it's throttled. If it exceeds memory limit, it's OOMKilled.

Always set both. No requests = scheduler can't plan. No limits = one bad pod can starve all others on the node.
resources:
  requests:
    memory: "256Mi"  # reserved
    cpu: "250m"     # 0.25 cores reserved
  limits:
    memory: "512Mi"  # OOMKilled if exceeded
    cpu: "500m"     # throttled if exceeded
🚧 Taints, Tolerations & Node Affinity
Taint & Toleration
Taint — mark a node as "not for general use." Only pods with a matching toleration can be scheduled there.

Use case: Dedicate GPU nodes only to ML workloads. Taint the GPU node. Only ML pods tolerate it.
Node Affinity
Schedule pods preferring or requiring specific nodes based on labels. Less strict than taints — you express preference, not exclusion.

Use case: "Schedule payment service pods on nodes in us-east-1a only."
🔧 More Essential kubectl Commands
kubectl top pods                        # real-time CPU/memory per pod
kubectl top nodes                       # real-time CPU/memory per node
kubectl get events --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' # latest events first
kubectl cordon <node>                    # prevent new pods on node (no drain)
kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets   # evict all pods, then maintenance
kubectl uncordon <node>                   # re-allow scheduling
kubectl get pvc                          # persistent volume claims
kubectl get hpa                          # horizontal pod autoscalers
kubectl auth can-i create pods              # check RBAC permissions
📦 Resource Requests & Limits — CRITICAL
Requests — what the container is guaranteed. The Scheduler uses this to decide which node has enough capacity for the pod.
Limits — the maximum the container can use. If it exceeds the memory limit, it gets OOMKilled. If it exceeds CPU limit, it gets throttled (not killed).
resources:
  requests:
    memory: "128Mi"       # guaranteed RAM
    cpu: "250m"           # guaranteed CPU (250 millicores = 0.25 CPU)
  limits:
    memory: "512Mi"       # max RAM — exceed this → OOMKilled
    cpu: "1000m"          # max CPU — exceed this → throttled (not killed)
🔢 More K8s Objects You'll Be Asked About
OBJECTWHAT IT DOES
DaemonSetEnsures one pod runs on every node in the cluster. Use for: log collectors (Fluentd), monitoring agents (node-exporter), network plugins. When a new node joins, DaemonSet automatically schedules a pod on it.
JobRuns one or more pods to completion. Pod must finish successfully, then the Job is done. Use for: database migrations, batch processing, one-off tasks. Unlike Deployment, pods are not restarted after success.
CronJobRuns a Job on a cron schedule. schedule: "0 2 * * *" = daily at 2 AM. Use for: nightly backups, scheduled reports, cache warming.
Init ContainerRuns before the main app container starts. Must complete successfully. Use for: wait until DB is ready, download config files, set up permissions. Multiple init containers run sequentially.
SidecarA second container in the same pod as the main app. Shares network + storage. Use for: log shippers, service mesh proxies (Envoy/Istio), secret injection, monitoring agents.
NetworkPolicyControls which pods can talk to which pods. By default, all pods can talk to all pods. NetworkPolicy lets you say "only the frontend service can talk to the API service on port 3000." Needs a CNI plugin that supports it (Calico, Cilium).
🎯 Taints, Tolerations & Node Affinity
Taints & Tolerations
Taint a node to repel pods: kubectl taint nodes gpu-node gpu=true:NoSchedule

Pods won't be scheduled there UNLESS they have a toleration for that taint. Use for: dedicating GPU nodes only to ML workloads, isolating production nodes.
Node Affinity
Attract pods to specific nodes based on labels. Softer than taints — "prefer to run on SSD nodes" or "must run on us-east-1a nodes".

nodeSelector is the simpler version: only schedule this pod on nodes with label disktype=ssd.
📊 kubectl top — Live Resource Usage
kubectl top nodes                # CPU/RAM usage across all nodes
kubectl top pods -n production      # CPU/RAM per pod in namespace
kubectl top pods --sort-by=memory   # sort by memory usage (find hogs)

🎭 Real Scenarios — Learn Kubernetes by Solving the Problem First
Read the situation, think about what you'd actually run, then click ▶ Run to reveal the command and its real output.
1
The situation: A pod keeps entering CrashLoopBackOff, restarting over and over, and you need to know why.
What would you run?
kubectl logs web-7d8f9c6b5d-abcde --previous
Error: Cannot find module 'express'
at Function.Module._resolveFilename
Why this command: --previous shows the log from the container that already crashed, not the fresh restart attempt — which usually has no output yet. This is exactly the same idea as "docker logs" needing the crashed container's own output.
2
The situation: A pod has been stuck in "Pending" status for several minutes and never actually starts.
What would you run?
kubectl describe pod web-7d8f9c6b5d-abcde
Events:
Warning FailedScheduling 0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient memory.
Why this command: describe's Events section is where the scheduler explains exactly why it couldn't place the pod — here, every node is genuinely out of free memory to fit it.
3
The situation: Another pod can't reach a service, and you suspect there might be no healthy pods actually behind it.
What would you run?
kubectl get endpoints web
NAME ENDPOINTS
web <none>
Why this command: An empty endpoints list confirms nothing is actually behind the service — no pod currently matches its selector, so any traffic sent to it simply has nowhere to go.
4
The situation: You need to test a service directly from your laptop, without setting up a public LoadBalancer or Ingress.
What would you run?
kubectl port-forward svc/web 8080:80
Forwarding from 127.0.0.1:8080 -> 80
Forwarding from [::1]:8080 -> 80
Why this command: port-forward tunnels a local port straight to the service inside the cluster — no public exposure needed, perfect for a quick local check.
5
The situation: A deployment you just pushed is clearly broken in production, and you need to recover immediately.
What would you run?
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web
deployment.apps/web rolled back
Why this command: This instantly reverts to the last known-good revision — no rebuild, no re-deploy script, just one command while you investigate the real fix.
6
The situation: You need to change an app's log level without rebuilding or redeploying its container image.
What would you run?
kubectl create configmap app-config --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=debug
configmap/app-config created
Why this command: ConfigMaps keep config outside the image entirely — changing one (then restarting the pods that read it) never requires touching the image at all.
7
The situation: You're about to run a risky delete command and want to confirm you're actually allowed to first.
What would you run?
kubectl auth can-i delete pods --namespace production
no
Why this command: Confirming access ahead of time beats finding out only after the real command fails — and here, it just saved you from a permission error mid-incident.
8
The situation: A big sale is coming up, and pods need to scale up and down automatically as traffic rises and falls.
What would you run?
kubectl autoscale deployment web --min=2 --max=10 --cpu-percent=70
horizontalpodautoscaler.autoscaling/web autoscaled
Why this command: This sets up a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler that reacts to real CPU load automatically — no one has to be online during the sale to manually run kubectl scale.

🏦
No physical servers
Rent compute from AWS
→
⚡

⚡ Core AWS Services — DevOps Essentials
SERVICEWHAT IT IS
EC2Virtual machine in the cloud. You pick the OS, size, and specs. The foundation of cloud compute.
S3Object storage — files, backups, static websites, Docker layer cache, Terraform state files. Infinitely scalable.
IAMWho can do what. Users, roles, policies. Always follow least privilege principle — give only the permissions needed, nothing more.
VPCYour private isolated network inside AWS. Subnets, routing tables, gateways. Everything sits inside a VPC.
Security GroupVirtual firewall for EC2/RDS. Controls inbound and outbound traffic by port/protocol/source.
CloudWatchAWS monitoring, logging, and alerting. Like Prometheus + Grafana but native AWS. Collects metrics, stores logs, fires alarms.
ECSAWS-native container orchestration. Simpler than K8s. Two modes: EC2 (you manage the VMs) and Fargate (serverless, AWS manages infra).
EKSManaged Kubernetes on AWS. AWS handles the control plane. You manage worker nodes. Best when you need full K8s compatibility.
ALBApplication Load Balancer. HTTP/HTTPS routing, health checks, path-based routing. Works with ECS and EKS.
LambdaServerless compute. Run code without managing servers. Event-triggered. Pay per invocation. Great for lightweight background tasks.
RDSManaged relational database. Postgres, MySQL, Aurora. AWS handles backups, patching, failover.
Region / AZRegion = geographic area (us-east-1). AZ = isolated data center within a region. Deploy across AZs for High Availability.
🛡️ High Availability vs Disaster Recovery
High Availability (HA)
Cluster is always accessible even if one or more servers are down. Achieved by:
• Multi-AZ deployment within a region
• Redundant instances + auto-scaling
• Load balancers routing around failed nodes
Disaster Recovery (DR)
Continue service even during a regional outage. Achieved by:
• Multi-region deployment
• Data replication across regions
• DNS failover to backup region
🌐 AWS Networking Summary
VPCisolation
Virtual Private Cloud — your isolated network. Resources (EC2, RDS) live inside subnets within the VPC. Public subnets face internet. Private subnets are internal only.
Security Groupsfirewall
Virtual firewall. Controls inbound/outbound traffic by port, protocol, source IP. Stateful — if you allow inbound, outbound response is auto-allowed.
Load Balancer (ALB)traffic
Distributes HTTP(S) traffic across multiple instances. Health checks remove unhealthy instances. Path-based routing. SSL termination.
IAMaccess control
Least privilege principle: Give only the permissions needed. IAM Roles attach to EC2/Lambda — never hardcode access keys in code. Use roles for service-to-service auth.
🔥 Full DevOps Deployment Workflow on AWS
User → ALB → ECS/EKS (App) → RDS (DB)
                             ↓
                             S3

1. Network Setup — VPC → Public subnet (ALB) + Private subnet (ECS + RDS)
2. Security — IAM roles for ECS/EC2. Security groups: Allow ALB→ECS (port 3000), Allow ECS→RDS (port 5432)
3. Database — Launch RDS (Postgres) in private subnet (never public)
4. App Deployment — Build Docker image → Push to ECR → Deploy on ECS Fargate (or EKS for K8s)
5. Traffic — Create ALB → Route /api → backend service, / → frontend service
6. Storage — S3 for static assets (React build), file uploads, logs
7. Monitoring — CloudWatch: logs + CPU/memory metrics + alerts
8. Automation — Lambda for background jobs (image resize, cron tasks)
🃏 Service Quick-Reference Cards
EC2compute
A computer in the cloud. You pick OS + size. Host apps, run Docker, CI/CD runners.
Think: "Renting a computer on AWS"
S3storage
Unlimited file storage. Images, videos, React builds, Terraform state, logs, build artifacts.
Think: "Google Drive for servers"
IAMaccess
Controls who can do what. Dev can deploy but not delete DB. EC2 can read S3 but nothing else. Rule: least privilege.
Think: "Bouncer for AWS"
VPCnetwork
Your private isolated network in AWS. Public subnet → web servers. Private subnet → database (never expose DB to internet).
Think: "Your own mini internet inside AWS"
Security Groupfirewall
Virtual firewall. Allow port 80 (HTTP), allow port 22 (SSH from your IP only). Lock down servers.
Think: "Firewall rules per instance"
CloudWatchmonitoring
Logs + metrics + alerts. CPU > 80% → send alert. App logs stored and searchable. Debug issues, monitor uptime.
Think: "Eyes + ears of your system"
ECS Fargatecontainers
Run Docker containers — AWS manages the servers. You just provide the image. Simpler than K8s.
Think: "Docker hosting without managing VMs"
EKSkubernetes
Managed Kubernetes. AWS handles the control plane. Use when you need full K8s power for complex microservices.
Think: "Powerful ECS with full K8s"
Lambdaserverless
Run code without servers. Upload image → auto resize. API endpoints. Cron jobs. Pay per invocation.
Think: "Run code only when needed"
RDSdatabase
Managed SQL database (Postgres, MySQL). No manual setup. Auto backups, patching, failover handled by AWS.
Think: "Database without the headache"
ALBload balancer
Distributes traffic. Route /api → backend, / → frontend. Health checks remove failed instances. SSL termination.
Think: "Traffic police for requests"
Region / AZgeography
Region = location (us-east-1). AZ = data center inside region. Deploy in 2+ AZs → if one fails, app still works.
Think: "Spread load to survive failures"
🌐 Global Infrastructure — Regions & AZs
🌍 Regions
Geographic locations around the world — us-east-1 (N. Virginia), eu-west-1 (Ireland), ap-southeast-1 (Singapore). Each is a massive cluster of data centers.

Choose your region based on: latency to users, data residency laws, and service availability.
🏢 Availability Zones (AZs)
Within each Region there are multiple physically isolated data centers: us-east-1a, us-east-1b, us-east-1c. Independent power, cooling, networking.

If a disaster hits one AZ, the others stay online. Good DevOps = always deploy across 2+ AZs.
💾 Storage Types — Which to Use When
SERVICETYPEUSE CASE
S3Object storageInfinitely scalable file bucket. Accessed via API. Perfect for backups, static assets, logs, Terraform state, Docker build cache. Not a filesystem.
EBSBlock storageVirtual hard drive attached directly to one EC2 instance. Holds the OS and local databases. Like a laptop's hard drive. Fast, but tied to one instance and one AZ.
EFSNetwork filesystemShared network drive. Multiple EC2 instances or K8s pods across different AZs can mount and read/write simultaneously. Like NFS in the cloud.
⚖️ L4 vs L7 Load Balancers (NLB vs ALB)
⚡ L4 — NLB (Fast, Blind)
Only looks at the IP address and TCP/UDP port. Has no idea what the user is asking for. Just grabs the packet and sends it to the next server as fast as possible.

Pros: Blazing fast, low latency, millions of req/sec.
When to use: Raw speed matters, or non-HTTP traffic (gaming servers, database connections).
AWS = NLB (Network Load Balancer)
🧠 L7 — ALB (Smart, Reading)
Opens the packet and reads the HTTP request. Understands the request content and can make smart routing decisions.

Path-based routing: /images → Image Servers. /api → API Servers.
When to use: Web apps and microservices routing by URL, headers, or cookies.
AWS = ALB (Application Load Balancer)
🏗️ VPC Architecture — Step by Step
Golden rule: Never put a database on the public internet. Design a network that separates public-facing traffic from secure backend resources.
1
Create the VPC
Create a Virtual Private Cloud with a CIDR block like 10.0.0.0/16. This is your isolated slice of AWS — nothing gets in or out without your permission. Use /16 for enough IPs for all subnets.
2
Carve out Subnets
Public Subnet 10.0.1.0/24 → Web server / Load Balancer lives here.
Private Subnet 10.0.2.0/24 → Database lives here. Repeat in each AZ for HA.
3
Attach Internet Gateway (IGW)
A VPC is completely locked down by default. Attach an IGW to give the public subnet internet access. Think of it as the modem for your cloud network. Private subnet gets no IGW route — stays safely offline.
4
Security Groups (Bouncers)
Web SG: Allow port 80/443 from internet (0.0.0.0/0).
Interview Gold: DB SG — allow port 3306 only from the Web Security Group ID, not from an IP. Only instances wearing the "Web SG badge" can talk to the DB. Never open the DB to 0.0.0.0/0.
5
Launch EC2 + User Data
Select AMI (Amazon Machine Image — the OS blueprint, e.g. Ubuntu 22.04), choose instance type (t3.micro), place in correct subnet. User Data = a bash script that runs on first boot. Use it to automatically apt install nginx — no SSH needed. This is bootstrapping.
Your DevOps job: automate all of this in Terraform.
6
NAT Gateway (Private → Internet)
Private subnet resources (app servers, DBs) can't reach the internet directly. A NAT Gateway in the public subnet allows outbound internet access (for package updates, API calls) without exposing the private resources to inbound traffic.
Architecture diagram:
Internet → IGW → ALB (public subnet) → App servers (private subnet) → RDS (private subnet)
Private subnet → NAT Gateway (public subnet) → IGW → Internet (for outbound only)
🔒 Security Groups vs NACLs
FEATURESECURITY GROUPNACL (Network ACL)
LevelInstance-level (attached to EC2)Subnet-level (all traffic in/out)
StateStateful — return traffic auto-allowedStateless — must allow both directions
RulesAllow only. Default deny all.Allow and explicit Deny rules.
Use casePrimary security mechanismLayered defense, blocking specific IPs
📡 CDN — Content Delivery Network
A CDN caches static assets (images, JS, CSS, HTML) at edge locations globally. When a user requests a file, it's served from the nearest edge location — not from your origin server.

Benefits: Dramatically reduces latency (user in Singapore gets content from Singapore edge, not your US server). Reduces origin server load. Protects against traffic spikes.

AWS CloudFront (AWS CDN), Cloudflare, Fastly are the major players.

DevOps gotcha: After a deployment, CDN may serve stale cached files. You need to invalidate the cache or use cache-busting (e.g., hashed filenames like app.a3f9d2.js).
🔒 Firewall vs Reverse Proxy
🛡️ Firewall
Controls which traffic is allowed into/out of a network based on rules (IP, port, protocol). Does NOT see the content of requests — just the "envelope". AWS Security Groups and NACLs are firewalls.
🔀 Reverse Proxy
Sits in front of servers and forwards client requests to them. Reads the request content. Used for: load balancing, SSL termination, caching, hiding backend topology. Nginx is often both. ALB acts as L7 reverse proxy.
📊 SLI / SLO / SLA
TERMFULL NAMEWHAT IT IS
SLIService Level IndicatorA measurable metric. Examples: error rate, p99 latency, uptime percentage. The raw number you track.
SLOService Level ObjectiveA target for an SLI. "99.9% of requests complete in under 200ms." Internal goal. If you miss SLOs, your error budget is consumed.
SLAService Level AgreementContractual commitment with customers. "We guarantee 99.9% uptime or you get a credit." SLOs are internal targets. SLAs are external promises with financial consequences.
🏗️ AWS CloudFormation — Native IaC
CloudFormation is AWS's native IaC service. Define AWS resources in JSON/YAML templates → provisioned as a Stack. Updates as change sets. Deep AWS integration, free. vs Terraform: CloudFormation = AWS-only. Terraform = multi-cloud HCL.
📡 More AWS Services — Also Asked
SERVICEWHAT IT IS
Route 53AWS DNS service. Register domains, manage DNS records, health-check-based routing (failover to backup region), weighted routing, latency-based routing.
ECRElastic Container Registry — AWS's private Docker image registry. Integrates tightly with ECS/EKS. IAM-controlled access. Scan images for vulnerabilities automatically.
SQSSimple Queue Service — managed message queue. Decouples microservices. Producer puts messages in queue; consumers poll and process. Handles traffic spikes without dropping requests.
SNSSimple Notification Service — pub/sub messaging. Publish once, fan out to many subscribers (SQS queues, Lambda, email, HTTP). Used for event-driven architectures.
ElastiCacheManaged Redis or Memcached. In-memory cache for session storage, query caching, leaderboards. Massively reduces DB load for read-heavy workloads.
CloudTrailLogs every API call made in your AWS account — who did what, when, from where. "Who deleted that security group?" Answer is in CloudTrail. Essential for security auditing.
AWS ConfigContinuously records configuration changes to AWS resources. Set rules that alert or auto-remediate when resources drift from compliance (e.g., "alert if any S3 bucket is public").
Auto Scaling GroupAutomatically adds/removes EC2 instances based on load. Set min/max/desired capacity. Define scaling policies (add instance if CPU > 70%). Works with ALB to distribute traffic across new instances.
SSM (Systems Manager)Connect to EC2 instances without SSH or opening port 22. Use Session Manager from AWS console. Store and access secrets via Parameter Store. Run commands across many instances simultaneously.
🌐 Route53 — AWS DNS
AWS's highly available DNS service. More than just DNS — it also does health-based routing: if your primary server goes down, Route53 detects the health check failure and automatically reroutes traffic to a backup server or region.

Routing policies:
Simple — one record, one IP. Basic.
Weighted — 70% traffic to us-east-1, 30% to eu-west-1. Good for canary deploys.
Latency — route to the region with lowest latency for that user.
Failover — primary/secondary. If primary fails health check, Route53 switches to secondary. Core of disaster recovery.
Geolocation — route EU users to EU servers, US users to US servers.
📦 ECR — Elastic Container Registry
AWS's private Docker image registry. Like Docker Hub but inside your AWS account.

Key benefits: Integrated with IAM (control who can push/pull), no bandwidth cost for images pulled by ECS/EKS in same region, image vulnerability scanning built-in, lifecycle policies to auto-delete old images.
# Authenticate Docker to ECR (run before push/pull):
aws ecr get-login-password --region us-east-1 | docker login \
  --username AWS --password-stdin 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com

# Tag and push:
docker tag myapp:v2 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/myapp:v2
docker push 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/myapp:v2
⏱️ RTO & RPO — Disaster Recovery Targets
RTO — Recovery Time Objective
How long can the system be down?
"After a disaster, we must be back online within 4 hours." This drives decisions about hot standby (minutes) vs cold backup (hours). Lower RTO = more expensive infra.
RPO — Recovery Point Objective
How much data can we afford to lose?
"We can tolerate losing up to 1 hour of data." This drives backup frequency. RPO = 1 hour → backups every hour. RPO = 0 → real-time replication required.
💬 SQS & SNS — Messaging Services
SQS — Simple Queue Service
Message queue. Producer sends message to queue. Consumer polls queue and processes it. Decouples services — if consumer is slow or down, messages wait in the queue. Use for: background jobs, order processing, task workers.
SNS — Simple Notification Service
Pub/Sub messaging. One publisher sends to a topic, many subscribers receive it simultaneously. Use for: fan-out (one event triggers multiple actions), sending emails/SMS, triggering Lambda functions.

⚙️ Terraform Workflow
1
Configuration FilesHCL / JSON
Define your infrastructure using .tf files written in HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language) or JSON. Describe servers, networks, databases — everything as code.
main.tfvariables.tfoutputs.tf
2
Execution Planterraform plan
Terraform generates a plan showing exactly what will be created, changed, or destroyed to reach the desired state. Review before applying — no surprises.
terraform initterraform plan
3
Resource Provisioningterraform apply
Terraform applies the plan — provisions and configures all the resources. Creates EC2 instances, VPCs, S3 buckets, whatever you defined.
terraform apply
4
State Managementterraform.tfstate
Terraform tracks current infrastructure state in a state file. This is how it knows what exists and what needs to change. In teams, store state in a remote backend (S3 + DynamoDB lock) — never commit it to Git.
5
Version ControlGit
Store configuration files in Git. Review infra changes via PRs. Full audit trail. Never hardcode secrets — use environment variables or a secrets manager.
🌐 Multi-Cloud with Terraform
1. Define Providers — add provider blocks for each cloud (AWS, Azure, GCP). Each configures how Terraform interacts with that cloud.
2. Resource Definitions — define resources per cloud in the same or separate .tf files.
3. Remote State — use a remote backend (S3, Azure Blob) to share state across team members. Critical for multi-cloud consistency.
4. Networking — configure VPCs, VPNs, or VPC peering for cross-cloud communication.
5. Authentication — use environment variables or a secrets manager for cloud credentials. Never hardcode access keys.
⌨️ Core Terraform Commands
terraform init             # Initialize, download providers
terraform plan             # Preview changes
terraform apply            # Apply changes (provisions infra)
terraform destroy          # Tear down all resources
terraform fmt              # Format .tf files
terraform validate         # Validate configuration syntax
terraform state list       # List all managed resources
🏗️
IaC = Infrastructure as Code. Code → Plan → Apply → State
Infra changes go through code review in Git PRs — same as app code. Full audit trail. Reproducible: one command recreates any environment. Never click the AWS console for critical infra.
⚔️ Terraform vs Ansible — They're Teammates, Not Rivals
The golden rule: Use Terraform to build the house. Use Ansible to arrange the furniture.
🏗️ Terraform — Provisioning
Best for: Managing the lifecycle of infrastructure itself — VPCs, EC2 instances, S3 buckets, RDS, load balancers.

Declarative: You describe the end state ("I want 5 servers"). Terraform figures out how.

State-aware: Keeps a .tfstate file. Knows exactly what exists. If you manually delete something, Terraform sees the "drift" and recreates it.

Immutable: Change a server's size? Terraform destroys the old one and creates a new one. Prevents config drift.
⚙️ Ansible — Configuration Management
Best for: Configuring the software inside servers once they exist — installing Nginx, updating packages, managing users, deploying app code.

Procedural: Follows a playbook step-by-step. Like running shell commands across 100 servers at once.

Stateless: Doesn't track infra in a database. Logs into target, checks state, applies changes. If you delete a server, Ansible won't know until it tries to reach it.

Agentless: No agent to install on target servers. Just SSH.
QUESTIONTERRAFORMANSIBLE
What does it manage?Infrastructure (servers, networks)Software inside servers
StyleDeclarative (describe end state)Procedural (step-by-step)
State trackingYes — .tfstate fileNo — stateless
Infra modelImmutable (destroy + recreate)Mutable (update in place)
Agent needed?NoNo (agentless via SSH)
🔒 DevSecOps — Security Baked Into the Pipeline
DevSecOps = security integrated throughout the development and deployment process — not bolted on at the end. Security at every stage, automated in the pipeline.
⬅️Shift Left SecuritySAST / Lint
Perform security checks early — static code analysis, dependency scanning, secret detection during the build phase. Catch vulnerabilities at commit, not in production.
🤖Automated Security TestsDAST / Snyk
Vulnerability scans and dynamic application security testing (DAST) run automatically in CI. Identify issues before they reach production.
📊Continuous MonitoringPrometheus / Grafana
Monitor pipeline and deployed apps for security incidents. Use specialized security monitoring tools alongside Prometheus/Grafana.
🏗️IaC Security ScanningCheckov / tfsec
Scan Terraform/CloudFormation templates for misconfigurations and vulnerabilities (like hardcoded passwords, overly permissive policies) before they're applied.
🔑Access ControlRBAC / IAM
Strict access controls using RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) or ABAC. Enforce least privilege principle across the entire pipeline — humans and services.
🚨Incident ResponsePagerDuty / Alerts
Clear incident response plan integrated into the pipeline. Security alerts fire automatically. Quickly address potential breaches. Runbooks for common scenarios.
🔀 Reverse Proxy — Nginx
A reverse proxy sits between clients and backend servers, forwarding requests to the appropriate server and returning responses to the client.

What it provides:
• Load balancing — distribute requests across backend servers
• SSL termination — handle HTTPS at the proxy, HTTP behind it
• Caching — serve cached responses without hitting backends
• Security — hide backend server IPs, rate limiting, WAF

Example (Nginx): Web app on 3 backend servers. Nginx distributes incoming HTTP requests evenly. If one server fails, Nginx routes around it. SSL cert lives on Nginx — backends don't need it.
🔒
DevSecOps = Shift Left + Automate + Monitor
Security isn't a final gate — it's woven into every stage. Secret detection at commit → vulnerability scan in CI → IaC scan before apply → RBAC in prod → security monitoring alerts. Never hardcode secrets anywhere — ever.
🚀 Deployment Strategies
Rolling Deploy
Take one server out of rotation, update it, add back. Repeat for each server. No downtime but there's a brief period running two versions simultaneously.

✅ Simple, safe. ⚠️ Brief version mismatch.
Blue / Green
Two full environments. LB routes to green (live). Deploy to blue. Test blue. Flip LB to blue. Rollback = flip LB back instantly.

✅ Instant rollback. ⚠️ Double infra cost.
Canary
Route 5% of traffic to new version via weighted rules. Monitor errors/latency. Expand % if healthy. Limits blast radius — if it breaks, only 5% of users affected.

✅ Safe for high-risk changes. ⚠️ More complex setup.
A/B Testing
Route users by header/cookie to different versions. Like canary but measuring user behavior, not just errors. Used to test feature impact on metrics (clicks, conversions).
⚖️ Load Balancing Algorithms
ALGORITHM HOW IT WORKS BEST FOR
Round Robin Req 1 → A, Req 2 → B, Req 3 → C, repeat. Evenly distributed. Stateless apps, equal server capacity
Least Connections Route to server with fewest active connections. Smarter than round robin. Requests vary in duration (some slow, some fast)
IP Hash Same client IP always hits same server. Deterministic routing. Sticky sessions when state isn't centralized
Weighted Server A gets 70%, Server B gets 30%. You define the ratio. Different server capacities, canary deployments
⚙️ How to Set Up a CI/CD Pipeline from Scratch
1
Set up CIJenkins / GitLab CI / GitHub Actions
Select a CI tool and connect it to your VCS. Write a build script: code checkout → dependency install → compile → run tests. Set up automated testing on every commit or PR.
2
Artifact StorageDocker Hub / AWS S3 / ECR
Decide where to store build artifacts (Docker images, binaries). Configure the pipeline to package and upload artifacts to storage after a successful build.
3
Set up CDSame tool or extend
Define deployment scripts for each environment (dev → staging → prod). Configure triggers after successful builds. Set up environment-specific configs and secrets management.
4
InfrastructureTerraform / CloudFormation
Provision infrastructure using IaC. Ensure environments are consistent and reproducible — spinning up a new one should be a single command, no human intervention.
5
Monitoring & LoggingPrometheus / Grafana / ELK
Implement monitoring for apps and infrastructure. Configure alerts for critical issues — monitoring without alerting is pointless, you need to react to problems.
6
Security & DocsSnyk / OWASP
Integrate security scanning tools (Snyk, OWASP). Document the pipeline, configuration, and deployment steps — to onboard new team members and maintain the system.
🕸️Service MeshIstio / Linkerd
A service mesh is a dedicated infrastructure layer for handling service-to-service communication in microservice architectures.

As your microservice count grows, orchestrating reliable communication between them becomes complex — load balancing, retries, timeouts, encryption, observability. A service mesh handles all this automatically, without changing your application code.

Think of it as a network of sidecar proxies attached to each service, intercepting all traffic and adding observability, security (mTLS), and routing capabilities.
sidecar proxy patternservice-to-service commsmTLS encryptionobservabilityIstio / Linkerd

⚙️ GitHub Actions — Key Keywords
KEYWORD WHAT IT DOES
nameDisplay name for the workflow or step. Shows in GitHub Actions UI.
onTrigger — what event starts the workflow. push, pull_request, schedule, workflow_dispatch
jobsTop-level grouping. A workflow has multiple jobs. Jobs run in parallel by default.
runs-onWhich runner (machine) to use. ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest
stepsOrdered list of tasks within a job. Run sequentially top to bottom.
runShell command to execute. run: npm test, run: docker build .
usesUse a pre-built action. uses: actions/checkout@v3, uses: docker/login-action@v2
withInput parameters for a uses action. Key-value pairs passed to the action.
envSet environment variables. Can be at workflow, job, or step level.
needsJob dependency. needs: build means this job waits for 'build' job to succeed first.
📄 Example GitHub Actions Workflow
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [main, develop]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Install deps
        run: npm install
      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test
  deploy:
    needs: build-and-test # waits for above
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: docker build -t myapp .
📄
Pipelines automate: Build → Test → Deploy
Workflow = the whole file. | Trigger (on) = what starts it. | Jobs = parallel work units. | Steps = sequential commands inside a job. | needs = job ordering.

🐧 Linux & OS Scenarios
S01A server's CPU is spiking to 100% and it's unresponsive. Walk me through how you find the culprit.▼
APPROACH
1. SSH into the box (if you can — if completely unresponsive, use cloud console/serial access).
2. top or htop — sort by CPU. Identify the PID consuming it. Note the process name.
3. ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head -10 — non-interactive version, good for scripting.
4. strace -p <PID> — see what system calls the process is actually making right now. Is it stuck in a loop? Waiting on I/O?
5. dmesg | tail -50 or cat /var/log/messages — check for kernel-level errors (OOM kills, hardware errors, driver issues).
6. If it's a runaway process: kill -9 <PID> as last resort.

top/htop → PIDstrace = what it's doingdmesg = system errors
S02"No space left on device" error, but df -h shows 20% disk space free. What's going on?▼
APPROACH
This is the classic inode exhaustion problem — and interviewers love it because most people don't know it exists.

Every file on Linux takes up one inode (an index node — metadata entry). You can have physical disk space free but run out of inodes if there are millions of tiny files.

Verify: df -i — shows inode usage. If Use% is 100% on a filesystem, that's your culprit.
Find the directory: find / -xdev -printf '%h\n' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head — shows which directory has the most files.

Second possibility: A deleted file is being held open by a running process — the disk space isn't reclaimed until the process closes the file handle.
Check: lsof | grep deleted — find processes holding deleted file handles. Restart that process to free the space.

df -i = inode usageinode exhaustion = millions of tiny fileslsof | grep deleted = held-open files
S03The OOM killer keeps terminating your main application. How do you troubleshoot and fix it?▼
APPROACH
1. Confirm the OOM killer fired:
dmesg | grep -i "oom\|killed" — you'll see "Out of memory: Kill process <PID> (<name>)"
cat /var/log/syslog | grep oom-killer

2. Investigate the cause:
• Memory leak? — watch free -h over time. If memory steadily climbs, the app has a leak. Profile it.
• Container limits too low? — if containerized, the cgroup memory limit might be set lower than the app needs. Check docker stats or kubectl describe pod for resource limits.
• Server genuinely lacks RAM? — the app's actual requirements exceed the server's memory. Scale up or optimize.

3. Short-term fix: Increase memory limits or add swap (not ideal but buys time).
4. Long-term fix: Fix the memory leak, right-size container limits, or upgrade instance.

dmesg → confirm OOM killfree -h over time = leak detectioncgroup limits too low = container issue
🌐 Networking & Web Scenarios
S04Users are getting 502 Bad Gateway. LB → Nginx → upstream app server. How do you isolate it?▼
APPROACH
502 = Nginx received an invalid/no response from the upstream server. The LB is fine. Nginx is fine. The upstream app is the problem.

1. cat /var/log/nginx/error.log | tail -50 — what error is Nginx actually seeing? "connect() failed", "upstream timed out", "no live upstreams"?
2. Check the upstream app: systemctl status appname — is it running?
3. curl -v http://localhost:<app-port>/health — is the app responding on its port locally?
4. netstat -tlnp | grep <port> or ss -tlnp — is anything listening on that port?
5. Check firewall/security groups — is internal traffic between Nginx and the app being blocked?

502 = upstream problem, not Nginxnginx error.log firstcurl localhost to test app directlyss -tlnp = what's listening
S05Service can't connect to database. What's the difference between "Connection Refused" and "Connection Timeout"?▼
APPROACH
This tests TCP/IP fundamentals — a classic question.

Connection Refused — the packet reached the destination, but nothing is listening on that port. The server actively rejected it. Causes: DB service is down, DB is bound to 127.0.0.1 (localhost only) instead of 0.0.0.0.
Debug: Is the DB process running? What IP is it bound to? (ss -tlnp | grep 5432)

Connection Timeout — the packet never arrived or was silently dropped. No response at all. Causes: firewall blocking, security group denying traffic, wrong IP/port, routing issue.
Debug: Check security groups/firewall rules. Can you reach the host at all? (ping <db-host>)

Test both: telnet <db-host> 5432 or nc -zv <db-host> 5432

Refused = reached but nothing listeningTimeout = packet never arrivednc -zv to test TCP connectivity
S06Ping by hostname fails. Ping by IP works. nslookup resolves correctly. What's the issue?▼
APPROACH
This tests DNS resolution order — a subtle but important distinction.

nslookup queries DNS directly. But ping uses the OS resolver, which follows the resolution order defined in /etc/nsswitch.conf.

The OS might be checking /etc/hosts BEFORE querying DNS. If there's a stale or incorrect entry for that hostname in /etc/hosts, ping will use that wrong IP and fail — while nslookup queries DNS directly and gets the correct answer.

1. cat /etc/hosts — is there a hardcoded entry for this hostname with a wrong IP?
2. cat /etc/nsswitch.conf — check the hosts: line. It likely says files dns — meaning check files (/etc/hosts) first, then DNS.
Fix: Remove the bad entry from /etc/hosts, or reorder nsswitch.conf to query DNS first.

nslookup = DNS directping = OS resolver ordercheck /etc/hosts for stale entry/etc/nsswitch.conf = resolution order
☸️ Kubernetes Scenarios
S07A pod is stuck in CrashLoopBackOff. Walk through the exact commands.▼
APPROACH
1. kubectl get pods — confirm the state. CrashLoopBackOff means the container starts, crashes, K8s tries to restart, crashes again, with increasing delays.
2. kubectl describe pod <name> — read the Events section. Look for liveness probe failures, missing secrets/configmaps, resource limit kills.
3. kubectl logs <pod> --previous — crucial: shows logs of the container before it crashed. Current logs may be empty if the crash is immediate.
4. Common causes:
• App error on startup (bad env var, missing config, DB not reachable)
• Liveness probe misconfigured (fails before app is ready)
• Secret/ConfigMap referenced but doesn't exist
• OOMKilled — container hit memory limit

describe pod = events = root causelogs --previous = before crashOOMKilled → increase memory limit
S08Pod is stuck in ImagePullBackOff. What are the potential reasons?▼
APPROACH
ImagePullBackOff = the worker node is trying to pull your Docker image and failing.

Reason 1 — Typo in image name or tag: Most common. myapp:lates instead of myapp:latest. Double-check the image name in your deployment YAML.

Reason 2 — Node can't reach the registry: Worker node has no internet access to Docker Hub / ECR. Check network/security group rules from the node.

Reason 3 — Private registry, missing imagePullSecrets: The registry requires authentication, but the pod spec doesn't have imagePullSecrets pointing to the credentials secret.
Fix: Create a K8s Secret with registry credentials and add imagePullSecrets to the deployment.

Debug: kubectl describe pod <name> — the Events section will say "Failed to pull image" with the exact reason.

typo in image namenode network blocks registrymissing imagePullSecretsdescribe pod = exact error
S09Pod A is healthy but pod B in the same namespace can't reach it via Service name. How do you debug?▼
APPROACH
1. First, try the Service IP from pod B:
kubectl exec -it <pod-b> -- curl <service-ip>
If IP works but name doesn't → it's a DNS issue (CoreDNS).

2. Check if CoreDNS is running:
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep coredns

3. Check the Service selector — does it actually match the target pod's labels?
kubectl get endpoints <service-name>
If the endpoints list is empty, the selector doesn't match any pod labels. This is a very common mistake.

4. Check the Service port matches the container's exposed port.

IP works, name fails = CoreDNSkubectl get endpoints = selector matchempty endpoints = selector mismatch
🔧 CI/CD & Infrastructure Scenarios
S10CI pipeline fails randomly ~10% of the time on integration tests. How do you fix flaky tests?▼
APPROACH
Do NOT just add retries — that masks the problem and makes the pipeline non-deterministic.

Find the pattern: Which tests? Which CI runner? What time of day? Collect data.

Common root causes:
• Shared state: Multiple test runs hitting the same database and stepping on each other's data. Fix: each test run gets its own isolated DB/schema.
• Race conditions: Tests that depend on async operations completing without proper waits.
• External API timeouts: Tests calling real external services. Fix: mock them.
• CI runner resource starvation: CPU/memory contention between parallel jobs.

Reproduce locally: Run the failing test in an isolated Docker container to match the CI environment.

no retries = fix the root causeshared state = isolated DB per runmock external APIs
S11Docker build pipeline went from 2 minutes to 15 minutes. What do you investigate?▼
APPROACH
1. Check the Dockerfile first: Did someone change an instruction high up in the file (like adding an ENV, modifying a COPY, or changing a RUN command) that is busting the Docker layer cache? If a layer high in the file changes, every subsequent layer must rebuild. If the COPY command that copies source code was moved above the npm install step, every commit now reinstalls all dependencies.

2. Check CI runner health: Is the runner starved for CPU or disk I/O? top during the build — is something competing for resources?

3. Is the cache actually being used? Many CI systems don't persist Docker layer cache between runs by default. You may need to explicitly configure BuildKit cache mounts or use a registry-based cache.

4. New large dependency added? A massive npm/pip install that didn't exist before?

layer cache busted = most commonorder matters: deps before codeCI runner resource starvation
S12Deployment succeeded in the pipeline, but users still see the old version. Where do you look?▼
APPROACH
The pipeline said "success" — but "deployed" and "released" are not the same thing.

Frontend/static assets:
• Browser cache: User's browser cached the old JS/CSS. Force-refresh (Ctrl+Shift+R) to test.
• CDN cache: Cloudflare or CloudFront is serving stale files. Check CDN cache settings. Trigger a cache purge.

Backend/Kubernetes:
• Did the new deployment actually roll out? kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp
• Is the new pod actually running? kubectl get pods — is the new pod in Running state while old ones are Terminating?
• Is the Service selector pointing to the new pods? Are there 2 versions running simultaneously (old pods still serving traffic)?

browser cache = force refreshCDN cache = purgekubectl rollout statusold pods still serving?
S13Someone manually deleted an AWS Security Group rule, breaking the app. You use Terraform. How do you fix it?▼
APPROACH
This is a Terraform drift detection scenario.

1. terraform plan — Terraform compares its state file (.tfstate) against the real AWS environment. It will detect the missing rule as "drift" and propose recreating it. You'll see something like: ~ aws_security_group_rule.allow_app: rule missing, will add

2. Review the plan output carefully, then terraform apply to recreate the deleted rule.

3. Prevent future manual changes:
• Lock down AWS Console write access for the Security Group resources
• Use AWS Config Rules to detect and alert on manual changes
• Set up CloudTrail to audit all API calls — you'll know exactly who deleted it

terraform plan = drift detectionterraform apply = fixrestrict Console write accessCloudTrail = audit who did it
S14EC2 instance gets "Access Denied" trying to write to S3. Walk through checking permissions.▼
APPROACH
IAM permission debugging is layered — check each layer in order:

1. IAM Role on EC2: Go to EC2 → check the attached Instance Profile. Does it have a Role? Does that Role have a policy with s3:PutObject on this bucket?

2. S3 Bucket Policy: Even if the IAM role allows it, the bucket policy can explicitly DENY access. An explicit Deny overrides any Allow. Check the bucket's Permissions → Bucket Policy.

3. KMS Encryption: If the bucket uses KMS encryption, the EC2 role also needs kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt permissions on that specific KMS key.

4. VPC Endpoint / Network: If the bucket has a VPC endpoint policy, the EC2 might be blocked at the network level.

Tip: Use AWS IAM Policy Simulator to test permissions without making real API calls.

IAM role → s3:PutObjectbucket policy explicit Deny overridesKMS = needs kms permissions too
S152 AM page: total drop in incoming traffic to your main application. Walk through your incident response.▼
APPROACH
This tests your incident response process as much as your technical knowledge.

1. Acknowledge the alert — mark it in your incident tool (PagerDuty, etc.). Start a war room (Slack channel, call).

2. Establish blast radius — are ALL users affected or a subset? One region? One service?

3. Work from the outside in:
• DNS first: Did the domain expire? nslookup app.com — does it resolve? whois app.com — when does it expire?
• Load balancer / CDN: Is traffic hitting the edge? Check LB access logs and health checks in AWS CloudWatch.
• App layer: If traffic hits the LB but fails — check backend health. kubectl get pods or ECS service status.
• Database: Is RDS/database reachable? Failover triggered?

4. Communicate — update stakeholders every 15-30 minutes with status even if you have nothing new.
5. Fix, verify, post-mortem — after restoring service, schedule a blameless post-mortem. Never blame people.

acknowledge firstDNS → LB → app → DBcommunicate oftenblameless post-mortem
🌐 The "google.com" Question
S16What happens exactly when you type google.com into your browser and hit Enter?▼
APPROACH
This tests DNS, networking, HTTP, and server knowledge end-to-end.

1. Browser cache: Is google.com already cached from a recent visit?
2. DNS Resolution: Browser asks OS → OS checks /etc/hosts, then queries the local DNS resolver → resolver checks its cache → queries root nameservers → TLD nameservers (.com) → Google's authoritative nameserver → returns IP address (e.g., 142.250.80.46).
3. TCP Connection: Browser opens a TCP connection to port 443 (HTTPS) via a 3-way handshake (SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK).
4. TLS Handshake: Client and server negotiate encryption. Server sends its TLS certificate. Browser verifies it against a CA. Session keys are exchanged.
5. HTTP Request: Browser sends GET / HTTP/2 Host: www.google.com
6. Load Balancer: Request hits Google's edge load balancer, routes to a backend server.
7. Response: Server returns HTML. Browser parses it, finds CSS/JS/image references, and makes more requests for those resources.
8. Render: Browser constructs the DOM, applies CSS, runs JS, displays the page.

DNS → TCP → TLS → HTTP → LB → server → render
🐳 Docker Scenarios
S17Your Docker container exits immediately after starting. How do you debug it?▼
APPROACH
1. docker ps -a — lists all containers including exited ones. Check the STATUS column — see the exit code. Exit code 0 = clean exit. Exit code 1 = error. Exit code 137 = OOM killed (out of memory).

2. docker logs <container-id> — read the output the container produced before dying. This usually has the actual error.

3. docker inspect <container-id> — look at the State section. Check ExitCode, OOMKilled, Error.

Common causes:
• CMD/ENTRYPOINT error — process exits immediately if the startup command fails
• Missing environment variable — app crashes on start because DB_URL is not set
• Missing required file — app can't find config file that wasn't COPYed into image
• Port already in use — app can't bind to the port
• OOMKilled — container hit memory limit

docker ps -a → exit codedocker logs → actual errorexit 137 = OOM killed
S18Your Docker image is 3GB. A teammate asks how to reduce it. What do you suggest?▼
APPROACH
1. Use a smaller base image: Switch from node:18 (~350MB) to node:18-alpine (~50MB). Alpine Linux is minimal by design.

2. Multi-stage build: Build in a heavy image, copy only the compiled artifact into a minimal production image. Build tools (compilers, npm dev-deps) stay in the builder stage and are discarded.

3. Add .dockerignore: Exclude node_modules/, .git/, tests/, docs/, *.md from being COPYed into the image.

4. Combine RUN commands: Each RUN = a layer. RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* — install and clean up in one layer, not three.

5. Don't install dev dependencies in prod: npm install --omit=dev or pip install --no-dev.

alpine base = tinymulti-stage = only artifact.dockerignore = exclude junkcombine RUN layers
S19Two Docker containers need to communicate. Container A can't reach Container B. How do you debug?▼
APPROACH
1. Check if they're on the same network: docker network ls then docker inspect <network-name>. If containers are on different networks, they can't talk by default.

2. If using docker-compose: Services in the same docker-compose.yml are automatically on a shared network and can reach each other by service name (e.g., http://db:5432).

3. Manual network connection: docker network connect my-network container-b

4. Test from inside container A: docker exec -it container-a sh then ping container-b or curl http://container-b:3000. Use service/container name, not IP — IPs change on restart.

5. Check EXPOSE/port mapping: EXPOSE in Dockerfile just documents the port — it doesn't bind it. For external access use -p 3000:3000. Container-to-container on same network doesn't need -p.

same network = can communicateuse container name not IPexec inside to test curl
☸️ Kubernetes Scenarios
S20A pod is in Pending state and never starts. How do you debug it?▼
APPROACH
Pending means the Scheduler cannot find a suitable node to place the pod.

1. kubectl describe pod <name> → read the Events section. It will say exactly why it's pending.

Common causes:
• "Insufficient CPU/memory" — the pod's resource request exceeds available capacity on all nodes. Fix: reduce requests, add nodes, or reduce other pod limits.
• "No nodes matching nodeSelector/affinity" — pod has a label constraint that no node satisfies. Fix: check your nodeSelector.
• "Unschedulable" — node is tainted and pod has no matching toleration. Fix: add toleration or remove taint.
• "PVC not bound" — pod needs a Persistent Volume Claim that hasn't been fulfilled. Fix: check kubectl get pvc.

2. kubectl get nodes — are all nodes Ready? A NotReady node won't accept pods.

Pending = Scheduler can't place poddescribe pod → Events sectioncheck resources, taints, PVC
S21Your Kubernetes cluster is running out of resources. Pods keep failing to schedule. What do you do?▼
APPROACH
1. Verify the problem: kubectl top nodes — which nodes are at capacity? kubectl describe nodes — look for "Allocatable" vs "Requests" section.

2. Find resource hogs: kubectl top pods --all-namespaces --sort-by=memory — which pods are consuming the most?

3. Right-size pod requests: Are pods requesting 4GB but only using 200MB? Over-requesting waste cluster capacity. Reduce requests to match actual usage.

4. Add nodes:
• AWS EKS: add to the Auto Scaling Group (manually or via cluster-autoscaler)
• kubectl scale won't help — that scales pods, not nodes

5. Enable Cluster Autoscaler: Watches for unschedulable pods and automatically provisions new EC2 instances. Scales down when nodes are underutilized.

6. Evict idle pods: Check for pods in namespaces you might have forgotten to clean up.

kubectl top nodesreduce over-requestingcluster-autoscaler for auto-scale
S22You deployed a new version and users are getting errors. How do you roll back in Kubernetes?▼
APPROACH
Immediate rollback (do this first):
kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp — rolls back to the previous version immediately. Kubernetes keeps the last 10 revision history by default.

Roll back to a specific version:
kubectl rollout history deployment/myapp — list all revisions
kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp --to-revision=3 — go to specific revision

Watch the rollback:
kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp — watch pods come up
kubectl get pods -w — watch pods update in real time

After stabilizing: Check what went wrong. Was it the code? A bad environment variable? A database migration that can't be reversed? Fix the issue before pushing v3.0.

kubectl rollout undo = instant rollback--to-revision for specific versionfix root cause before next deploy
S23A pod is OOMKilled repeatedly. What does it mean and how do you fix it?▼
APPROACH
OOMKilled = Out Of Memory Killed. The container exceeded its memory limit and was forcibly terminated by the Linux kernel (OOM killer). The pod will restart, hit the limit again, get killed again — CrashLoopBackOff.

Verify: kubectl describe pod <name> → look for OOMKilled: true in the State section.

Investigate:
• kubectl top pods — what was the actual memory usage before it was killed?
• Check application code — is there a memory leak? Does memory grow over time or spike suddenly?

Fix options:
• Short term: Increase the memory limit in the pod spec. limits.memory: "1Gi" instead of "512Mi".
• Long term: Fix the memory leak. Profile the app, find what's growing, and fix it in code.

OOMKilled = exceeded memory limitdescribe pod → OOMKilled: trueincrease limit short-term, fix leak long-term
☁️ AWS / Cloud Scenarios
S24A developer accidentally pushed API keys to a public GitHub repo. What do you do immediately?▼
APPROACH
Assume the secret is already compromised — bots scan GitHub 24/7 and pick up leaked secrets within seconds. Deleting the commit is NOT enough — the history exists and the key is already stolen.

Immediate actions (do in parallel):
1. Revoke the key IMMEDIATELY — go to AWS Console → IAM → Access Keys → Deactivate/Delete the compromised key. This is the most critical step. Do it before anything else.

2. Rotate all affected credentials — create a new key for the service that needed it. Update all places that were using the old key.

3. Check for unauthorized activity — AWS CloudTrail will show what API calls were made with the leaked key. Look for unusual regions, services, or large data exfil.

4. Make the GitHub repo private (if not already) and use git filter-branch or BFG Repo Cleaner to remove the secret from history (prevents future accidental exposure).

5. Post-mortem + Prevention — add .env to .gitignore. Use GitHub's secret scanning. Add pre-commit hooks to detect secrets before commit (tools: git-secrets, truffleHog).

revoke key FIRSTcheck CloudTrail for damagerotate credentialsprevent with pre-commit hooks
S25An EC2 instance can't connect to your RDS database. Walk through your debug steps.▼
APPROACH
Work through the layers systematically:

1. Is RDS actually running? AWS Console → RDS → check Status. Is it Available? If Stopped, start it. If Failing Over, wait.

2. Network connectivity: From the EC2, try nc -zv <rds-endpoint> 5432. Connection Refused or Timeout?

3. Security Group check (most common cause):
• RDS Security Group must allow port 5432 from the EC2's Security Group ID (not its IP — IPs change)
• EC2 Security Group must allow outbound to RDS

4. Subnet/VPC check: Are EC2 and RDS in the same VPC? If RDS is in a different VPC, you need VPC peering. Is RDS in a private subnet that has no route to EC2?

5. Check RDS endpoint and port: Is the connection string using the correct endpoint, port, DB name, username, password?

6. Check RDS parameter group: Is the DB accepting connections on the expected port?

Security Group = most common causereference SG ID not IPnc -zv to test port
S26Your Terraform state file is corrupted or locked. How do you handle it?▼
APPROACH
State file locked (most common): A previous terraform apply crashed and left a lock in DynamoDB. Terraform says "Error acquiring the state lock."
Fix: terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID> (the lock ID is shown in the error message). Only do this if you're certain no other apply is running.

State file corrupted:
1. First, DON'T panic and run terraform apply — you could make things worse.
2. Restore from backup — S3 has versioning enabled on your state bucket (it should). Go to S3, find the last good version, restore it.
3. If no backup: terraform import to rebuild state by importing existing resources one by one.

Prevention: Always use remote state (S3 + DynamoDB). Enable S3 versioning. Enable state encryption. Never manually edit the .tfstate file.

force-unlock if stuck lockS3 versioning = restore backupnever edit tfstate manually
S27Your ALB health checks are failing and all instances are being removed from rotation. What do you check?▼
APPROACH
ALB health checks periodically hit a specific endpoint (e.g., /health) on your instances. If it doesn't get 200 OK within the timeout, it marks the instance unhealthy.

1. What's the health check configured for? Go to ALB → Target Group → Health Check settings. Note the path, port, protocol, success codes, timeout, and threshold.

2. Test the health check endpoint manually: SSH into an EC2 instance. curl -v http://localhost:<health-check-port>/health. Does it return 200? What does it return?

3. Common causes:
• Health check path wrong — app has /healthz but ALB checks /health
• Wrong port — ALB checking port 80, app on port 3000
• App is starting slowly — health check fires before app is ready. Fix: increase HealthyThresholdCount or initial delay.
• Security Group — does the Security Group allow the ALB to reach the health check port on the instances?
• App genuinely broken — the app is actually returning 500, which is the real problem to fix.

curl localhost to test manuallycheck path + port configSG must allow ALB to instances
S28Your RDS database CPU is at 100%. How do you diagnose and respond?▼
APPROACH
Immediate (stop the bleeding):
1. AWS Console → RDS → Enhanced Monitoring or Performance Insights — see which queries are consuming the CPU.
2. Identify and kill the most expensive query: connect to the DB and run SELECT * FROM pg_stat_activity ORDER BY duration DESC; (Postgres). Kill with SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid);.

Diagnose root cause:
• Missing index: A query is doing a full table scan. Check with EXPLAIN ANALYZE. Add an index on the column being filtered.
• Sudden traffic spike: More connections = more queries. Scale up the instance type or add a read replica for read-heavy workloads.
• N+1 query problem: App code making hundreds of queries in a loop where one query would do.
• Runaway scheduled job: A background job launched a massive query.

Longer term: Enable slow query log, add connection pooling (PgBouncer), add read replicas for read traffic, cache frequently-read data in Redis/ElastiCache.

Performance Insights = identify queriesEXPLAIN ANALYZE = find missing indexesread replica for read scaling
S29Your CI/CD pipeline is deploying but the new code isn't reflecting in production. You've already ruled out browser cache. What next?▼
APPROACH
This is a "deployment succeeded but nothing changed" problem. Work through the delivery chain:

1. Was the right image built? Check the CI logs — did the Docker build actually pick up your latest code? Or did it use a cached layer that skipped your changes?

2. Was the new image pushed? Check ECR/Docker Hub — is there a new image tag with today's timestamp?

3. Was the deployment actually updated?
• Kubernetes: kubectl describe deployment myapp — what image tag is it using? Did the deployment get the new image tag or the same old one?
• Common mistake: always pushing to :latest tag. If the tag doesn't change, Kubernetes thinks it's the same image and won't pull a new one. Use a unique tag per build (commit hash or version number).

4. Force re-pull: kubectl rollout restart deployment/myapp — forces all pods to restart and pull the latest image.

5. CDN invalidation: Even for backend APIs, if there's a WAF or CDN in front, cached responses might be stale.

check CI logs for correct imagenever use :latest in K8srollout restart to force re-pull
S30You need to investigate an EC2 instance but port 22 is closed and you can't SSH. How do you get in?▼
APPROACH
Port 22 being closed is actually a good security practice. There are proper alternatives:

Option 1 — AWS Systems Manager Session Manager (best practice):
AWS Console → EC2 → Select instance → Connect → Session Manager. Opens a browser-based terminal session. No port 22 needed, no inbound security group rules, full audit log in CloudTrail. Requires SSM agent on instance (pre-installed on Amazon Linux 2+) and correct IAM role.

Option 2 — EC2 Instance Connect:
AWS Console → EC2 → Connect → EC2 Instance Connect. AWS pushes a temporary SSH key. Still requires port 22 but only from AWS IP ranges (not 0.0.0.0/0).

Option 3 — Bastion Host:
SSH into a bastion/jump host in the public subnet (which has port 22 open but restricted to your IP), then SSH from there to the private EC2.

Option 4 — EC2 Serial Console:
For instances that won't boot or are completely unreachable. Low-level access via AWS Console.

SSM Session Manager = best practiceno port 22 neededfull audit log
S31Your application suddenly starts throwing "too many open files" errors on Linux. What's happening?▼
APPROACH
Linux limits the number of file descriptors a process can have open simultaneously (files, network connections, sockets all count). When the limit is hit, the process can't open new connections or files.

1. Check current limits:
ulimit -n — shows current per-process limit (often 1024 by default)
cat /proc/<PID>/limits — limits for a specific process

2. Check actual usage:
lsof -p <PID> | wc -l — how many files/connections the process has open

3. Fix temporary:
ulimit -n 65536 — increase limit for current session

4. Fix permanent:
Edit /etc/security/limits.conf — add * soft nofile 65536 and * hard nofile 65536

Root cause: Usually a connection leak — app opens connections (DB, HTTP) but never closes them. Fix the leak in code; increasing limits is a bandaid.

ulimit -n = file descriptor limitlsof -p = what process has openfix the connection leak, not just the limit

📖

→
💡
