Was a new database migration part of this deploy? Did it add an unindexed column that a frequent query now uses? Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on slow queries. Check DB slow query log.

3. Check external dependencies:
Did the new code add calls to an external API? Is that API slow? Check connection pool settings.

4. Check resource saturation:
kubectl top pods — is the new code CPU/memory heavy? Is it hitting limits and being throttled?

5. Compare the diff:
git diff v1.0..v2.0 — what changed? Look for new database queries, removed caching, synchronous operations that were async, N+1 query bugs.

If urgent: rollback first, investigate in staging.

correlate timing with deploycheck DB slow queries + missing indexkubectl top for throttlinggit diff the changes
SC06An S3 bucket was accidentally made public. What is your incident response?▼
ANSWER
1. Block public access immediately:
S3 Console → Block Public Access settings → enable all four blocks. This is instant. Takes <1 minute.

2. Determine what was exposed:
S3 Server Access Logs or AWS CloudTrail Data Events → who accessed what files and when? Any GetObject requests from external IPs? What data was in that bucket?

3. Assess the data sensitivity:
PII, credentials, internal configs, customer data? Escalate accordingly. If PII was exposed, legal/compliance team must be notified (GDPR, etc.).

4. Rotate exposed secrets:
If any credentials, API keys, or tokens were in the bucket — rotate them all immediately.

5. Root cause and prevention:
Who made it public and how? Was it Terraform config? A console click? Enable AWS Config rule: s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited — alerts immediately when any S3 bucket is made public.

block public access firstcheck CloudTrail for accessrotate any exposed secretsAWS Config rule to prevent recurrence
SC07Your CI pipeline takes 45 minutes. How do you reduce it to under 10?▼
ANSWER
Profile first — find the bottleneck: Which step takes longest? Tests? Docker build? Lint? You can't optimize what you can't measure.

1. Parallelize jobs:
Run unit tests, lint, and security scan in parallel (separate jobs in GitHub Actions). Don't wait for lint to finish before starting tests.

2. Fix Docker layer caching:
Move COPY package.json and RUN npm install BEFORE COPY . .. If your source code changes but deps don't, the install layer is cached — saves 5-10 min.

3. Cache dependencies in CI:
GitHub Actions: actions/cache@v3 for node_modules, pip cache, Maven .m2. Avoid re-downloading on every run.

4. Split test suites:
Run unit tests in CI on every push. Run integration/e2e tests only on PRs to main. Don't run 5000 unit tests on every commit.

5. Use faster runners:
Larger GitHub Actions runners (4 CPU vs 2 CPU) for compute-heavy steps. Self-hosted runners close to your registries.

6. Fail fast:
Run the fastest checks (lint, type-check) first. Fail early before expensive steps.

profile firstparallelize jobsfix Docker layer cache ordercache dependencies
SC08All Kubernetes nodes are NotReady. What happened and how do you recover?▼
ANSWER
NotReady = Kubelet on the worker node has stopped communicating with the Control Plane, or the node itself is down.

1. Check node status:
kubectl get nodes → all NotReady.
kubectl describe node <name> → conditions section shows why (DiskPressure, MemoryPressure, NetworkUnavailable, KubeletNotReady).

2. SSH into a worker node and check:
systemctl status kubelet — is Kubelet running? If crashed: journalctl -u kubelet -f for error logs.
Common causes: disk full (df -h), node OOM, kubelet config error after upgrade.

3. Check the network:
Can nodes reach the API Server? Is the CNI plugin (Calico, Cilium) healthy? kubectl get pods -n kube-system — are networking pods crashing?

4. Cloud provider check:
Are the EC2 instances actually running? Check AWS console. Did an ASG policy terminate them all? Is there a cloud region incident?

5. Recovery:
Restart kubelet: systemctl restart kubelet. If disk full, clean up logs. If all else fails, replace the nodes via ASG.

describe node = conditionssystemctl status kubeletcheck disk full + CNIcheck cloud instance health
SC09You need to roll back a Kubernetes deployment that included a database migration. What's the problem and how do you handle it?▼
ANSWER
This is one of the most important DevOps topics and most candidates miss the nuance.

The problem: kubectl rollout undo rolls back the application code to v1.0. But the database migration already ran and added/modified schema. v1.0 code may not be compatible with the new schema — it might crash, produce errors, or corrupt data.

Best practice — write backwards-compatible migrations:
• Never drop a column in the same release that stops using it. First release: add new column, code uses both old + new. Second release: migrate data. Third release: remove old column.
• This allows safe rollback at any point — v1.0 code still works with the new schema because the old column still exists.

If you're already in trouble:
• Roll back the app first to stop user impact.
• Write a down migration (reverses the schema change) and run it manually.
• Ensure no data was migrated that would be lost by the rollback.

backward-compatible migrationsnever drop column in same releaseapp rollback ≠ DB rollback
SC10Your database is running out of connections under load. What do you investigate?▼
ANSWER
1. Confirm the error:
App logs: "too many connections" or "connection pool exhausted." DB metric: active connections approaching max_connections.

2. Check connection pool configuration:
Every app instance opens a pool of connections. If you have 20 pods × 50 pool size = 1000 connections. Does your DB support that? RDS Postgres default max_connections is often 100 for small instances.

3. Solutions:
• PgBouncer / RDS Proxy — connection poolers that sit between your app and DB. Many app connections → few real DB connections. 1000 app connections → 100 actual DB connections. This is the right fix at scale.
• Reduce pool size per pod — if you have many pods, reduce pool size so total connections fit within DB limits.
• Increase DB max_connections — temporary fix. Each connection uses RAM, so this has limits.

4. Find connection leaks:
Are connections being released after use? Check for code that opens connections but doesn't close them on error paths.

pods × pool size = total connectionsPgBouncer/RDS Proxy = multiplexingcheck for connection leaks
SC11A Kubernetes CronJob hasn't run in 3 days. How do you debug it?▼
ANSWER
1. Check the CronJob itself:
kubectl describe cronjob <name> — look at "Last Schedule Time" and "Active" count. Any events showing failures?

2. Check if Jobs were created:
kubectl get jobs — was a Job object created? If not, the schedule expression might be wrong. Verify the cron expression at crontab.guru.

3. Check missed deadline:
CronJob has a startingDeadlineSeconds field. If the cluster was down during the scheduled time and this window passed, K8s considers the job "missed" and won't run it retroactively.

4. Check failed Jobs:
kubectl get jobs --field-selector status.successful=0 — any failed jobs from recent runs? Check pod logs of the failed job.

5. concurrencyPolicy:
If set to Forbid and a previous run is still running → new runs are skipped. Check for stuck running jobs.

kubectl describe cronjobverify cron expressioncheck concurrencyPolicystartingDeadlineSeconds
SC12A new engineer accidentally ran `terraform destroy` in production. What's your recovery plan?▼
ANSWER
Don't panic. Act fast.

Immediate:
1. How much was destroyed? Run terraform plan to see what's missing vs what's in the state file.
2. Is there a Terraform workspace or state backup? S3 versioning on the state bucket → restore previous state version from S3.

Recovery:
1. terraform apply — recreates all resources defined in your .tf files. Terraform's declarative nature means this should reconstruct the infrastructure.
2. Databases: check AWS RDS automated backups (retention period). Restore from the latest snapshot. This is why you enable automated backups and test restores.
3. Restore DNS: if Route 53 records were destroyed, update them.

Prevention (what you implement after):
• Enable lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } on critical resources in Terraform.
• Require two-person approval for production applies (Atlantis with required approvers).
• Lock down terraform destroy in CI — never in automated pipelines, human-only.
• Enable AWS Delete Protection on RDS, ELB.

restore state from S3 versioningterraform apply recreatesrestore DB from snapshotprevent_destroy lifecycle rule
SC13Your application is deployed but the Kubernetes Service is returning "No endpoints available". Why?▼
ANSWER
"No endpoints" = the Service exists but has no pods backing it. The Service selector doesn't match any healthy pod labels.

1. Check the endpoints object:
kubectl get endpoints <service-name> — if it shows <none>, no pods are selected.

2. Check the Service selector vs Pod labels:
kubectl describe service <name> → look at "Selector" field (e.g., app=myapp)
kubectl get pods --show-labels → do any pods have that exact label?
Typo in the label or selector = no match = no endpoints. This is the most common cause.

3. Check pod readiness:
Even if labels match, pods must be Ready to receive traffic. If readinessProbe is failing, pods are excluded from endpoints even though they're running.
kubectl get pods → check the READY column (1/1 vs 0/1).

4. Check namespace:
Is the Service in the same namespace as the pods? By default, Services only select pods in the same namespace.

kubectl get endpoints = empty?selector label mismatchreadinessProbe failingsame namespace?
SC14You're asked to migrate a monolith to microservices on Kubernetes. How do you approach it?▼
ANSWER
This is a Strangler Fig migration — don't rewrite everything at once. Extract services gradually while the monolith still runs.

Phase 1 — Containerize the monolith first:
Before splitting anything, package the monolith in Docker and deploy to Kubernetes. This teaches your team K8s without the added complexity of microservices.

Phase 2 — Identify seams:
Find the parts of the monolith that are independently deployable: auth service, payment service, notification service. Start with the one that changes most frequently or causes the most pain.

Phase 3 — Extract one service at a time:
• Extract the service → deploy as a separate K8s Deployment.
• Route traffic to the new service via the Ingress (e.g., /api/payments → payment service).
• Keep the monolith running — both the monolith's payment code and the new service exist during transition.
• Once confident, disable the monolith's payment code.

Phase 4 — Data separation:
Each microservice should own its data — separate DB schemas or separate RDS instances.

Strangler Fig patterncontainerize monolith firstextract one service at a timeeach service owns its data
SC15You've been asked to set up a DevOps pipeline for a brand new project from scratch. Walk through everything you'd build.▼
ANSWER
The answer that shows you understand the full picture:

1. Source Control: GitHub repo, branch protection on main (require PR + CI pass to merge), .gitignore, conventional commits enforced via commit-msg hook.

2. CI Pipeline (GitHub Actions):
On every push: lint → unit tests → build Docker image → push to ECR.
On PR: additionally run integration tests + security scan (Trivy, Snyk).

3. Infrastructure (Terraform):
VPC + subnets + security groups + EKS cluster + RDS in private subnet + ALB. Remote state in S3 + DynamoDB lock. Separate workspaces for dev/staging/prod.

4. CD (GitHub Actions + kubectl/Helm):
On merge to main → deploy to staging automatically. Manual approval gate → deploy to production. Kubernetes rolling update, zero downtime.

5. Secrets: GitHub Actions secrets for CI. AWS Secrets Manager for production app secrets. Never hardcoded.

6. Monitoring: Prometheus + Grafana for metrics. CloudWatch for AWS infra. Alertmanager → PagerDuty. Liveness + readiness probes on all pods.

7. Documentation: Runbook for on-call. README with setup instructions. Architecture diagram.

Git → CI → IaC → CD → Secrets → Monitor → Docs
🏆 Final Exam — The Hardest Questions
These are the questions that separate junior from mid/senior DevOps engineers. Read every answer. Own every concept.
🔥 Deep Design Questions
FE01Design a zero-downtime database migration strategy for a production app with millions of users.▼
ANSWER
This tests understanding of backward compatibility, deployment sequencing, and rollback safety.

The core problem: You can't take the DB offline. You can't deploy app + DB migration simultaneously — the old app will hit new schema during rollout, and the new app will hit old schema before migration completes.

The Expand-Contract Pattern (3 phases):

Phase 1 — Expand (backward compatible change):
Add the new column/table as nullable. Deploy nothing yet. Existing app still works with old schema. Run the migration to add the column.

Phase 2 — Migrate (dual-write or backfill):
Deploy new version of app that writes to BOTH old and new columns. Backfill existing rows with a background job. Once backfill completes and new column has all data, both versions of the app work.

Phase 3 — Contract (remove old column):
Deploy app version that only reads/writes new column. Then drop the old column in a separate migration.

Key rule: Never deploy a breaking schema change and application change simultaneously. Always make schema changes backward compatible first.

expand → migrate → contractbackward compatible firstnever simultaneous app + schema deploy
FE02How do you secure a Kubernetes cluster end-to-end? Walk through every layer.▼
ANSWER
Layer 1 — API Server access:
Disable anonymous authentication. Use RBAC — no wildcard permissions. Audit logging on. Never expose the API server to the internet — use a bastion or VPN.

Layer 2 — Node security:
Workers in private subnets. Security groups block all but necessary ports. OS hardened. Automated patch management via managed node groups (EKS handles this).

Layer 3 — Pod security:
Run containers as non-root (runAsNonRoot: true). Read-only root filesystem. Drop all Linux capabilities, add back only what's needed. Pod Security Admission enforces these standards.

Layer 4 — Network security:
NetworkPolicies — by default all pods can talk to all pods. Apply least-privilege NetworkPolicies: payment service can only talk to DB, not to the logging service.

Layer 5 — Secrets:
Never store real secrets in K8s Secrets unencrypted. Use Sealed Secrets or External Secrets Operator (sync from AWS Secrets Manager). Encrypt etcd at rest.

Layer 6 — Images:
Only pull from trusted registries. Scan images for CVEs in CI (Trivy, Snyk). Use image digest pinning instead of mutable tags (:latest is dangerous).

Layer 7 — Audit + Monitoring:
K8s audit logs → Cloudwatch/SIEM. Runtime threat detection (Falco watches for suspicious syscalls). Alert on privilege escalation attempts.

RBAC + no wildcardsnon-root podsNetworkPoliciesencrypted secretsimage scanning
FE03Design a disaster recovery plan for a multi-region AWS application with an RTO of 1 hour and RPO of 5 minutes.▼
ANSWER
RTO (Recovery Time Objective) = how long can you be down? 1 hour max.
RPO (Recovery Point Objective) = how much data can you lose? 5 minutes max.

Data strategy (RPO = 5 mins):
RDS Multi-AZ for same-region HA (synchronous replication, ~0 RPO). Cross-region: enable RDS Read Replica in us-west-2 with async replication (lag ~1-3 mins, meets 5 min RPO). For S3: enable Cross-Region Replication with versioning.

Compute strategy (RTO = 1 hour):
Run a "warm standby" in the secondary region — ECS/EKS cluster at minimum capacity (1 pod per service). Can scale up in ~10 minutes. Keep AMIs replicated cross-region for fast EC2 launch.

Networking:
Route 53 health checks on primary region. Failover routing policy: if primary health check fails, Route 53 automatically routes traffic to secondary region's ALB. DNS TTL set to 60 seconds so failover propagates in ~1 min.

Runbook automation:
Pre-written runbook (ideally automated with AWS Systems Manager). Promotes RDS read replica to primary. Scales up secondary compute. Updates any hardcoded endpoints. Target: RTO under 15 minutes in practice.

Regular DR drills:
Test the failover quarterly. "Game days" — actually fail over to secondary. A DR plan never tested is not a DR plan.

RDS cross-region replica (5 min lag)warm standby computeRoute 53 health check + failoverdrill quarterly
FE04Your microservices system has 50 services. Deploys have become slow and risky. How do you redesign the CI/CD architecture?▼
ANSWER
Problem analysis: With 50 services, a monorepo pipeline that rebuilds everything on every commit is catastrophic. A polyrepo without shared standards leads to 50 different pipeline configs.

Solution: Service-specific pipelines with shared templates:

1. Affected-only builds: Only build and deploy services whose code actually changed. Use tools like Nx, Turborepo (monorepo) or trigger detection scripts that check which directories changed via git diff.

2. Pipeline templates: Create reusable GitHub Actions workflow templates / Jenkins shared libraries. Every service uses the same tested template. Change the template once, all services get it.

3. GitOps for deployments: Separate application code repos from deployment config repos. CI writes the new image tag to the deployment repo. ArgoCD picks it up and syncs. Rollback = revert a Git commit.

4. Parallel execution: Independent services build and test in parallel. Only sequential steps are: test → build image → deploy to staging → integration test → deploy to prod.

5. Contract testing: Instead of expensive full integration tests, use consumer-driven contract tests (Pact). Each service tests its interface contracts independently — no full stack needed.

6. Progressive delivery: All production deploys via canary (5% → 25% → 100%). Automated rollback if error rate spikes. Operators monitor, not babysit.

affected-only buildsshared pipeline templatesGitOps for deploycanary everywhere
FE05How would you migrate a legacy monolith from bare-metal servers to AWS with zero downtime?▼
ANSWER
Phase 1 — Lift and Shift (0 risk):
Mirror the monolith to EC2 first. Don't refactor yet. Use AWS Server Migration Service or manually replicate. Set up the same environment. Validate it works identically.

Phase 2 — Database migration:
Use AWS DMS (Database Migration Service) to continuously sync the on-premise DB to RDS with CDC (Change Data Capture) replication running live. Zero data loss.

Phase 3 — Traffic shifting:
Both environments running simultaneously. Use weighted DNS (Route 53) to shift 5% → 25% → 50% → 100% of traffic to AWS. Monitor error rates at each step. Rollback = flip DNS weight back.

Phase 4 — Cutover:
Once 100% traffic on AWS, freeze on-premise writes, run final DB sync, promote RDS as primary. Decommission on-premise.

Phase 5 — Containerize (optional, later):
Once stable on AWS, containerize into Docker/ECS. Then, if needed, break apart into microservices (Strangler Fig pattern).

Key principle: Lift and shift first. Optimize after. Never try to refactor AND migrate at the same time — too risky.

lift and shift firstDMS for live DB syncweighted DNS cutovercontainerize after
🔥 More Scenario Questions
FE06A Kubernetes pod is stuck in "Pending" state for 20 minutes. Walk through every possible cause.▼
ANSWER
Pending = the pod has been accepted by K8s but no node has been assigned yet. The Scheduler couldn't place it.

Run first: kubectl describe pod <name> — read the Events. The answer is almost always in there.

Cause 1 — Insufficient resources: Pod requests 4 CPU but no node has 4 free CPUs. Events say "Insufficient cpu" or "Insufficient memory". Fix: scale up the node group or reduce resource requests.

Cause 2 — No matching node (NodeSelector/Affinity): Pod has a nodeSelector requiring type: gpu but no GPU nodes exist. Fix: add the right nodes or remove the constraint.

Cause 3 — Taints and Tolerations: All nodes have taints the pod doesn't tolerate. Fix: add tolerations to the pod spec.

Cause 4 — PVC not bound: Pod requires a PersistentVolumeClaim that hasn't been provisioned yet or the StorageClass can't provision in this AZ. Events say "waiting for volume to be created". Fix: check PVC status with kubectl get pvc.

Cause 5 — Image pull limit (indirect): Sometimes indirectly — if init containers are failing during scheduling evaluation.

Cause 6 — Cluster autoscaler delay: Node group needs to scale up to accommodate the pod. Check if a new node is being provisioned with kubectl get nodes.

describe pod = look at Eventsinsufficient resourcesnodeSelector mismatchPVC not bound
FE07Your Docker image is 2.4GB. The team wants it under 100MB. How do you do it?▼
ANSWER
Step 1 — Diagnose first: docker image history myapp:latest — see which layers are large. dive myapp:latest (tool) for interactive layer inspection.

Step 2 — Switch to Alpine or Distroless base:
FROM node:18 = ~950MB. FROM node:18-alpine = ~170MB. FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs18 = ~100MB. This alone often cuts 80%.

Step 3 — Multi-stage build:
Build in a full image (with compilers, dev dependencies). Copy only the final compiled artifact to a minimal runtime image. The build tools never end up in production.

Step 4 — .dockerignore:
Add node_modules/, .git/, tests/, *.md, coverage/. These shouldn't be COPY'd into the image.

Step 5 — Combine RUN commands:
Each RUN is a layer. Combine: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*. Cleaning up in the same layer prevents the garbage from persisting.

Step 6 — Don't install dev dependencies:
npm install --production or npm ci --only=production. Dev packages can be 10x the size of prod packages.

dive to inspect layersalpine/distroless basemulti-stage build.dockerignorecombine RUN commands
FE08You run `terraform apply` and it destroys a production database. It wasn't supposed to. Why did this happen and how do you prevent it?▼
ANSWER
Why it happened — common causes:

1. Resource rename: Someone renamed the Terraform resource block (e.g., resource "aws_db_instance" "db" → resource "aws_db_instance" "prod_db"). Terraform sees the old one as deleted and new one as created. Result: destroy + create.

2. Force-replace flag: Someone ran terraform apply -replace=aws_db_instance.db.

3. Changed an immutable attribute: Some AWS resource attributes can't be updated in-place (e.g., changing RDS engine version). Terraform destroys and recreates.

Prevention — multiple layers:

lifecycle prevent_destroy:
resource "aws_db_instance" "prod_db" {
  lifecycle {
    prevent_destroy = true
  }
}
Terraform will refuse to destroy this resource. Any plan attempting to destroy it will fail.

Require plan review: Never run terraform apply directly in prod. CI/CD pipeline generates a plan, posts it as PR comment, requires human approval before applying.

terraform state mv: If you need to rename a resource, use terraform state mv old_name new_name to rename it in the state file without destroying it.

Separate state per environment: Prod infra in a completely separate state file and workspace. Mistakes in dev don't affect prod.

prevent_destroy lifecycleplan before applyterraform state mv for renamesseparate state per env
FE09Your AWS bill doubled this month with no new features shipped. How do you investigate?▼
ANSWER
1. AWS Cost Explorer: Filter by service. Which service increased most? Filter by resource tag to find the specific resource.

2. Common culprits to check:
• NAT Gateway: Often a hidden cost driver. Every GB processed costs money. Check if something is routing unnecessary traffic through NAT (e.g., EC2 downloading S3 data via NAT instead of VPC endpoint).
• Data transfer: Cross-AZ or cross-region data transfer adds up. Are services unnecessarily talking across AZs?
• EC2 instances left running: Someone spun up large instances for testing and forgot. Check for untagged resources.
• CloudWatch Logs: An app logging verbosely — millions of log events per day. Check log ingestion costs.
• RDS storage: RDS auto-storage-scaling kicked in, can't scale back down.
• Snapshot/backup accumulation: Old AMI snapshots or DB snapshots accumulating for months.

3. AWS Cost Anomaly Detection: Enable this — it uses ML to detect unusual spending patterns and alerts you before the bill arrives.

4. Tagging enforcement: Every resource should have Environment, Owner, Project tags. Without tags, you can't trace which team/service caused the cost.

Cost Explorer by serviceNAT Gateway = hidden costcheck untagged resourcesCost Anomaly Detection
FE10Explain how you would implement a GitOps workflow for Kubernetes from scratch.▼
ANSWER
The components you need:

1. Two Git repos:
• App repo: source code, Dockerfile, tests
• Config repo: Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts, Kustomize overlays per environment

2. CI pipeline (in app repo):
On merge to main: run tests → build Docker image → push to ECR with commit SHA as tag → update the image tag in the config repo (automated PR or direct commit to a branch)

3. ArgoCD (in the cluster):
Install ArgoCD. Create an Application resource pointing at your config repo + path + target namespace. ArgoCD continuously polls the config repo. When image tag changes, ArgoCD syncs the cluster to the new state.

4. Environment promotion:
Config repo has envs/staging/ and envs/production/ directories. CI auto-updates staging. Promotion to prod = merge PR that updates prod's image tag. ArgoCD detects and deploys.

5. Rollback:
git revert the tag update commit in the config repo. ArgoCD detects and rolls the cluster back. No kubectl needed in production.

Security benefit: No CI/CD system needs write access to the cluster. The cluster pulls from Git. Much smaller attack surface.

app repo + config repo separateCI updates config repo image tagArgoCD polls + syncsrollback = git revert
FE11How would you debug a memory leak in a Dockerized production application?▼
ANSWER
Step 1 — Confirm it's a leak:
kubectl top pods or docker stats — watch memory over time. Does it grow continuously and never come down? That's a leak. Does it grow and then GC kicks in and it drops? That's normal.

Step 2 — Confirm via container restarts:
kubectl get pods — high RESTARTS count + OOMKilled in describe = memory is hitting the container limit. Immediate evidence of a leak.

Step 3 — Correlate with traffic:
Does memory grow proportionally with requests? Might be a connection or object that's not being properly released per request.

Step 4 — Language-specific profiling:
• Node.js: --inspect flag → Chrome DevTools heap snapshots
• Java: JVM heap dumps (jmap -dump) → VisualVM or Eclipse MAT
• Python: tracemalloc, objgraph

Step 5 — Short-term mitigation:
Set memory limits and enable automatic pod restarts. HPA or scheduled restart as a bandage while you fix the root cause. Communicate to the team — don't silently paper over it.

Step 6 — Fix and verify:
Deploy fix, run extended load test, verify memory stays flat over time. Only then close the ticket.

kubectl top pods = memory over timeOOMKilled = hitting limitheap dump for root causememory limits = short-term mitigation
FE12Production is getting DDoS'd. Traffic is 50x normal. Walk through your response.▼
ANSWER
Immediate (first 5 minutes):
Check CloudWatch — is this real user traffic or attack traffic? Look at request patterns: same IP? Same User-Agent? Same endpoint being hammered? Bots usually have patterns.

Layer 1 — AWS Shield:
AWS Shield Standard is already on by default — protects against L3/L4 DDoS. If attacks are sophisticated, AWS Shield Advanced (paid) adds 24/7 DRT (DDoS Response Team) support and cost protection.

Layer 2 — AWS WAF (Web Application Firewall):
Attach WAF to CloudFront or ALB. Create rate-based rules: block IPs sending more than 1000 req/5min. Create geo-blocking rules if traffic is from unexpected countries. Enable AWS managed rule groups (bot protection).

Layer 3 — CloudFront:
If not already in front of your app, enable CloudFront. Acts as a buffer — absorbs traffic at the edge, not at your origin. Enable cache for static content (takes load off origin).

Layer 4 — Auto Scaling:
If legitimate traffic is also spiking (viral event), ensure ASG and HPA are configured to scale fast enough. ALB spreads the load.

Layer 5 — Rate limiting at application level:
API gateway rate limiting per IP. Nginx limit_req_zone.

After the attack:
Review WAF logs to understand the attack pattern. Tune rules. Add Cloudflare or AWS Shield Advanced if appropriate. Post-mortem.

WAF rate-based rulesCloudFront as DDoS bufferAWS Shield Standard = free baselinegeo-blocking for bot traffic
FE13How do you handle configuration management across 4 environments (dev/staging/uat/prod) without duplicating Terraform code?▼
ANSWER
The problem: If you copy-paste your Terraform for each environment, you have 4x maintenance burden and they drift apart.

Solution 1 — Terraform Workspaces:
Same code, different state files. terraform workspace new staging creates an isolated state. Use terraform.workspace variable to vary config per environment.
Downside: all environments share the same code — risky if environments need very different configurations.

Solution 2 — Terraform Modules + Separate Variable Files (recommended):
Write reusable modules (e.g., module "vpc", module "ecs_service"). Each environment has its own directory with a main.tf that calls the modules and a terraform.tfvars with environment-specific values.
envs/
  prod/main.tf     # calls modules, uses prod.tfvars
  staging/main.tf  # calls same modules, uses staging.tfvars
modules/
  vpc/
  ecs_service/
Solution 3 — Terragrunt:
DRY wrapper for Terraform. Define common config once, inherit and override per environment. Manages remote state config automatically.

modules = reusable codetfvars per environmentseparate state per envTerragrunt for DRY
FE14You need to run a one-time data migration job in Kubernetes. What's the right way to do it?▼
ANSWER
Use a Kubernetes Job, not a Deployment.

A Job runs one or more pods to completion and then stops. It's designed for batch work: database migrations, data transformations, one-off scripts.

Key properties:
• restartPolicy: OnFailure — retry on failure, but don't restart after success
• completions: 1 — need exactly 1 successful run
• backoffLimit: 3 — retry up to 3 times before marking as failed

For database migrations specifically:
Use an Init Container in your deployment — runs the migration before the main containers start. This ensures the schema is always up to date before the app starts serving traffic. But it runs on every pod restart, so the migration must be idempotent.

Alternatively, run the migration as a Helm hook (helm.sh/hook: pre-upgrade) — runs the migration job before Helm applies the new deployment.

What NOT to do: Don't run migrations inside the app on startup (race condition with multiple replicas). Don't use a Deployment (keeps restarting after success).

Job = runs to completionInit Container = before main app startsHelm pre-upgrade hooknever Deployment for one-time work
FE15What is observability and how is it different from monitoring? What are the three pillars?▼
ANSWER
Monitoring = watching known things. You define what metrics to collect and alert on. You can only answer questions you thought to ask in advance. "Is CPU above 80%?"

Observability = understanding a system's internal state from its external outputs. You can answer questions you didn't think to ask. "Why is user 12345 getting slow responses only when making requests from Germany at 3 PM on Tuesdays?"

The 3 Pillars of Observability:

1. Metrics — numerical measurements over time. CPU, memory, request rate, error rate. Good for alerting, dashboards, trending. Tools: Prometheus, CloudWatch.

2. Logs — timestamped events. "User X failed to authenticate at 14:32:11". Good for debugging specific incidents. Tools: ELK Stack, Loki, CloudWatch Logs.

3. Traces (Distributed Tracing) — follow a single request as it travels through multiple microservices. Shows exactly where time was spent and which service caused a slowdown. Tools: Jaeger, Zipkin, AWS X-Ray. This is the pillar most teams are missing.

Correlation: The real power is when you can go from a metric alert → the relevant logs → the trace for the slow request. Tools like Grafana Tempo or Datadog connect all three.

observability = understand why3 pillars: metrics + logs + tracestraces = most valuable for microservices

🐳 TASK 1 — Containerize a Node.js App (End-to-End)
The Scenario: You have a Node.js app. Your interviewer says: "Containerize this so it runs the same everywhere — locally, on CI, and in production." Here's exactly what you do.
📁
STEP 01 Understand your app RECON
Before writing a single line of Dockerfile, answer 3 questions:
1. What runtime does it need? (Node 18? Python 3.11?)
2. What port does it listen on? (3000? 8080?)
3. What command starts it? (node index.js? npm start?)
💡 Say this out loud in your interview. It shows you think before you type — that's senior behavior.
📝
STEP 02 Write the Dockerfile DOCKERFILE
Create a file literally called Dockerfile (no extension) in your project root:
# 1. Base image — the OS + runtime your app needs
FROM node:18-alpine

# 2. Set the working directory INSIDE the container
WORKDIR /app

# 3. Copy dependency files FIRST (layer caching trick)
COPY package*.json ./

# 4. Install dependencies
RUN npm install --production

# 5. Copy the rest of your app code
COPY . .

# 6. Tell Docker which port your app uses
EXPOSE 3000

# 7. The command that starts your app
CMD ["node", "index.js"]
💡 Why COPY package.json BEFORE COPY . ? Docker caches layers. If your code changes but dependencies don't, it skips npm install on rebuild — saving minutes every time.
🚫
STEP 03 Add a .dockerignore OPTIMIZE
Create .dockerignore in your project root — tells Docker what NOT to copy into the image:
node_modules
.git
.env
*.log
README.md
💡 Without this, node_modules (sometimes 500MB+) gets copied in, bloating your image. This is a common interview gotcha.
🔨
STEP 04 Build the image docker build
Run this from the directory containing your Dockerfile:
# Syntax: docker build -t name:tag context
docker build -t myapp:latest .

# With your Docker Hub username (needed for pushing):
docker build -t ibrahiem/myapp:v1.0 .
Breaking it down:
-t myapp:latest → tag the image with name:version
. → build context (current directory)
💡 You'll see each Dockerfile instruction execute as a numbered step. Each step = one layer. Failed step = fix that layer and rebuild from cache.
▶️
STEP 05 Run the container docker run
Spin up a container from your image:
# Run detached + map port + name it
docker run -d -p 3000:3000 --name my-container myapp:latest

# Run with env variable
docker run -d -p 3000:3000 -e NODE_ENV=production myapp:latest
Port mapping: -p 3000:3000 = host:container
So localhost:3000 on your machine → hits port 3000 inside the container
💡 -d runs it in the background. Without it, logs flood your terminal and Ctrl+C kills the container.
🐛
STEP 06 Debug when things break DEBUG 
# See all containers (including stopped)
docker ps -a

# Read crash output
docker logs my-container

# Follow logs in real-time
docker logs -f my-container

# Open a shell INSIDE the running container
docker exec -it my-container sh

# Inspect container details (IP, env vars, mounts)
docker inspect my-container
💡 docker exec -it <name> sh is your "get inside the box" command — exactly like SSH into a server. Check files, test network, verify env vars.
☁️ TASK 2 — Push Your Image to Docker Hub
# 1. Login
docker login

# 2. Tag with your Docker Hub username
docker tag myapp:latest ibrahiem/myapp:v1.0

# 3. Push
docker push ibrahiem/myapp:v1.0

# 4. Pull on another machine / CI server
docker pull ibrahiem/myapp:v1.0
docker run -d -p 3000:3000 ibrahiem/myapp:v1.0
🎼 TASK 3 — Multi-Container App with Docker Compose
Scenario: Your app needs a Node.js backend + MongoDB database. Docker Compose wires them together with one file. 
# docker-compose.yml
version: '3.8'

services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      - MONGO_URL=mongodb://db:27017/myapp
    depends_on:
      - db

  db:
    image: mongo:6
    ports:
      - "27017:27017"
    volumes:
      - mongo-data:/data/db

volumes:
  mongo-data:
docker compose up -d          # start everything
docker compose down           # stop everything
docker compose down -v        # stop + wipe volumes
docker compose up -d --build  # rebuild after code change
⚡ TASK 4 — GitHub Actions: Auto Build & Push on Push to main
# .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
name: Build and Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}/myapp:latest
⚠️ Secrets: Go to GitHub → Repo Settings → Secrets and Variables → Actions → add DOCKER_USERNAME and DOCKER_TOKEN. The workflow reads them as ${{ secrets.X }} — never visible in logs.
🎯 Interview Q&A — What They're Really Testing
HO01"Walk me through how you'd containerize an application."▼
ANSWER SCRIPT
"First I'd understand the app — runtime, port, start command. Then write a Dockerfile: official base image like node:18-alpine, set WORKDIR, copy package files first for layer caching, run npm install, copy remaining code. Add .dockerignore to exclude node_modules and .env. Build with docker build -t myapp:latest ., run with docker run -d -p 3000:3000 myapp. For production I'd also do a multi-stage build — build stage installs dev deps, final stage only copies the compiled output."

explain the whymention layer caching.dockerignoremention multi-stage
HO02"What's the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT in a Dockerfile?"▼
ANSWER
CMD = the default command to run. It can be fully overridden at docker run: docker run myapp node other.js replaces CMD entirely.

ENTRYPOINT = the executable that always runs. Arguments from docker run are appended to it, not replacing it.

Best practice combo: 
ENTRYPOINT ["node"]
CMD ["index.js"]
# docker run myapp           → node index.js
# docker run myapp server.js → node server.js
CMD = overridable defaultENTRYPOINT = always runscombine both for flexibility
HO03"How do you minimize Docker image size?"▼
ANSWER
4 techniques in order of impact:

1. Alpine base images — node:18-alpine is ~50MB vs node:18 at ~350MB.

2. Multi-stage builds — build in one stage, copy only output to a clean final stage. Dev deps never reach production: 
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm install && npm run build

FROM node:18-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist
CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]
3. .dockerignore — exclude node_modules, .git, test files, logs.

4. Chain RUN commands — each RUN = one layer. Use && and clean up in the same layer.

alpine basemulti-stage builds.dockerignorechain RUN commands
HO04"Your container starts but crashes immediately. How do you debug it?"▼
DEBUG SCRIPT
1. docker ps -a — confirm container exists, check its status (Exited? Restarting?)
2. docker logs <container> — read the crash output. 90% of the time the error is right there.
3. If it exits too fast: docker run -it myapp sh — override CMD with a shell, investigate manually.
4. docker inspect <container> — check env vars, mounts, network config.
5. Check if port is already used on host: lsof -i :3000

docker logs firstdocker ps -a for statusexec -it sh to get insideinspect for env/config
HO05"How do containers differ from VMs?"▼
ANSWER
VMs virtualize hardware. Containers virtualize the OS.

VM: Each VM has its own full OS kernel. A hypervisor manages hardware. Heavy — gigabytes each, minutes to boot.

Container: All containers share the host OS kernel. Docker isolates processes using Linux namespaces and cgroups. Lightweight — megabytes, seconds to start.

The analogy: VMs = separate houses (own plumbing, electricity). Containers = apartments in one building — shared infrastructure, isolated living spaces.

VMs = full OS per instancecontainers = shared kernelcontainers = faster + lighterVMs = stronger isolation

🐧 TASK 5 — Set Up a Linux Server from Scratch
The Scenario: You just got SSH access to a fresh Ubuntu server. The interviewer says: "It's yours — secure it and make it production-ready."
① Update the system first
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
Always start here. Stale packages = unpatched vulnerabilities.
② Create a non-root user
adduser ibrahiem
usermod -aG sudo ibrahiem
su - ibrahiem
Never run apps as root. Blast radius of a hack = everything if you do.
③ Set up SSH key auth
# On your LOCAL machine:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "ibrahiem@dev"
ssh-copy-id ibrahiem@SERVER_IP
Keys can't be brute-forced. Passwords can. Disable password auth after this.
④ Harden SSH config
# /etc/ssh/sshd_config
PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
Port 2222          # optional: change default port

sudo systemctl restart sshd
⑤ Configure UFW firewall
sudo ufw allow OpenSSH
sudo ufw allow 80      # HTTP
sudo ufw allow 443     # HTTPS
sudo ufw enable
sudo ufw status
Deny all by default, allow only what you need. Principle of least privilege.
⑥ Install & manage a service
sudo apt install nginx -y
sudo systemctl enable nginx   # start on boot
sudo systemctl start nginx
sudo systemctl status nginx
⑦ Monitor system health
top / htop          # CPU & memory live
df -h               # disk usage
free -h             # RAM usage
lsof -i :80         # what's using port 80?
journalctl -xe      # system logs
⑧ Set up cron job
crontab -e
# Run backup every day at 2am:
0 2 * * * /home/ibrahiem/backup.sh

# Check cron format: min hr day month weekday
🌿 TASK 6 — Git: The Real-World Feature Branch Workflow
The Scenario: "Show me how you'd work on a new feature without breaking main." This is the workflow used at every real company. 
# 1. Always start from an updated main
git checkout main
git pull origin main

# 2. Create a feature branch
git checkout -b feature/user-auth

# 3. Work, commit with meaningful messages
git add .
git commit -m "feat: add JWT authentication middleware"
git commit -m "test: add unit tests for auth service"

# 4. Keep your branch up to date with main (avoid merge conflicts later)
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main        # replay your commits on top of latest main

# 5. Push your branch
git push origin feature/user-auth

# 6. Open a Pull Request on GitHub → code review → merge

# 7. After merge, clean up
git checkout main
git pull origin main
git branch -d feature/user-auth
git push origin --delete feature/user-auth
🔥 Fix a merge conflict
git merge feature/other
# CONFLICT → open the file, find <<<< markers
# Edit to keep the right code
git add conflicted-file.js
git commit -m "resolve merge conflict"
⏪ Undo last commit (keep changes)
git reset --soft HEAD~1
# Changes go back to staging area
# git reset --hard HEAD~1 = DESTROYS changes
🚑 Stash work mid-task
git stash              # save dirty state
git checkout main      # switch to hotfix
# ... fix hotfix ...
git checkout feature/x
git stash pop          # restore your work
🏷️ Tag a release
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Production release"
git push origin v1.0.0
# List all tags:
git tag

STEP 01Launch EC2 instanceAWS Console
EC2 → Launch Instance → Ubuntu 22.04 LTS → t2.micro (free tier)
Key pair: create new → download .pem file (you can't get it again)
Security group: Allow SSH (22), HTTP (80), HTTPS (443) — from 0.0.0.0/0 for public
💡 Security groups are stateful firewalls. Inbound rule for port 80 = HTTP traffic can reach your app.

⚡ TASK 8 — Full CI/CD Pipeline: Test → Build → Deploy
The Scenario: "Set up a pipeline that runs tests on every PR, and deploys to production only when merged to main." 
# .github/workflows/ci-cd.yml
name: CI/CD Pipeline

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]          # runs tests on every PR
  push:
    branches: [main]          # deploys only when merged

jobs:
  # ─── JOB 1: Test (runs on every PR) ───────────────────────
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Setup Node
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '18'
          cache: 'npm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci              # faster + stricter than npm install

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

      - name: Run linter
        run: npm run lint

  # ─── JOB 2: Build & Push (only on merge to main) ──────────
  build-and-push:
    needs: test                 # only runs if test job passes
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Login to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: |
            ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}/myapp:latest
            ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}/myapp:${{ github.sha }}

  # ─── JOB 3: Deploy to EC2 ─────────────────────────────────
  deploy:
    needs: build-and-push
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: SSH into EC2 and redeploy
        uses: appleboy/ssh-action@v1
        with:
          host: ${{ secrets.EC2_HOST }}
          username: ubuntu
          key: ${{ secrets.EC2_SSH_KEY }}
          script: |
            docker pull ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}/myapp:latest
            docker stop app || true
            docker rm app || true
            docker run -d -p 80:3000 --name app --restart=always \
              ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}/myapp:latest
Secrets needed: DOCKER_USERNAME, DOCKER_TOKEN, EC2_HOST (public IP), EC2_SSH_KEY (contents of your .pem file)
The flow: PR opened → tests run → PR blocked if fail → merge to main → build image → push to Hub → SSH into EC2 → pull new image → restart container ✅
☸️ TASK 9 — Deploy an App to Kubernetes
The Scenario: "You have a Dockerized app. Deploy it to Kubernetes with 3 replicas and expose it via a Service." 
# deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: myapp
spec:
  replicas: 3                       # 3 copies running at all times
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: myapp
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: myapp
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: myapp
          image: ibrahiem/myapp:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
          env:
            - name: NODE_ENV
              value: "production"
          resources:
            requests:
              memory: "128Mi"
              cpu: "250m"
            limits:
              memory: "256Mi"
              cpu: "500m"
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 3000
            initialDelaySeconds: 10
            periodSeconds: 15

---
# service.yaml — exposes the app
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: myapp-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: myapp                      # routes to pods with label app=myapp
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80                      # Service port
      targetPort: 3000              # container port
  type: LoadBalancer                # gives a public IP (on cloud), NodePort (local)
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml   # create/update deployment
kubectl apply -f service.yaml      # create/update service

kubectl get pods                   # verify pods are Running
kubectl get svc                    # get external IP
kubectl describe pod myapp-xyz     # debug a specific pod
kubectl logs myapp-xyz             # see pod logs
kubectl rollout status deploy/myapp  # watch rollout progress

# Scale up/down
kubectl scale deployment myapp --replicas=5

# Rolling update (change image version)
kubectl set image deployment/myapp myapp=ibrahiem/myapp:v2.0
kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp  # rollback if broken
🚨 K8s Pod Not Starting — Debug Flow
kubectl get pods                         # STATUS = CrashLoopBackOff / Pending / Error?
kubectl describe pod <pod-name>          # Events section at the bottom — the real error
kubectl logs <pod-name>                  # App crash output
kubectl logs <pod-name> --previous       # Logs from crashed previous instance
kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -- sh        # Shell into the pod (if it's running)

# Common causes:
# CrashLoopBackOff = app crashes on startup → check logs
# Pending = no node has enough resources → check resource requests
# ImagePullBackOff = image name wrong or registry auth missing
# OOMKilled = container exceeded memory limit → raise limits
🏗️ TASK 10 — Provision Infrastructure with Terraform
The Scenario: "Provision an EC2 instance and S3 bucket on AWS using Terraform. No clicking in the console." 
# main.tf
terraform {
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 5.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = var.aws_region
}

# ── EC2 Instance ───────────────────────────────────────────
resource "aws_instance" "app_server" {
  ami           = "ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0"   # Ubuntu 22.04 us-east-1
  instance_type = var.instance_type

  tags = {
    Name        = "myapp-server"
    Environment = var.environment
  }
}

# ── S3 Bucket ──────────────────────────────────────────────
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "app_assets" {
  bucket = "ibrahiem-app-assets-${var.environment}"
  tags = {
    Environment = var.environment
  }
}

# variables.tf
variable "aws_region"     { default = "us-east-1" }
variable "instance_type"  { default = "t2.micro" }
variable "environment"    { default = "staging" }

# outputs.tf
output "ec2_public_ip" {
  value = aws_instance.app_server.public_ip
}
output "s3_bucket_name" {
  value = aws_s3_bucket.app_assets.bucket
}
terraform init        # download providers
terraform plan        # preview what will be created/changed/destroyed
terraform apply       # actually create resources (asks for confirmation)
terraform apply -auto-approve   # skip confirmation (use in CI)
terraform destroy     # tear everything down
terraform output      # print output values after apply
terraform state list  # see all resources in state
⚠️ Never commit terraform.tfstate to Git. It contains secrets and resource IDs. Store it in S3 with DynamoDB locking for team use:
terraform { backend "s3" { bucket = "my-tf-state" key = "prod/terraform.tfstate" region = "us-east-1" dynamodb_table = "tf-locks" } }
🌐 TASK 11 — Configure Nginx as a Reverse Proxy
The Scenario: "Your Node app runs on port 3000. Make it accessible on port 80 (HTTP) so users don't need to type :3000." 
# /etc/nginx/sites-available/myapp
server {
    listen 80;
    server_name yourdomain.com www.yourdomain.com;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://localhost:3000;    # forward to your app
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header Connection 'upgrade';
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_cache_bypass $http_upgrade;
    }
}
# Enable the config (symlink to sites-enabled)
sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/myapp /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/

# Test config for syntax errors BEFORE reloading
sudo nginx -t

# Apply config
sudo systemctl reload nginx

# Add HTTPS with Let's Encrypt (free SSL)
sudo apt install certbot python3-certbot-nginx -y
sudo certbot --nginx -d yourdomain.com
Why a reverse proxy? Your app can't run on port 80 without root (security risk). Nginx runs on 80 as root, then forwards to your unprivileged app on 3000. Bonus: Nginx also handles SSL termination, rate limiting, gzip compression, and can load balance across multiple app instances.
⌨️ TASK 12 — Write a DevOps Bash Script
The Scenario: "Write a script that checks if a service is running and restarts it if not." A classic DevOps automation task. 
#!/bin/bash
# healthcheck.sh — auto-restart a service if it dies

SERVICE="nginx"
LOG_FILE="/var/log/healthcheck.log"
TIMESTAMP=$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')

# Check if the service is running
if systemctl is-active --quiet "$SERVICE"; then
    echo "[$TIMESTAMP] $SERVICE is running ✅" >> "$LOG_FILE"
else
    echo "[$TIMESTAMP] $SERVICE is DOWN. Restarting..." >> "$LOG_FILE"
    systemctl restart "$SERVICE"

    # Check if restart succeeded
    if systemctl is-active --quiet "$SERVICE"; then
        echo "[$TIMESTAMP] $SERVICE restarted successfully ✅" >> "$LOG_FILE"
    else
        echo "[$TIMESTAMP] CRITICAL: $SERVICE failed to restart ❌" >> "$LOG_FILE"
        # Send an alert (email, Slack webhook, etc.)
    fi
fi
Script essentials
#!/bin/bash          # shebang line
chmod +x script.sh   # make executable
./script.sh          # run it

set -e    # exit on any error
set -u    # error on undefined vars
set -o pipefail  # catch pipe failures
Variables & conditionals
NAME="ibrahiem"
echo "Hello, $NAME"

if [ "$ENV" == "prod" ]; then
  echo "production mode"
elif [ "$ENV" == "dev" ]; then
  echo "dev mode"
fi
Loops & functions
for server in web1 web2 web3; do
  echo "Deploying to $server"
  ssh $server "docker pull myapp:latest"
done

backup() {
  tar -czf backup-$(date +%F).tar.gz /app

backup

📊 TASK 13 — Set Up Monitoring with Prometheus + Grafana
The Scenario: "How would you set up monitoring for your application? What metrics would you track?" 
# docker-compose.monitoring.yml
version: '3.8'

services:
  prometheus:
    image: prom/prometheus:latest
    ports:
      - "9090:9090"
    volumes:
      - ./prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml
    command:
      - '--config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml'

  grafana:
    image: grafana/grafana:latest
    ports:
      - "3001:3000"
    environment:
      - GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD=admin
    volumes:
      - grafana-data:/var/lib/grafana
    depends_on:
      - prometheus

  node-exporter:               # exports Linux system metrics
    image: prom/node-exporter:latest
    ports:
      - "9100:9100"

volumes:
  grafana-data:
# prometheus.yml — tells Prometheus what to scrape
global:
  scrape_interval: 15s

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'node-exporter'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['node-exporter:9100']

  - job_name: 'myapp'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['app:3000']      # your app must expose /metrics endpoint
The 4 Golden Signals
Latency — how long requests take
Traffic — requests per second
Errors — error rate (4xx/5xx)
Saturation — how full is your system (CPU/memory at limit?)
PromQL — key queries
# CPU usage %
100 - (avg(rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m])) * 100)

# HTTP error rate
rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])

# Memory used
node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes
Access Grafana
Open http://localhost:3001
Login: admin / admin
Add Prometheus as data source: http://prometheus:9090
Import dashboard ID 1860 (Node Exporter Full) — instant system dashboard

🤔 WHY — The Problem They Solve
😰 Without monitoring
Your app crashes at 3am. You find out when a customer tweets about it.

Users say "it's slow." You have no idea what is slow, when it started, or why.

Memory leak eats up your server over 3 days. You find out when it crashes.
✅ With Prometheus + Grafana
Alert fires at 3am before the crash — memory was trending up.

You open Grafana, see exactly which endpoint got slow and which commit caused it.

You spot the memory leak on a graph a week before it becomes a crisis.
💼 Why interviewers care
Any production system needs monitoring. If you can say "I set up Prometheus + Grafana, wrote PromQL queries, and configured alerts" — you're describing real production work that most juniors have never touched.
🏛️ How It All Fits Together
🖥️ 🐳 ☸️
Your App / Services
exposes /metrics
→
📡
Prometheus

→
📊
Grafana

Also in the stack: Node Exporter — runs on each Linux server, exports CPU/RAM/disk/network metrics to Prometheus.  |  cAdvisor — exports Docker container metrics.  |  kube-state-metrics — exports Kubernetes object metrics (pod status, deployment replicas, etc.)
📡 PROMETHEUS — Deep Dive
🔄 Pull-Based Scraping
Prometheus pulls metrics from targets — targets don't push to Prometheus.

Each target exposes a /metrics HTTP endpoint. Prometheus hits it every 15s (configurable) and stores the data.

Why pull, not push? Prometheus knows if a target goes down (it stops responding). Push-based systems don't know if silence = healthy or dead.
🗄️ Time-Series Database (TSDB)
All data stored as metric_name + labels + timestamp + value.

Example entry: http_requests_total{method="GET", status="200", endpoint="/api"} 1452 1714000000

Labels let you slice data: "show me only POST errors on /login". Stored efficiently on disk — compresses well since values change slowly.
📏 4 Metric Types
Counter — only goes up. Total requests, total errors. Use rate() to get per-second rate.
Gauge — goes up and down. Current memory, active connections, queue size.
Histogram — samples observations into buckets. Request duration, response size. Enables p95/p99 latency.
Summary — like histogram but calculates quantiles client-side. Less flexible.
🎯 Service Discovery
In Kubernetes you don't hardcode targets. Prometheus uses service discovery to auto-find pods with the right annotations:

prometheus.io/scrape: "true"
prometheus.io/port: "3000"

Any new pod with these annotations gets automatically scraped.
📄 What a /metrics endpoint looks like
# HELP http_requests_total Total number of HTTP requests
# TYPE http_requests_total counter
http_requests_total{method="GET",status="200",path="/api/users"} 8473
http_requests_total{method="POST",status="201",path="/api/users"} 312
http_requests_total{method="GET",status="404",path="/api/users"} 17
http_requests_total{method="POST",status="500",path="/api/login"} 3

# HELP process_resident_memory_bytes Resident memory size in bytes
# TYPE process_resident_memory_bytes gauge
process_resident_memory_bytes 52428800

# HELP http_request_duration_seconds HTTP request latency
# TYPE http_request_duration_seconds histogram
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.05"} 7231
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.1"} 7890
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.5"} 8450
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="+Inf"} 8473
💡 Prometheus scrapes this URL on your app every 15s and stores every line as a time-series data point. Your app exposes this — you add a library like prom-client (Node.js) or prometheus_client (Python).
🔍 PromQL — The Query Language
PromQL is how you ask Prometheus questions about your data. Grafana uses PromQL to build its panels. Alertmanager uses PromQL to decide when to fire alerts. You don't need to memorize all of it — you need to understand the patterns.
📈 Request Rate (most used)
# Requests per second over last 5 mins
rate(http_requests_total[5m])

# Only GET requests
rate(http_requests_total{method="GET"}[5m])

# Error rate (5xx only)
rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])
rate() takes a counter (always increasing) and calculates per-second rate. Always use rate() on counters — never the raw value.
💾 Memory & CPU
# Memory used (bytes)
node_memory_MemTotal_bytes - node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes

# Memory used %
(1 - (node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes /
      node_memory_MemTotal_bytes)) * 100

# CPU usage % (all cores, 5m avg)
100 - (avg by(instance)(
  rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m])
) * 100)
⏱️ Latency (p95 / p99)
# 95th percentile latency over 5m
histogram_quantile(0.95,
  rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])
)

# 99th percentile (the "worst" users)
histogram_quantile(0.99,
  rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])
)
p95 = 95% of requests are faster than this. Interviewers love when you talk p99 instead of average — average hides pain.
💽 Disk Usage
# Disk used %
(1 - (node_filesystem_avail_bytes{mountpoint="/"} /
      node_filesystem_size_bytes{mountpoint="/"})) * 100

# Predict when disk will fill (linear extrapolation)
predict_linear(
  node_filesystem_avail_bytes[6h], 4*3600
)
🐳 Container Metrics
# Container CPU usage
rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{
  name="my-container"
}[5m])

# Container memory usage
container_memory_usage_bytes{name="my-container"}

# Kubernetes pod restarts (bad sign!)
kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total
🔢 Aggregation Functions
sum(metric)         # total across all instances
avg(metric)         # average
max(metric)         # worst case
min(metric)
count(metric)       # number of time series

# Group by a label:
sum by(endpoint)(rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
# → request rate per endpoint
⚙️ prometheus.yml — The Config File Explained
# prometheus.yml
global:
  scrape_interval: 15s          # how often to scrape all targets
  evaluation_interval: 15s      # how often to evaluate alert rules
  scrape_timeout: 10s

# Rules files (alert rules live here)
rule_files:
  - "alert_rules.yml"

# Alertmanager connection
alerting:
  alertmanagers:
    - static_configs:
        - targets: ['alertmanager:9093']

# What to scrape
scrape_configs:
  # Prometheus monitors itself
  - job_name: 'prometheus'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['localhost:9090']

  # Linux server metrics via Node Exporter
  - job_name: 'node-exporter'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['node-exporter:9100']

  # Your Node.js application
  - job_name: 'myapp'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['app:3000']
    metrics_path: '/metrics'     # default — can be changed

  # Docker containers via cAdvisor
  - job_name: 'cadvisor'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['cadvisor:8080']

  # Kubernetes auto-discovery
  - job_name: 'kubernetes-pods'
    kubernetes_sd_configs:
      - role: pod
    relabel_configs:
      - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_scrape]
        action: keep
        regex: 'true'
🚨 Alert Rules — When Prometheus Pages You
# alert_rules.yml
groups:
  - name: application_alerts
    rules:

      # Fire if error rate > 1% for 5 minutes
      - alert: HighErrorRate
        expr: rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]) > 0.01
        for: 5m                   # must be true for 5 mins before firing
        labels:
          severity: critical
        annotations:
          summary: "High error rate on {{ $labels.instance }}"
          description: "Error rate is {{ $value | humanizePercentage }}"

      # Fire if CPU > 80% for 10 minutes
      - alert: HighCPU
        expr: |
          100 - (avg by(instance)(
            rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m])
          ) * 100) > 80
        for: 10m
        labels:
          severity: warning
        annotations:
          summary: "High CPU on {{ $labels.instance }}"

      # Fire if disk will fill within 4 hours
      - alert: DiskFillingSoon
        expr: predict_linear(node_filesystem_avail_bytes[6h], 4*3600) < 0
        for: 30m
        labels:
          severity: warning
        annotations:
          summary: "Disk filling up on {{ $labels.instance }}"

      # Fire if pod is crash-looping
      - alert: PodCrashLooping
        expr: rate(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total[15m]) > 0
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: critical
        annotations:
          summary: "Pod {{ $labels.pod }} is crash-looping"
📬 Alertmanager — Route Alerts to Slack
# alertmanager.yml
global:
  slack_api_url: 'https://hooks.slack.com/services/YOUR/WEBHOOK'

route:
  group_by: ['alertname']
  group_wait: 30s               # wait before sending first alert in group
  group_interval: 5m            # time before re-sending grouped alerts
  repeat_interval: 4h           # time before re-sending unresolved alerts
  receiver: 'slack-notifications'

receivers:
  - name: 'slack-notifications'
    slack_configs:
      - channel: '#alerts'
        title: '{{ .GroupLabels.alertname }}'
        text: '{{ range .Alerts }}{{ .Annotations.description }}{{ end }}'
📊 GRAFANA — Deep Dive
🎨 What Grafana actually does
Grafana is purely a visualization layer. It stores no metrics itself.

It connects to data sources (Prometheus, CloudWatch, Loki, MySQL, ElasticSearch — 50+ supported) and turns query results into panels: graphs, gauges, stat numbers, tables, heatmaps, geo maps.
📋 Dashboards
A dashboard = collection of panels.
Each panel = a PromQL query + visualization type.

Variables — dropdowns at the top. $instance lets you switch which server you're viewing without editing queries. Defined as label values from Prometheus.
📦 Pre-built Dashboards (use these!)
grafana.com/dashboards has thousands of community dashboards. Import by ID:

1860 — Node Exporter Full (Linux server)
3119 — Docker + cAdvisor containers
315 — Kubernetes cluster overview
6417 — Kubernetes pod resources
11074 — Node Exporter for Prometheus
🔔 Grafana Alerting
Grafana has its own alert engine (separate from Prometheus Alertmanager). You define alert rules on panels — if the PromQL value crosses a threshold, fire an alert.

Routes to Slack, PagerDuty, email, webhooks. In modern setups, teams pick one: Grafana alerts OR Prometheus Alertmanager. Not both.
🐳 Full Monitoring Stack — Docker Compose
# docker-compose.monitoring.yml
version: '3.8'

services:
  # ── Prometheus ──────────────────────────────────────────────
  prometheus:
    image: prom/prometheus:latest
    container_name: prometheus
    ports:
      - "9090:9090"
    volumes:
      - ./prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml
      - ./alert_rules.yml:/etc/prometheus/alert_rules.yml
      - prometheus-data:/prometheus          # persist data
    command:
      - '--config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml'
      - '--storage.tsdb.retention.time=15d'  # keep 15 days of data
    restart: unless-stopped

  # ── Grafana ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
  grafana:
    image: grafana/grafana:latest
    container_name: grafana
    ports:
      - "3001:3000"
    environment:
      - GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_USER=admin
      - GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD=securepassword
      - GF_USERS_ALLOW_SIGN_UP=false
    volumes:
      - grafana-data:/var/lib/grafana
    depends_on:
      - prometheus
    restart: unless-stopped

  # ── Node Exporter (Linux server metrics) ───────────────────
  node-exporter:
    image: prom/node-exporter:latest
    container_name: node-exporter
    ports:
      - "9100:9100"
    volumes:
      - /proc:/host/proc:ro
      - /sys:/host/sys:ro
      - /:/rootfs:ro
    command:
      - '--path.procfs=/host/proc'
      - '--path.rootfs=/rootfs'
      - '--path.sysfs=/host/sys'
    restart: unless-stopped

  # ── cAdvisor (Docker container metrics) ────────────────────
  cadvisor:
    image: gcr.io/cadvisor/cadvisor:latest
    container_name: cadvisor
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    volumes:
      - /:/rootfs:ro
      - /var/run:/var/run:ro
      - /sys:/sys:ro
      - /var/lib/docker/:/var/lib/docker:ro
    restart: unless-stopped

  # ── Alertmanager ────────────────────────────────────────────
  alertmanager:
    image: prom/alertmanager:latest
    container_name: alertmanager
    ports:
      - "9093:9093"
    volumes:
      - ./alertmanager.yml:/etc/alertmanager/alertmanager.yml
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  prometheus-data:
  grafana-data:
docker compose -f docker-compose.monitoring.yml up -d

# Access:
# Prometheus UI:    http://localhost:9090
# Grafana:          http://localhost:3001  (admin / securepassword)
# Alertmanager:     http://localhost:9093
# Node Exporter:    http://localhost:9100/metrics
# cAdvisor:         http://localhost:8080
🔧 Instrument Your App — Add /metrics to Node.js
Key insight: Prometheus can only collect metrics that your app exposes. You need to instrument your code — add a /metrics endpoint. This is a 10-minute task with the prom-client library. 
// Install: npm install prom-client
const express = require('express');
const client = require('prom-client');

const app = express();

// ── Auto-collect default Node.js metrics (CPU, memory, GC, etc.)
client.collectDefaultMetrics({ prefix: 'myapp_' });

// ── Custom counter: track HTTP requests
const httpRequests = new client.Counter({
  name: 'http_requests_total',
  help: 'Total number of HTTP requests',
  labelNames: ['method', 'route', 'status']
});

// ── Custom histogram: track request duration
const requestDuration = new client.Histogram({
  name: 'http_request_duration_seconds',
  help: 'Duration of HTTP requests in seconds',
  labelNames: ['method', 'route'],
  buckets: [0.005, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5]
});

// ── Middleware to auto-instrument all routes
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  const end = requestDuration.startTimer({ method: req.method, route: req.path });
  res.on('finish', () => {
    httpRequests.inc({ method: req.method, route: req.path, status: res.statusCode });
    end();
  });
  next();
});

// ── The /metrics endpoint Prometheus will scrape
app.get('/metrics', async (req, res) => {
  res.set('Content-Type', client.register.contentType);
  res.end(await client.register.metrics());
});

app.listen(3000);
🗂️ Step-by-Step: First Time Setup
1
STEP 01Start the stack
docker compose -f docker-compose.monitoring.yml up -d
docker compose ps   # verify all containers are Up
2
STEP 02Verify Prometheus targets
Open http://localhost:9090/targets — every scrape target should show UP in green. If a target is DOWN, check: is the service running? Is the port correct? Is the container on the same Docker network?
3
STEP 03Test a PromQL query
Open http://localhost:9090/graph, type a query: up — shows all targets (1=up, 0=down). Then try node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes. Click "Graph" tab to see the time series.
4
STEP 04Connect Grafana to Prometheus
Open http://localhost:3001 → login → Connections → Data Sources → Add new → Prometheus
URL: http://prometheus:9090 (use container name, not localhost — they're on the same Docker network)
Click Save & Test — should show green checkmark.
5
STEP 05Import a dashboard
Dashboards → Import → Enter ID: 1860 → Load → Select Prometheus data source → Import
You now have a full Linux server dashboard with CPU, memory, disk, network — all live.
6
STEP 06Create your own panel
Dashboard → Add panel → Enter PromQL query → pick visualization type
Try: rate(http_requests_total[5m]) with "Time series" chart. Add a title. Save. You just built a custom panel.
💡 Save dashboards as JSON and commit to Git. This is "dashboards as code" — reproducible across environments.
🎯 Interview Q&A — Prometheus + Grafana
PG01"Why would you choose Prometheus over CloudWatch or Datadog?"▼
ANSWER
Prometheus advantages: Open source (free), runs on your infra (data never leaves), massively popular in Kubernetes ecosystems, huge community + pre-built dashboards, pull-based model gives better insight into target health.

CloudWatch advantages: Zero setup for AWS services (EC2, Lambda, RDS auto-report to it), tight AWS integration, managed service — no ops overhead.

Datadog advantages: Managed, one platform for metrics + logs + traces + APM, great UI, works across cloud providers. Expensive.

Real answer: Prometheus + Grafana for on-prem or K8s-heavy setups. CloudWatch when you're fully AWS serverless. Datadog when the company has money and wants one tool for everything.

Prometheus = free + K8s nativeCloudWatch = AWS managedDatadog = expensive but unified
PG02"What's the difference between a counter and a gauge? Give examples."▼
ANSWER
Counter — only ever increases (or resets to 0 on restart). Total requests served, total errors, total bytes sent. You never query the raw value — use rate(counter[5m]) to get a meaningful per-second rate.

Gauge — can go up or down freely. Current memory usage, current active connections, current temperature, queue depth. You query the raw value directly.

Memory trick: If the metric can decrease on its own during normal operation — gauge. If it only decreases when the app restarts — counter.

counter = total ever, use rate()gauge = current value, query directly
PG03"An alert fired for high memory at 3am. Walk me through your response."▼
ANSWER SCRIPT
"First I'd open Grafana and check the memory panel — is it still climbing or has it stabilized? I'd check the time range: did it start after a deployment? Did it correlate with a traffic spike?

I'd check container-level memory — which pod/container is consuming it. docker stats or kubectl top pods.

If memory is still climbing: check for a memory leak — is the app holding references it shouldn't? Restart the pod as a short-term fix. Open a ticket for root cause analysis.

If it was a one-time spike: check if a batch job ran. Was there an unusual traffic pattern? Document it and adjust the alert threshold if it was a false positive.

Post-incident: write a brief blameless post-mortem, note what the alert fired on, what caused it, what we fixed."

Grafana firstcorrelate with deploys/trafficcontainer-level drill-downblameless post-mortem
PG04"Why is average latency a bad metric? What should you use instead?"▼
ANSWER
Average hides the worst user experiences. If 999 requests take 10ms and 1 takes 10,000ms, the average is ~20ms — looks fine. But that 1 user had a terrible experience.

Use percentiles instead:
p50 (median) — half of users are faster/slower. Better than average.
p95 — 95% of users are faster than this. Your typical "slow" experience.
p99 — the experience of your worst 1%. Often what SLOs are written against.

PromQL: histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))

Interviewers love this answer — it shows you understand how real performance works.

average = hides outliersp95/p99 = real user experienceSLOs written against percentiles
PG05"What are the 4 Golden Signals and what would you alert on?"▼
ANSWER
1. Latency — how long requests take. Alert: p99 latency > 500ms for 5 minutes.

2. Traffic — how many requests per second. No alert directly — use it as context. A latency spike during 10x traffic is different from a spike during normal load.

3. Errors — error rate (4xx/5xx). Alert: error rate > 1% for 5 minutes. 5xx is user-facing failure. 4xx is usually client error (less critical unless it's 401 auth failures = potential attack).

4. Saturation — how full is the system. Alert: CPU > 80% for 10 minutes, memory > 85%, disk > 90%, connection pool utilization > 90%.

These come from Google's SRE book. Saying "4 Golden Signals" in an interview is an instant signal you've thought seriously about production systems.

latency + traffic + errors + saturationGoogle SRE origintraffic = context, not alert target
📡
The setup that impresses interviewers
Spin up the full stack locally with Docker Compose. Add prom-client to one of your projects. Write 3 alert rules. Import dashboard 1860. Take a screenshot of your working Grafana dashboard. That screenshot has gotten engineers hired.

📁 Navigation & Directory
CommandCategoryWhat it does & how to use it

lsnavigateList directory contents. ls -la = show hidden files + permissions + size. ls -lh = human-readable sizes. ls -lt = sorted by time (newest first).
cd /path/to/dirnavigateChange directory. cd .. = go up one level. cd ~ = go home. cd - = go back to previous directory.

cp -r src/ dest/copyCopy files or directories. -r = recursive (required for dirs). cp file.txt /backup/ = copy file to backup dir.
mv old newmoveMove or rename. mv app.js server.js = rename. mv dist/ /var/www/ = move directory.
find / -name "*.log"searchFind files. find . -name "*.env" = find .env files from here. find /var -size +100M = files over 100MB. find . -mtime -1 = modified in last day.

📄 Reading & Editing Files
CommandCategoryWhat it does & how to use it
cat file.txtreadPrint entire file to terminal. For large files use less instead.
less file.txtreadPage through a large file. j/k=down/up, g=top, G=bottom, /keyword=search, q=quit. Use for logs.

tail -n 50 filereadShow last N lines. tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log = follow log in real-time (live stream).
grep "error" file.logsearchSearch for pattern. grep -i=case insensitive, grep -r "text" ./dir=recursive, grep -n=show line numbers, grep -v "ok"=exclude matches.
grep -rn "TODO" ./srcsearchRecursive grep with line numbers. DevOps use: find all hardcoded secrets, TODOs, or config references across a codebase.
awk '{print $1}' fileprocessColumn extractor. $1=1st column, $2=2nd. awk -F: '{print $1}' /etc/passwd=print all usernames.

wc -l file.txtcountCount lines. wc -w=words, wc -c=bytes. cat file | wc -l=count lines in output.
