uniqprocessRemove duplicate consecutive lines. Always pipe from sort first: sort file | uniq -c=count occurrences.
cut -d',' -f2 file.csvprocessCut columns by delimiter. -d','=delimiter, -f2=second field. Extract columns from CSVs or colon-separated files.
diff file1 file2compareShow differences between files. diff -u=unified format (like git diff). Use to compare config files.
nano file.txteditSimple terminal editor. Ctrl+O=save, Ctrl+X=exit. Use for quick edits on servers.
vim file.txteditPowerful editor. i=insert mode, Esc=normal mode, :w=save, :q!=quit no save, :wq=save+quit, /word=search.
🔗 Pipes, Redirects & Combining Commands
CommandCategoryWhat it does & how to use it
cmd1 | cmd2pipePipe output of cmd1 as input to cmd2. cat access.log | grep "500" | wc -l = count 500 errors in log.
cmd > file.txtredirectRedirect stdout to file (overwrites). echo "hello" > output.txt
cmd >> file.txtredirectAppend stdout to file. echo "new line" >> log.txt
cmd 2> error.logredirectRedirect stderr to file. 2>&1 = redirect stderr to stdout (combine both streams).
cmd1 && cmd2chainRun cmd2 only if cmd1 succeeds. npm test && npm run build = build only if tests pass.
cmd1 || cmd2chainRun cmd2 only if cmd1 fails. docker stop app || true = don't fail if container not running.
cmd &backgroundRun command in background. Returns to prompt immediately. Use jobs to list, fg to bring back.
xargsprocessBuild and run commands from stdin. find . -name "*.log" | xargs rm = delete all found log files.
tee file.txtsplitWrite to file AND stdout simultaneously. ./deploy.sh | tee deploy.log = see output AND save it.
🔐 Permissions & Ownership
CommandCategoryWhat it does & how to use it
chmod 755 filepermissionsChange permissions. 755=rwxr-xr-x (owner=all, group+others=read+exec). chmod +x script.sh=make executable. chmod 600 key.pem=owner read/write only (required for SSH keys).
chown user:group fileownershipChange file owner and group. chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www = recursively give nginx user ownership of web root.
ls -lainspectSee permissions for all files. Format: -rwxr-xr-x 1 user group size date name. First char: -=file, d=dir, l=symlink.
sudo commandprivilegeRun as superuser. Required for system changes. sudo -i=become root (stay root). sudo !!=rerun last command as sudo.
su - usernameprivilegeSwitch user. - loads the user's full environment. Exit back with exit.
whoamiinspectPrint current user. Useful to confirm you're running as the right user in scripts.
id usernameinspectShow user ID, group ID, and all groups. id ubuntu = see ubuntu user's groups.
adduser usernameusersCreate new user interactively. useradd -m -s /bin/bash user = non-interactive version.
usermod -aG sudo userusersAdd user to a group. -a=append (don't remove from other groups), -G=group. Essential for granting sudo access.
passwd usernameusersChange user password. Run as root to change any user's password.
⚙️ Processes & System Resources
CommandCategoryWhat it does & how to use it
topmonitorLive process monitor. CPU + memory usage. Press q=quit, k=kill process (enter PID), P=sort by CPU, M=sort by memory.
htopmonitorBetter top with colors + mouse support. Install: apt install htop. F6=sort, F9=kill, F10=quit.

df -hdiskDisk space usage per filesystem. -h=human readable. Check "Use%" column. >90% = danger zone.

uptimeinspectHow long server has been running + load averages (1m/5m/15m). Load > number of CPU cores = overloaded.

envinspectPrint all environment variables. printenv VAR_NAME=print specific var. export KEY=value=set for current session.
crontab -escheduleEdit cron jobs for current user. crontab -l=list all cron jobs. Format: MIN HR DAY MON DOW command.
historyutilShow command history. !42=run command #42. history | grep docker=search history. Ctrl+R=reverse search.

CommandCategoryWhat it does & how to use it

🔑 SSH — Secure Shell Remote Access
CommandCategoryWhat it does & how to use it
ssh user@hostconnectConnect to remote server. Uses default key (~/.ssh/id_rsa) or password. ssh ubuntu@54.12.34.56

ssh -N -f -L tunneltunnel-N=no remote command, -f=background. Create background tunnel without interactive shell.
💡 ~/.ssh/config — create this file to save connection aliases:
Host myserver
  HostName 54.12.34.56
  User ubuntu
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/my-key.pem
Now just run ssh myserver instead of the full command every time.
⌨️ Bash Scripting Essentials Automation
Command / SyntaxCategoryWhat it does & how to use it
#!/bin/bashshebangFirst line of every bash script. Tells the OS which interpreter to use. Without it, the script may run in sh (different behavior).
chmod +x script.shexecuteMake script executable. Then run with ./script.sh. Or run without chmod: bash script.sh.
set -euo pipefailsafetyPut at top of scripts. -e=exit on any error, -u=error on undefined variable, -o pipefail=catch errors in pipes. Production scripts always have this.
VAR="value"variableSet variable. No spaces around =. Access with $VAR or ${VAR}. ${VAR:-default}=use default if unset.
export VAR="value"variableExport variable to child processes. Without export, only current shell sees it.
echo "text $VAR"outputPrint text. echo -n=no newline. echo -e "\n"=interpret escape sequences. Use for debug output in scripts.
if [ "$X" == "y" ]; thenconditionIf statement. Spaces inside [ ] are required. -eq=numeric equal, -z=string empty, -f=file exists, -d=dir exists.
[[ "$X" == "y" ]]conditionDouble brackets — safer, supports regex. Use [[ ]] in bash scripts instead of [ ]. [[ "$s" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]=regex match.
for i in 1 2 3; doloopFor loop. for f in *.log; do echo "$f"; done. for i in {1..5}=range. for i in $(cat hosts.txt)=loop over file lines.
while [ condition ]loopWhile loop. while true; do check; sleep 5; done=polling loop. Common for health checks.
function name() { }functionDefine function. Call it by name. $1 $2=positional args. $@=all args. $#=arg count.
$(command)subshellCommand substitution — capture output. DATE=$(date +%F)=store today's date. echo "Pods: $(kubectl get pods | wc -l)"
read -r varnameinputRead user input into variable. read -p "Enter name: " NAME. -r=raw (don't interpret backslashes).
exit 0 / exit 1controlExit script with code. 0=success, non-zero=error. CI/CD systems check exit codes — a non-zero exit fails the pipeline step.
trap 'cleanup' EXITcontrolRun cleanup function on exit (even on error). Use to delete temp files, stop services, send notifications when script ends.
source ./file.shimportLoad another script in current shell (so its variables/functions become available). . ./file.sh is the same.
logger "message"loggingWrite to system log (/var/log/syslog). Use in cron jobs so output is preserved in system logs.

git rebase mainrebaseReplay your commits on top of main. Cleaner history than merge. Don't rebase shared branches. Used to keep feature branch up to date.
git rebase -i HEAD~3rebaseInteractive rebase — squash/edit/reorder last 3 commits. Use before opening a PR to clean up messy commits.
git cherry-pick abc1234cherry-pickApply a single commit from another branch onto current branch. Hotfix use case: cherry-pick a fix from develop to main without merging all of develop.
🔄 Remote Operations
CommandCategoryWhat it does & how to use it
git fetch originsyncDownload changes from remote WITHOUT merging. Safe — doesn't change your working directory. Then git merge or git rebase separately.
git pull origin mainsyncFetch + merge in one step. git pull --rebase=fetch + rebase (cleaner history). Use before starting work each day.
git push origin feature/xpushPush branch to remote. git push -u origin branch=set upstream (then just git push). git push --force-with-lease=safe force push after rebase.
git push origin --delete brdeleteDelete remote branch after PR is merged.
⏪ Undoing & Recovery
CommandCategoryWhat it does & how to use it
git reset --soft HEAD~1undoUndo last commit, keep changes staged. Useful to re-commit with different message.
git reset --mixed HEAD~1undoUndo last commit, keep changes unstaged. Default reset behavior.
git reset --hard HEAD~1undoUndo last commit, DISCARD all changes. Destructive — files are gone. Use git reflog to recover if needed.
git revert abc1234undoCreate new commit that undoes a previous commit. Safe — doesn't rewrite history. Use on shared/main branches.
git stashstashSave dirty working state temporarily. git stash pop=restore. git stash list=see all stashes. git stash drop=delete stash.
git stash push -m "name"stashStash with a descriptive name. Makes it easy to find later with git stash list.
git reflogrecoveryLog of ALL HEAD movements — even after hard reset. Your last resort for recovering "deleted" commits. Find the SHA, then git checkout SHA.
git clean -fdcleanDelete untracked files and directories. -n=dry run (preview what will be deleted). Irreversible.
🏷️ Tags & Releases

git push origin v1.0.0tagPush a specific tag. git push origin --tags=push all tags.
git tag -d v1.0.0tagDelete tag locally. git push origin --delete v1.0.0=delete remote tag.

⚠️ Never commit terraform.tfstate to Git. It contains secrets and resource IDs. Use S3 backend + DynamoDB locking for team usage. Add *.tfstate and *.tfstate.backup to .gitignore.

Command / QueryCategoryWhat it does & how to use it

🌑 The 3:00 AM Mindset — Why VPC Matters

To truly understand a VPC practically, you have to look at it the way a DevOps engineer does at 3:00 AM when a server suddenly goes offline.

When you launch a server in AWS and it cannot connect to the internet — or you cannot connect to it — 99% of the time it is a VPC configuration issue.

A VPC isn't just a container; it's a series of checkpoints. For a packet of data to travel from your laptop to your AWS server, it must successfully pass through three distinct layers of networking. Fail any one layer and traffic dies silently. No error message. Just timeout.

🔗 The 3 Checkpoint Layers — Practical Breakdown
1
Internet Gateway (IGW) — The Front Door
VPC → Internet
By default, a VPC is completely sealed off from the outside world. It is a private island. If you want any server inside that VPC to talk to the internet, you must create an Internet Gateway and attach it to the VPC.

What it does: Acts as the bridge between your VPC and the public internet. Without it, no traffic can flow in or out — regardless of any other setting.

How to fix it: EC2 → VPC → Internet Gateways → Create → Attach to your VPC. Then your VPC has a door.

🏠 Practical equivalent: Plugging the modem into the wall of your house.
2
Route Table — The Map
Subnet routing rules
Just because the house has a modem doesn't mean your laptop knows how to use it. A Route Table is a literal list of rules attached to your Subnet. You have to explicitly add a rule that says: "If a packet is trying to go to the public internet (represented as 0.0.0.0/0), send it to the Internet Gateway."

What it does: Determines where traffic goes. Local traffic stays in the VPC. Internet-bound traffic must have a route to the IGW.

How to fix it: VPC → Route Tables → Select your subnet's table → Routes → Add route: Destination 0.0.0.0/0, Target = your IGW.

📶 Practical equivalent: Telling your devices the Wi-Fi password and router IP address.
3
Security Group (SG) — The Bouncer
Per-instance firewall
Even if traffic makes it into the VPC and knows where to go, every single EC2 server has a personal firewall wrapped around it called a Security Group. By default, Security Groups deny all incoming traffic. You must write a rule allowing specific traffic — like Port 80 for web traffic, or Port 22 for SSH.

What it does: Controls exactly which ports and protocols can reach your specific instance. Stateful — if you allow inbound port 80, the response traffic is automatically allowed back out.

How to fix it: EC2 → Security Groups → Inbound Rules → Add rule: Port 80, Source 0.0.0.0/0 for HTTP. Port 22 restricted to your IP only for SSH.

🔐 Practical equivalent: The lock on your specific bedroom door.
The 3am checklist when a server is unreachable:
① Does the VPC have an Internet Gateway attached?
② Does the subnet's Route Table have a route 0.0.0.0/0 → IGW?
③ Does the Security Group have an inbound rule for the port you're trying to reach?
④ Does the EC2 instance have a public IP or Elastic IP assigned?
If all four are yes and it still doesn't work — check your local firewall, or try nc -zv IP PORT to test port reachability.

🖥️ EC2 — A Computer in an Amazon Warehouse

At its absolute simplest, EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) is just a computer sitting in an Amazon warehouse that you rent by the minute.

When you strip away the fancy cloud terminology, launching an EC2 instance is no different than buying a blank Dell laptop, installing Linux on it, and plugging it into the wall.

However, how a regular person uses EC2 and how a DevOps engineer uses EC2 are two completely different things.

😓 The Normal Way (Manual)
Go into AWS Console → click "Launch EC2" → select t2.micro → AWS gives you an IP and key → SSH in → type commands to install Docker → pull image → run it.

The problem: If the server crashes at 3:00 AM, your app is dead until you wake up, click "Launch" again, SSH back in, and type all those commands again. Not scalable. Not automatable. Not DevOps.
✅ The DevOps Way (User Data)
When you launch an EC2 instance, there is a hidden feature called User Data — a text box where you paste a Bash script.

When the EC2 server boots for the first time, before you can even log in, it automatically runs every command in that script as the root user. Self-configuring, self-deploying, zero SSH required.
📝 The User Data Script — Practical Code
If you were launching an EC2 instance for a Node.js app, this is exactly what your User Data script would look like — pasted into the "User Data" field before clicking Launch: 
#!/bin/bash
# 1. Update the operating system
yum update -y

# 2. Install Docker
yum install -y docker

# 3. Start the Docker background service
systemctl start docker
systemctl enable docker

# 4. Pull our application image and run it on Port 80
docker run -d -p 80:3000 my-company/my-node-api:v1
The DevOps milestone this achieves: You never have to SSH into the server. It boots up, configures itself, downloads your app, and starts serving traffic completely automatically. If the server dies, you just tell AWS to launch a new one with the exact same script. This is the foundation of immutable infrastructure.

🏗️ Full VPC Architecture — Production Pattern
AWS Account
└── VPC (10.0.0.0/16)
    │
    ├── Internet Gateway ◄── attached to VPC
    │
    ├── Public Subnet A (10.0.1.0/24) — AZ-1
    │   ├── Route Table: 0.0.0.0/0 → IGW  ◄── internet access
    │   ├── ALB (Application Load Balancer)
    │   └── NAT Gateway  ◄── lets private subnets reach internet (outbound only)
    │
    ├── Public Subnet B (10.0.2.0/24) — AZ-2  ◄── multi-AZ for HA
    │   └── ALB (second AZ)
    │
    ├── Private Subnet A (10.0.10.0/24) — AZ-1
    │   ├── Route Table: 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT GW  ◄── NO direct internet
    │   └── EC2 App Servers (behind ALB)
    │       └── Security Group: allow port 3000 from ALB SG only
    │
    ├── Private Subnet B (10.0.11.0/24) — AZ-2
    │   └── EC2 App Servers (same)
    │
    └── Private Subnet DB (10.0.20.0/24)
        └── RDS Postgres
            └── Security Group: allow port 5432 from App SG only
Interview gold: "Public subnets have a route to the IGW — private subnets don't. The NAT Gateway in the public subnet lets private EC2s reach the internet for updates without being exposed. Security Groups reference each other by ID — the database SG only allows traffic from the app SG, not from any IP. This means even if an attacker gets into the VPC, they can't reach the database directly."
🤖 GitHub Actions in one sentence
👀
GitHub watches your repo
for things happening — pushes, PRs
→
📋
and runs a checklist for you
a file you wrote, top to bottom
→
✅
free CI/CD, built into GitHub
no separate server to run yourself
This tab is the "start from zero" foundation for GitHub Actions specifically — what it is, why teams bother with it, exactly when to introduce it into a project, what every piece of vocabulary means, how to build a workflow file line by line, and what everything looks like when you click around the real GitHub UI. If you want the syntax cheat-sheet keyword table, that's in 📄 YAML/CI. If you want to see it used inside one full realistic pipeline, that's in 🎬 How It's Used → Example 3. This tab is the "why does any of this exist, and when do I even need it" layer underneath both.
🤔 WHY GitHub Actions Exists — The Problem It Solves
😰 Without it
You push code. You hope you remembered to run the tests locally. You hope the app still builds. If you're deploying, you SSH in and run commands by hand, hoping you don't fat-finger a step. Nobody checks your work until a user finds the bug.
✅ With it
You push code. GitHub automatically runs your tests, on a clean machine, the exact same way every single time — human memory removed from the process entirely. You get a green ✅ or red ❌ before anyone even looks at the code.
Why GitHub Actions specifically (and not just "a CI tool" in general): it lives inside GitHub. No separate server to install, no separate account to make, no separate URL to remember. The workflow file lives in your repo, next to your code, versioned in Git like everything else. You already have a GitHub account — you already have GitHub Actions.
🪜 At What Stage Should You Actually Add This?
This is the part most tutorials skip. You don't need this on day one — and turning on the wrong stage too early just adds friction with no payoff.
1
Solo hobby project, just you, still learningSKIP IT FOR NOW
You're the only person touching the code and there's nothing automated to check yet. Adding a workflow here is busywork that teaches you YAML, not the thing you're actually trying to learn. Focus on writing code first.
2
You have at least one automated test, or a second person joinsADD THIS FIRST
This is the real starting line. Add one workflow: run the test suite on every push and every pull request. This single workflow alone removes most "oops, I forgot to test that" bugs before they ever reach a teammate — or you, a week from now.
on: [push, pull_request]
3
You have a Dockerfile or a real build stepADD BUILD
Tests passing doesn't guarantee the app actually builds — a missing import can pass tests and still break the build. Add a second job that builds the image (or runs the build command) so that's checked automatically too.
docker build .
4
You deploy somewhere real people can reachADD DEPLOY — CAREFULLY
Only automate deployment once you genuinely trust stages 2 and 3. Auto-deploying broken code faster is worse than deploying it slowly by hand. This is also the stage where Secrets (API keys, server credentials) start to matter — never type those directly into the YAML file.
5
The team grows, or the project actually matters nowADD GUARDRAILS
Turn on branch protection so nobody can merge to main unless the workflow passes. Add linting and security-scan jobs. Require a second person's review. The workflow stops being a convenience and starts being the thing that actually protects production.
🎯
The one rule that matters: start with tests-on-push, nothing else
Every tutorial that opens with a full deploy pipeline is skipping the part that actually builds your foundation. | Test automation first. | Build checking second. | Deploy automation last, once you trust the first two.
🧠 Core Vocabulary — What Everything Is Called
TermThink of it asWhat it actually is
WorkflowThe whole recipeOne YAML file in .github/workflows/. A repo can have several — one per file. Each is independent.
Event / Trigger"When does this start?"What causes a workflow to run: push, pull_request, workflow_dispatch (manual button), schedule (cron).
JobA section of the checklistA group of steps that all run on the same machine. A workflow can have multiple jobs — by default they all start at once, in parallel.
StepOne line of the checklistA single task inside a job. Steps inside one job always run in order, top to bottom — if one fails, the rest of that job stops.
RunnerThe machine doing the workA fresh, temporary virtual machine GitHub spins up just for your job, then throws away when it's done. ubuntu-latest is the default — free and disposable.
ActionA reusable step someone else wroteA packaged step you drop in with uses: instead of writing it yourself — e.g. actions/checkout@v4 pulls your code onto the runner in one line.
SecretA password the YAML never sees directlyStored encrypted in Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions, referenced as ${{ secrets.NAME }}. Never appears in logs, never lives in the file.
ArtifactA file the run hands back to youBuild output worth keeping — a test report, a compiled binary. Uploaded with actions/upload-artifact, downloadable from the run page afterward.
Matrix"Run this same job, many times"Runs one job across multiple combinations automatically — e.g. Node 18 and 20, on Ubuntu and Windows — without copy-pasting the job four times.
Marketplace ActionA pluginA pre-built action anyone can publish and reuse — Docker login, Slack notify, deploy-to-AWS. Search them at github.com/marketplace/actions.
EnvironmentA named deploy target with rulese.g. "production" — can require a human to click approve before a job touching it is allowed to run. Your safety switch on real deploys.
Concurrency"Don't let two of these overlap"Cancels or queues runs so two deploys can't race each other — important once deploy automation exists (Stage 4 above).
📄 Building Your First Workflow File, One Piece at a Time
Click any card below to open it — click again to close it. Each one adds exactly one new idea on top of the last.
01
The absolute minimum workflow that runs
No checkout, no tests — just proof the machine works and something fires
.github/workflows/hello.yml
FILE
.github/workflows/hello.yml
name: Hello Workflow on: push jobs: say-hello: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - run: echo "Hello from GitHub Actions"
WHY
Four ideas, nothing else: name is just a label. on: push means "run every time someone pushes." runs-on picks the machine. run is one shell command. Commit this file and push — a real run appears in the Actions tab within seconds.
↓ a workflow that can't see your code isn't useful yet — fix that
02
Give it your actual code first
A fresh runner starts completely empty — it has to be told to fetch your repo
actions/checkout
FILE
.github/workflows/hello.yml
jobs: say-hello: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: ls
WHY
The runner is a brand new, empty machine every single time — it does not automatically have your repo on it. uses: actions/checkout@v4 is the official action that clones your repo onto the runner. It's the first step in almost every real-world workflow that has ever been written.
↓ now make it actually check something meaningful
03
Install dependencies, then run your real tests
This is the version worth actually committing to a real project
setup-node + npm test
FILE
.github/workflows/hello.yml
jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: '20' - run: npm install - run: npm test
WHY
setup-node installs a specific Node.js version onto the runner — the runner has an OS but not necessarily the exact toolchain your app needs. with: passes options into an action, the same way arguments get passed into a function. From here, npm test is the same command you'd run on your own laptop — it just now runs automatically, on a clean machine, every single push.
↓ last touch — be specific about when this should actually fire
04
Narrow down exactly when it should run
"Every push" includes branches you may not care about yet
on: branches
FILE
.github/workflows/hello.yml
name: Run Tests on: push: branches: [main] pull_request: branches: [main]
WHY
This says: run when someone pushes straight to main, and run on every pull request that targets main — which means every PR gets tested before it's even merged, not after. This is the exact version of the workflow used as Step 1 of Example 3 in the "How It's Used" tab.
🖱️ Click-by-Click: Where Everything Actually Lives in GitHub's UI
Every screen below is described exactly as the real GitHub UI looks and is laid out — so nothing here looks unfamiliar the first time you open the real thing.
01
Where the file physically goes
One folder, one exact name — GitHub only looks in this one place
folder structure
PATH
your-repo/ ├── .github/ │ └── workflows/ │ └── ci.yml ← any .yml file in here is a workflow ├── src/ ├── package.json └── README.md
WHY
That's the entire rule. .github/workflows/ — that exact folder name, that exact spelling, in the repo root. GitHub scans this one folder. You can have as many .yml files in there as you want; each one is a completely separate, independent workflow.
02
The Actions tab, the first time you ever open it
If a repo has no workflows yet, GitHub offers to help you write one
Actions tab
UI
Get started with GitHub Actions GitHub Actions can help you automate your workflow. ▸ Simple workflow a basic starter file ▸ Node.js test a Node.js project ▸ Docker image build and push an image ... more suggested templates, based on files already in your repo or set up a workflow yourself →
WHY
GitHub actually detects what's in your repo — if it sees a package.json, it suggests a Node.js template; if it sees a Dockerfile, it suggests a Docker template. Clicking "set up a workflow yourself" just opens a blank editor already pointed at .github/workflows/main.yml, ready to commit.
03
You push — a run appears in the list
Every push or PR that matches your trigger adds one row here
workflow runs list
UI — while it's running
● Run Tests #14 Push · main · you · 12s so far
UI — once it finishes
✓ Run Tests #14 Push · main · you · Success · 38s
WHY
A hollow yellow dot means it's currently in progress. A green checkmark means every job in that run finished with exit code 0. A red ✕ means at least one job failed. This exact list is what "the workflow ran" actually looks like in practice — this is what Step 4 of Example 3 walks through inside one real pipeline.
04
Click into the run → click into the job → live steps
Every single step you wrote shows up here, in order, with its own log
job step list
UI
✓ Set up job 1s ✓ Checkout code 1s ✓ Set up Node 3s ✓ npm install 14s ✓ npm test 17s ✓ Complete job 0s
WHY
"Set up job" and "Complete job" are added automatically by GitHub — everything between them is exactly the steps: list you wrote in the YAML, in the same order. Click any row to expand its full raw terminal output — genuinely the same output you'd see running it locally.
05
Where secrets actually live
Never in the YAML file — always in repo settings, encrypted
Settings → Secrets
UI PATH
Repo → Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions Repository secrets [ New repository secret ] DOCKERHUB_TOKEN Updated 2 days ago SERVER_SSH_KEY Updated 2 days ago
WHY
You type the value in once here — GitHub encrypts it. From then on, your workflow only ever references the name: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}. It's automatically masked as *** if it ever shows up in a log by accident. This is the only correct place for passwords, API keys, or tokens — never paste one directly into a .yml file.
06
Made a mistake? Re-run it, or cancel it
No need to push a new commit just to try again
••• menu
UI
On a finished run, top-right ••• ↻ Re-run all jobs ↻ Re-run failed jobs ⤓ Download log archive On a run that's still in progress, top-right ✕ Cancel run
WHY
"Re-run failed jobs" only re-runs what actually failed — useful when a test flaked for an unrelated reason and you don't want to wait for the whole thing again. "Cancel run" stops a run mid-flight, e.g. you just noticed the code isn't ready and don't want it to finish deploying.
🎯 Foundational Q&A
GA1What's the actual difference between a workflow, a job, and a step?▼
ANSWER
Workflow = one YAML file, the whole automation. Job = a group of steps that all run together on one machine — a workflow can have several jobs, and by default they all start in parallel. Step = one task inside a job, and steps inside a job always run in order, top to bottom.

workflow = filejob = machine + parallelstep = task in order
GA2What actually triggers a workflow to run?▼
ANSWER
An event defined under on:. Most common: push (code lands on a branch), pull_request (a PR is opened or updated), workflow_dispatch (someone clicks a manual "Run workflow" button), and schedule (a cron expression, e.g. "every night at 2am"). If none of these match, the workflow simply never runs.

pushpull_requestworkflow_dispatch = manualschedule = cron
GA3Why never hardcode an API key or password directly in the YAML file?▼
ANSWER
The workflow file is committed to Git — meaning it's in your repo's full history forever, visible to anyone with read access, even if you delete the line in a later commit. Secrets stored in Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions are encrypted, never appear in the file, and get automatically masked as *** in logs even if a step accidentally prints them.

git history is foreversecrets = encrypted + masked
GA4What is a "runner," exactly?▼
ANSWER
A temporary virtual machine GitHub spins up fresh, just to execute one job, then destroys the moment that job is done. Nothing you install or write to disk during a run survives to the next one — that's intentional, it guarantees every run starts from the exact same clean state. runs-on: ubuntu-latest is the free, default option; self-hosted runners (your own machine) are also possible for special hardware or private-network access.

fresh every rundisposableubuntu-latest = free default
GA5If a workflow has two jobs, do they run one after the other, or at the same time?▼
ANSWER
At the same time, by default — jobs are parallel unless you say otherwise. To force one job to wait for another, add needs: job-name. E.g. a deploy job with needs: test won't start until the test job has fully succeeded — exactly what stops broken code from ever reaching a deploy step.

jobs = parallel by defaultneeds: = wait for another job
GA6When should you NOT reach for GitHub Actions yet?▼
ANSWER
When you're the only person on the project and there's nothing automated to check yet — no tests, no build step. Writing a workflow at that point is practicing YAML syntax, not solving a real problem. Add it the moment there's a test suite to run automatically or a second person whose code you need checked before it lands next to yours.

see Stage 1 aboveautomation needs something to automate
🐙
Workflow file → trigger → runner → jobs → steps
Start with one workflow: tests on every push. | Add build-checking once there's something to build. | Add deploy only once you trust both of those. | Secrets always live in Settings, never in the YAML. | See it all wired into one real pipeline in 🎬 How It's Used → Example 3.
🐙 GitHub Actions for DevOps — built for someone who has never touched it. If the words "workflow," "job," "runner," or "on: push" mean nothing to you yet, you're exactly who this tab is for. No assumptions, no skipped steps.
🐣 Start Here — What Is GitHub Actions, Really?
🏫 Think of it like a homework auto-checker
📄
You turn in homework
(you push code to GitHub)
→
🤖
A robot checks it instantly
(runs the checklist you wrote)
→
✅
You get a pass/fail before anyone looks
(green ✅ or red ❌ on GitHub)
In plain words: GitHub Actions is a robot that lives inside GitHub and watches your repository. You write down a checklist once — "run the tests," "make sure it still builds" — save it as a file, and from then on, every time you push code, the robot automatically runs through that exact checklist on a brand-new, clean computer. It never forgets a step, never gets tired, and never skips something because it's in a rush. That's the entire idea. Everything else on this page is just details on top of that one concept.
Why does this even need to exist? Without it, "did I break anything?" only gets answered when a human remembers to check — by running tests by hand, or worse, after a real user hits the bug in production. GitHub Actions moves that check to happen automatically, on every single change, before a human ever needs to notice.
🔤 The 5 Words You Actually Need to Know First
Not a dense reference table yet — just five plain-English ideas, in the order they matter.
1. Workflow
The checklist itself. A single file that says what to check and when.
2. Trigger
The moment that starts the checklist — usually "someone pushed code."
3. Runner
The brand-new, empty computer GitHub gives you just for this one check.
4. Job
One whole section of the checklist, run entirely on one runner.
5. Step
One single line of that checklist — done in order, one at a time.
# the smallest possible workflow — read it top to bottom, out loud:
name: "Check my code"   # just a label, for humans
on: push                      # the TRIGGER — "run this whenever code is pushed"
jobs:
  check-it:                           # the JOB — you can name it anything
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest   # the RUNNER — a free, brand-new Linux machine
    steps:
      - run: echo "Hello!"     # a STEP — one single task
That's really it. Save that as .github/workflows/check.yml inside any GitHub repo, push it, and click the Actions tab on GitHub — you'll watch that exact file run, live, in your browser. Every other feature you'll ever use in GitHub Actions is just adding more steps, more jobs, or fancier triggers on top of this same four-part shape.

🎭 Real Scenarios — Learn GitHub Actions by Solving the Problem First
Read the situation, think about what you'd actually write, then click ▶ Run to reveal the YAML and why.
1
The situation: You just wrote your first test suite and want it to run automatically every time anyone pushes code.
What would you write?
on: push
jobs:
test:
runs-on: ubuntu-latest
steps:
- uses: actions/checkout@v4
- run: npm test
✓ Tests passed (12 passed, 0 failed) — 8s
Why this shape: checkout first (the runner starts empty), then run the actual test command — this is genuinely the single most common workflow that exists, and the right first one to add to any project.
2
The situation: Your test suite now takes 3 minutes because it reinstalls every npm package from scratch on every single run.
What would you write?
- uses: actions/cache@v4
with:
path: ~/.npm
key: npm-${{ hashFiles('package-lock.json') }}
Cache restored from key: npm-8f2a1c...
npm install completed in 4s (was 45s)
Why this shape: caching keys off the lockfile's hash — if dependencies haven't changed, the cache hits and install becomes nearly instant; change the lockfile, and a fresh cache is built automatically.
3
The situation: You need to verify your app works on both Node 18 and Node 20 before merging, without copy-pasting the whole job twice.
What would you write?
strategy:
matrix:
node-version: [18, 20]
steps:
- uses: actions/setup-node@v4
with:
node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
✓ test (node-version: 18) — passed
✓ test (node-version: 20) — passed
Why this shape: matrix runs the exact same job once per combination automatically — one job definition, two real runs, zero duplicated YAML.
4
The situation: Your deploy step needs a database password, and you know it can never go directly in the YAML file.
What would you write?
- run: ./deploy.sh
env:
DB_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.DB_PASSWORD }}
Deploying...
Connected to database *** (value automatically masked in every log)
Why this shape: the real value lives only in Settings → Secrets, encrypted — the YAML just references its name, and GitHub automatically hides it if a step ever accidentally prints it.
5
The situation: A deploy job must never run unless the test job passed first — no exceptions.
What would you write?
jobs:
test:
runs-on: ubuntu-latest
steps: [...]
deploy:
needs: test
runs-on: ubuntu-latest
steps: [...]
✓ test — passed
✓ deploy — started only after test succeeded
Why this shape: jobs run in parallel by default — needs: is the one line that forces an order, and if the job it needs fails, deploy is skipped entirely, automatically.
6
The situation: You want to build a Docker image and push it to a registry every time code lands on main.
What would you write?
on:
push:
branches: [main]
steps:
- uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
with:
push: true
tags: myapp:${{ github.sha }}
Successfully pushed myapp:a3f9d2c
Why this shape: tagging the image with the commit SHA means every build is uniquely traceable back to the exact code that produced it — no ambiguous "latest" guessing later.
7
The situation: Deploying to production should require a real human to click approve first — no fully automatic deploys to prod.
What would you write?
jobs:
deploy:
environment: production
runs-on: ubuntu-latest
steps: [...]
Waiting for approval on environment "production"...
Approved by ibrahiem17 — deploy proceeding
Why this shape: an environment with required reviewers configured in Settings pauses the job until someone with permission clicks approve — a real safety switch for real production.
8
The situation: Someone pushes three commits in quick succession, and you don't want three overlapping deploys racing each other.
What would you write?
concurrency:
group: deploy-production
cancel-in-progress: true
Canceling previous run in group "deploy-production"
Starting latest run
Why this shape: concurrency groups make sure only the newest run in that group survives — the two stale, in-between deploys get canceled automatically instead of racing to production.

🔧 Jenkins — The DevOps Workhorse
Jenkins is the world's most widely deployed open-source automation server. It's the engine that runs CI/CD pipelines at thousands of companies. While GitHub Actions is newer and simpler, Jenkins is still dominant in enterprise environments — and Pakistani software houses use it heavily. If you see "CI/CD" in a job description, there's a 60% chance it means Jenkins.
🤔 WHY Jenkins Exists — The Problem It Solves
😰 Without Jenkins
Dev pushes code → someone manually pulls it → manually runs tests → manually builds Docker image → manually deploys to server → manually checks if it works. Every. Single. Time. One person forgetting a step = broken production.
✅ With Jenkins
Dev pushes code → Jenkins automatically detects the push → runs tests → builds image → pushes to registry → deploys → notifies on Slack. Zero human involvement. Consistent every time. This is CI/CD.
⚖️ Jenkins vs GitHub Actions — When to Use Which
FactorJenkinsGitHub Actions
HostingSelf-hosted (you run the server)Cloud (GitHub manages it)
CostFree (but needs a server — ~$10-20/mo)Free for public repos, paid for private CI minutes
Setup timeHours (install, configure, plugins)Minutes (just add a .yml file)
FlexibilityExtreme — run anywhere, any pipelineHigh — but tied to GitHub ecosystem
Enterprise useDominant — most large companies use itGrowing but newer
Plugin ecosystem1,800+ plugins (Docker, K8s, AWS, Slack...)Marketplace actions
Private network accessYes — runs on your infra, inside VPCNeeds self-hosted runner for private resources
When to chooseEnterprise, complex pipelines, private infra, on-premStartups, public repos, GitHub-first teams
🧠 Core Concepts — What Everything Means
TermTypeWhat it is
PipelineCoreA script that defines your entire CI/CD workflow. Written in Groovy DSL in a file called Jenkinsfile. Lives in your repo root.
JenkinsfileCoreThe file that defines your pipeline. Checked into Git so pipeline changes are versioned alongside code. "Pipeline as Code."
StagePipelineA named phase of the pipeline: Build, Test, Deploy. Stages are shown as boxes in the Jenkins UI — makes failures easy to spot.
StepPipelineA single task inside a stage. sh 'npm test', docker.build(), git clone are all steps.
AgentExecutionWhere the pipeline runs. agent any = any available machine. agent { docker 'node:18' } = run inside a Docker container. agent none = define per stage.
Node / ExecutorInfrastructureA machine that runs jobs. The Jenkins master delegates work to agents/nodes. Each node can run N executors (parallel jobs).
BuildRunA single execution of a pipeline. Each build gets a number (#1, #2...) and a status: SUCCESS, FAILURE, UNSTABLE, ABORTED.
Job / ProjectConfigA configured task in Jenkins. Freestyle Job = click-based config. Pipeline Job = Jenkinsfile. Multibranch Pipeline = auto-creates jobs per branch.
WorkspaceFilesThe directory on the agent where the build runs and files are checked out. Cleaned between builds with cleanWs().
ArtifactOutputBuild output you want to keep: Docker images, .jar files, test reports. Archived with archiveArtifacts.
TriggerAutomationWhat kicks off a build. Git push (webhook), schedule (cron), manual, or upstream job completion.
WebhookIntegrationGitHub/GitLab pings Jenkins the second code is pushed. Jenkins then automatically starts the pipeline. No polling needed.
CredentialSecuritySecrets stored in Jenkins (passwords, tokens, SSH keys). Referenced in pipeline as credentials('myid') — never hardcoded.
PluginExtensionJenkins gets all its integrations from plugins. Docker, Kubernetes, AWS, Slack, GitHub, SonarQube — all plugins. 1,800+ available.
Blue OceanUIA modern Jenkins UI plugin that shows pipelines as visual flowcharts instead of raw console logs. Easier to understand.
Shared LibraryReuseReusable Groovy code shared across multiple Jenkinsfiles. Like a function library for your pipelines. Stored in a separate Git repo.

📝 Jenkinsfile Examples — From Simple to Production
Jenkinsfile — Basic Pipeline (start here)Groovy DSL
// Every Jenkinsfile starts with 'pipeline { }' pipeline { // 'agent any' = run on any available Jenkins node/executor agent any // environment block: define env vars available to all stages environment { APP_NAME = 'my-node-app' NODE_ENV = 'production' } stages { stage('Checkout') { steps { // Pull the code from Git (Jenkins does this automatically // if you set up a Multibranch Pipeline — or call it explicitly) git branch: 'main', url: 'https://github.com/ibrahiem/myapp.git' } } stage('Install') { steps { // sh = run a shell command on the agent sh 'npm ci' } } stage('Test') { steps { sh 'npm test' } post { // always runs regardless of test result always { // Publish JUnit test results to Jenkins UI junit 'test-results/**/*.xml' } } } stage('Build') { steps { sh 'npm run build' } } } // post: runs after ALL stages finish post { success { echo '✅ Pipeline succeeded!' // slackSend channel: '#deploys', message: "Build #${BUILD_NUMBER} passed" } failure { echo '❌ Pipeline FAILED — check console output' mail to: 'team@company.com', subject: "Build Failed: ${JOB_NAME}" } always { // Clean up workspace to save disk space cleanWs() } } }
💡 Key rule: The pipeline only fails if a sh command exits with a non-zero code. npm test failing → exits 1 → stage fails → pipeline stops. This is why your tests must exit properly.
Jenkinsfile — Docker Build + Push to RegistryGroovy DSL
pipeline { agent any environment { // credentials() fetches a Jenkins credential by ID // NEVER put passwords directly in the Jenkinsfile DOCKER_HUB_CREDS = credentials('docker-hub-credentials') IMAGE_NAME = "ibrahiem/myapp" IMAGE_TAG = "${BUILD_NUMBER}" // Jenkins built-in: build number } stages { stage('Checkout') { steps { checkout scm // auto-checks out the triggering branch } } stage('Build Docker Image') { steps { script { // Using the Docker Pipeline plugin dockerImage = docker.build("${IMAGE_NAME}:${IMAGE_TAG}") } } } stage('Push to Docker Hub') { steps { script { // withRegistry logs in, pushes, then logs out automatically docker.withRegistry('https://registry.hub.docker.com', 'docker-hub-credentials') { dockerImage.push("${IMAGE_TAG}") dockerImage.push('latest') // also tag as 'latest' } } } } stage('Cleanup') { steps { // Remove local image to free disk space on the Jenkins agent sh "docker rmi ${IMAGE_NAME}:${IMAGE_TAG} || true" } } } }
💡 credentials('id') injects the secret as env vars at runtime. For username/password credentials, Jenkins auto-creates _USR and _PSW suffixes. The raw password never appears in logs — Jenkins masks it with ****.
Jenkinsfile — Full Production CI/CD PipelineGroovy DSL
pipeline { agent any environment { DOCKER_CREDS = credentials('docker-hub-creds') AWS_CREDS = credentials('aws-credentials') EC2_KEY = credentials('ec2-ssh-key') IMAGE = "ibrahiem/myapp:${BUILD_NUMBER}" EC2_HOST = '54.12.34.56' } // Automatically trigger on Git push (requires GitHub webhook setup) triggers { githubPush() } options { timeout(time: 30, unit: 'MINUTES') // kill if takes > 30min disableConcurrentBuilds() // no parallel runs of same job buildDiscarder(logRotator(numToKeepStr: '10')) // keep last 10 builds } stages { stage('🔍 Checkout') { steps { checkout scm echo "Building branch: ${BRANCH_NAME}, commit: ${GIT_COMMIT}" } } stage('📦 Install') { steps { sh 'npm ci --prefer-offline' } } stage('🧪 Test') { steps { sh 'npm test -- --ci --reporters=jest-junit' } post { always { junit 'junit.xml' } } } stage('🔍 Code Quality') { steps { // SonarQube static analysis (requires SonarQube plugin + server) withSonarQubeEnv('SonarQube') { sh 'sonar-scanner -Dsonar.projectKey=myapp' } } } stage('🐳 Docker Build + Push') { when { // Only run this stage when on main branch branch 'main' } steps { script { docker.withRegistry('', 'docker-hub-creds') { def img = docker.build("${IMAGE}") img.push() img.push('latest') } } } } stage('🚀 Deploy to Staging') { when { branch 'main' } steps { // SSH into EC2 and redeploy sshagent(['ec2-ssh-key']) { sh """ ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no ubuntu@${EC2_HOST} ' docker pull ibrahiem/myapp:latest docker stop myapp || true docker rm myapp || true docker run -d -p 80:3000 --name myapp --restart=always ibrahiem/myapp:latest ' """ } } } stage('✅ Smoke Test') { when { branch 'main' } steps { // Hit the health endpoint after deploy — fail if not 200 sh """ sleep 10 curl --fail http://${EC2_HOST}/health || exit 1 """ } } stage('🚢 Deploy to Production') { when { branch 'main' } steps { // Manual approval gate before prod input message: 'Deploy to PRODUCTION? (approve within 30 min)', ok: 'Deploy', submitter: 'ibrahiem,senior-devops' sh './scripts/deploy-prod.sh' } } } post { success { slackSend( channel: '#deployments', color: 'good', message: "✅ Build #${BUILD_NUMBER} deployed: ${JOB_NAME}" ) } failure { slackSend( channel: '#deployments', color: 'danger', message: "❌ Build #${BUILD_NUMBER} FAILED at: ${STAGE_NAME}" ) } always { cleanWs() } } }
Jenkinsfile — Multi-Branch Strategy (real-world)Groovy DSL
// This single Jenkinsfile handles ALL branches differently // Set up a "Multibranch Pipeline" job in Jenkins to use this pipeline { agent any stages { stage('Test') { steps { sh 'npm ci && npm test' } } stage('Build Image') { // Only build Docker image on main or develop — not on every feature branch when { anyOf { branch 'main' branch 'develop' } } steps { sh "docker build -t myapp:${GIT_COMMIT[0..7]} ." } } stage('Deploy Staging') { // Auto-deploy develop branch to staging environment when { branch 'develop' } steps { sh './deploy.sh staging' } } stage('Deploy Production') { // Only main branch goes to production — and needs approval when { branch 'main' } steps { input 'Approve production deployment?' sh './deploy.sh production' } } } } /* Branch strategy with Multibranch Pipeline: feature/* → runs Test only develop → Test + Build + Deploy Staging (auto) main → Test + Build + Deploy Production (with approval) PR → Test only (Jenkins creates a PR job automatically) */
💡 Multibranch Pipeline is the most powerful Jenkins job type. It scans your repo, auto-creates a Jenkins job for every branch that has a Jenkinsfile, and deletes the job when the branch is deleted. One Jenkins job config → all branches covered automatically.
Jenkinsfile — Parallel Stages (faster pipelines)Groovy DSL
pipeline { agent any stages { stage('Checkout') { steps { checkout scm } } // Run unit tests, linting, and security scan simultaneously // Total time = slowest job (not sum of all) stage('Quality Checks') { parallel { stage('Unit Tests') { steps { sh 'npm run test:unit' } } stage('Lint') { steps { sh 'npm run lint' } } stage('Security Scan') { steps { // npm audit checks for known vulnerabilities sh 'npm audit --audit-level=high' } } stage('Integration Tests') { steps { sh 'npm run test:integration' } } } } // This stage only runs after ALL parallel stages above pass stage('Build & Deploy') { steps { sh 'docker build -t myapp:latest . && ./deploy.sh' } } } } /* Without parallel: Unit(45s) + Lint(12s) + Security(20s) + Integration(40s) = 117s With parallel: max(45s, 12s, 20s, 40s) = 45s total ← 60% faster */

🔌 Essential Jenkins Plugins — Know These by Name
📦 Pipeline
The core plugin. Enables the pipeline { } DSL in Jenkinsfiles. Without this, you only have Freestyle jobs. Installed by default in modern Jenkins.
🐳 Docker Pipeline
Adds docker.build(), docker.withRegistry(), agent { docker 'node:18' }. Lets you run build steps inside containers. Essential for any Docker workflow.
🌿 Git / GitHub
Git integration + GitHub webhook support. Enables checkout scm and auto-triggering pipelines on push. Usually one of the first plugins you install.
🔐 Credentials Binding
Enables credentials('id') and withCredentials(). Lets you securely inject secrets into pipelines as env vars. Values are masked in logs. Critical for security.
☁️ AWS Steps
Adds native AWS CLI steps. Push to ECR, update ECS services, invalidate CloudFront. Easier than raw shell AWS CLI calls in pipelines.
☸️ Kubernetes
Run Jenkins agents as Kubernetes pods. Each build spins up a fresh pod, runs, then destroys itself. No persistent agents to maintain. Modern Jenkins at scale.
💬 Slack Notification
Adds slackSend() step. Post build results, deployment notifications, and alerts directly to Slack channels. Most teams set this up day one.
🔍 SonarQube Scanner
Static code analysis integration. Adds withSonarQubeEnv(). Runs code quality + security vulnerability scans as a pipeline stage. Common in enterprise.
📊 Blue Ocean
Modern visual UI for pipelines. Shows stages as swimlanes, highlights failures clearly. Much better than the default Jenkins UI for understanding pipeline results.
🔑 SSH Agent
Adds sshagent() wrapper. Lets you SSH into servers using keys stored in Jenkins Credentials. Used for deploy-over-SSH workflows.
📌 Built-In Jenkins Environment Variables
VariableExample ValueWhat it contains
BUILD_NUMBER47Auto-incrementing build number. Use as Docker image tag: myapp:${BUILD_NUMBER}
BUILD_ID2024-01-15_10-30-00Build timestamp. Unique per build.
JOB_NAMEmy-app/mainFull job name including folder. Use in notifications.
BRANCH_NAMEfeature/authGit branch that triggered this build. Use in when { branch '...' } conditions.
GIT_COMMITa3f8c22d91b4...Full SHA of the triggering commit. Use first 7 chars as image tag for traceability.
GIT_BRANCHorigin/mainFull ref of the branch.
WORKSPACE/var/jenkins/workspace/jobAbsolute path to the build workspace on the agent.
JENKINS_URLhttp://jenkins:8080/Base URL of Jenkins. Useful for building links in notifications.
BUILD_URLhttp://jenkins:8080/job/47/Direct link to this build. Include in Slack messages so team can jump to logs.
STAGE_NAMETestName of the currently running stage. Use in failure notifications: "Failed at: ${STAGE_NAME}"
🔗 Setting Up GitHub → Jenkins Webhooks
① Jenkins side — expose it publicly
Jenkins must be accessible from GitHub's servers.
If running locally for testing: use ngrok: ngrok http 8080 → gets a public URL.
In production: expose Jenkins behind Nginx with a real domain + SSL.
Install the GitHub plugin in Jenkins.
② GitHub side — add webhook
GitHub repo → Settings → Webhooks → Add webhook
Payload URL: http://your-jenkins.com/github-webhook/
Content type: application/json
Trigger: Just the push event (or PR events too)
Click Add Webhook → GitHub sends a test ping.
③ Jenkins job — enable trigger
Job → Configure → Build Triggers → ✅ GitHub hook trigger for GITScm polling

Or in Jenkinsfile (Pipeline as Code):
triggers { githubPush() }

Now every push to GitHub instantly starts a Jenkins build. No polling. No delay.
🎯 Jenkins Interview Q&A
JK01"What is a Jenkinsfile and why should it be committed to Git?"▼
ANSWER
A Jenkinsfile is a text file that defines a Jenkins pipeline using Groovy DSL. It lives in the root of your repository.

Committing it to Git gives you Pipeline as Code: the pipeline definition changes are versioned alongside the application code. If you break the pipeline, you can git blame to find who changed it. You can have different Jenkinsfiles per branch — the main branch deploys to production, develop deploys to staging. New team members get the pipeline automatically when they clone the repo. No clicking in the Jenkins UI to set up a pipeline.

pipeline as codeversioned with appper-branch pipelinesno manual UI config
JK02"What's the difference between Declarative and Scripted pipelines?"▼
ANSWER
Declarative Pipeline — uses the structured pipeline { stages { stage { steps { } } } } syntax. Opinionated, easier to read, has built-in validation. Best practice for most teams. What all the examples in this cheatsheet use.

Scripted Pipeline — starts with node { }, is pure Groovy code. More flexible but harder to read and maintain. No structure enforcement. Used when you need to do something Declarative can't express.

Recommendation: Always use Declarative. If you need a one-off complex Groovy logic inside it, wrap it in a script { } block within a Declarative pipeline — best of both worlds.

Declarative = structured, recommendedScripted = flexible, legacyuse script{} block for complex logic
JK03"How do you store and use secrets in Jenkins? Why not hardcode them?"▼
ANSWER
Jenkins has a built-in Credentials store. You add secrets there (Manage Jenkins → Credentials) and give them an ID. In the Jenkinsfile you reference them by ID — the actual value is never in the code.

Types: Username/Password (Docker Hub, registries), Secret Text (API tokens, Slack tokens), SSH Private Key (deploy to servers), AWS Credentials.

Usage in pipeline: environment { CREDS = credentials('my-id') } — Jenkins injects as CREDS_USR and CREDS_PSW. Or use withCredentials([string(credentialsId: 'id', variable: 'TOKEN')]) { sh '...$TOKEN...' }

Why not hardcode: Secrets in a Jenkinsfile get committed to Git. Anyone with repo access sees them. Jenkins masks credential values in logs automatically — if you hardcode them, they print in plain text.

Jenkins Credentials storecredentials('id') in pipelinevalues masked in logsnever in Git
JK04"A Jenkins build is failing but you don't know why. Walk me through debugging it."▼
DEBUG SCRIPT
"First I check the Console Output of the failing build — the full log shows exactly which shell command failed and what error it returned. 90% of issues are visible here.

I look for the stage that turned red in Blue Ocean, then find the exact failed sh step and its exit code.

Common causes: missing credentials (check the Credentials store), Docker daemon not running on agent, network issue pulling image, test actually failing (which is correct behavior — fix the code), disk full on agent, permission denied on workspace.

If the error is unclear, I add a debug step: sh 'env' to print all env vars, or sh 'docker info' to check Docker status. I can also replay the build with modified Jenkinsfile using the Replay button — no code commit needed.

If the agent is the issue: check System → Nodes → view the agent log."

Console Output firstBlue Ocean for visualReplay to test fixescheck agent nodes
JK05"What is a Jenkins agent/node and why would you use multiple?"▼
ANSWER
The Jenkins master manages the UI, schedules jobs, and stores build history. Agents (nodes) are the machines that actually run the pipeline steps.

Why multiple agents: Isolation — each build gets a clean environment. Parallelism — run multiple builds simultaneously. Different environments — one agent for Node.js builds, one for Java, one with Docker. Security — production deployment agent can be in the private network, inaccessible from the internet. Resource scaling — add more agents when build queue grows.

Modern approach (Kubernetes agent): agent { kubernetes { yaml '...' } } — Jenkins spins up a fresh Kubernetes pod per build, runs the pipeline, then destroys the pod. Zero agent maintenance. Each build is perfectly isolated.

master = scheduler + UIagents = executionK8s agents = modern, ephemeralisolation per build
JK06"How do you trigger a Jenkins pipeline automatically on a Git push?"▼
ANSWER
Two approaches:

1. Webhook (recommended): GitHub sends an HTTP POST to http://jenkins/github-webhook/ the instant code is pushed. Jenkins receives it and immediately starts the build. Zero delay. Requires Jenkins to be publicly accessible or GitHub Enterprise with network access.

2. Polling (fallback): Jenkins checks Git on a schedule: triggers { pollSCM('H/5 * * * *') } = check every 5 minutes. Works even if Jenkins is behind a firewall. But introduces up to 5-minute delay.

In the Jenkinsfile: triggers { githubPush() } for webhooks or triggers { pollSCM('H * * * *') } for hourly polling.

Recommendation: Always set up webhooks for production. Use polling only when network constraints prevent webhooks (e.g., Jenkins is in a private VPC with no public IP).

webhook = instant, recommendedpolling = delayed, fallbacktriggers{} block in Jenkinsfile
🐳 Running Jenkins with Docker (fastest way to start)
docker-compose.yml — Jenkins + Docker-in-DockerYAML
# docker-compose.jenkins.yml version: '3.8' services: jenkins: image: jenkins/jenkins:lts # LTS = Long Term Support (stable) container_name: jenkins restart: unless-stopped ports: - "8080:8080" # Jenkins UI - "50000:50000" # Agent communication port volumes: - jenkins-data:/var/jenkins_home # Persist jobs, configs, builds - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock # Docker-in-Docker environment: - JAVA_OPTS=-Djenkins.install.runSetupWizard=false # skip wizard (optional) volumes: jenkins-data: --- # Start Jenkins: # docker compose -f docker-compose.jenkins.yml up -d # # Get initial admin password: # docker exec jenkins cat /var/jenkins_home/secrets/initialAdminPassword # # Open: http://localhost:8080 # Install suggested plugins → create admin user → done! # # IMPORTANT: Mount /var/run/docker.sock so Jenkins can run Docker commands # inside pipelines (docker build, docker push, etc.)
🔧
The path from zero to Jenkins in 30 minutes
Run Jenkins with Docker Compose above. Install suggested plugins. Create a Freestyle job first (just to understand the UI). Then create a Pipeline job pointing to a GitHub repo with a Jenkinsfile. Add a webhook. Push a commit. Watch it build automatically. That moment when your code push triggers a Jenkins build is when DevOps clicks.
