🐳 Docker — Practical Use Cases
01
Build a Docker Image from a Node.js App
Package your app into a portable image that runs anywhere
Dockerfile
FILE
./Dockerfile
# Use official Node.js 20 base image FROM node:20-alpine # Set working directory inside container WORKDIR /app # Copy package files and install dependencies FIRST (caching!) COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm install # Copy the rest of the source code COPY . . # Expose the port your app listens on EXPOSE 3000 # Command to start the app CMD ["node", "index.js"]
FILE
./.dockerignore
node_modules .git .env *.log
CMD
# Build the image — tag it as myapp:1.0 docker build -t myapp:1.0 . # List images to confirm it was created docker images
OUTPUT
[1/4] FROM docker.io/library/node:20-alpine [2/4] WORKDIR /app [3/4] RUN npm install [4/4] COPY . . => exporting to image => naming to docker.io/library/myapp:1.0 REPOSITORY TAG IMAGE ID SIZE myapp 1.0 a3f8c91b7e2d 185MB
WHY
COPY package*.json + RUN npm install before COPY . . — Docker caches each layer. If you change only app code, npm install layer is reused → much faster rebuilds.
02
Run a Container with Port Mapping & Env Vars
Start your image as a running container, map ports, inject config
docker run
CMD
# Run container: # -d = detached (background) # --name = give it a name # -p 8080:3000 = host:container port map # -e = inject environment variable docker run -d --name my-api -p 8080:3000 -e NODE_ENV=production -e PORT=3000 myapp:1.0 # Check it is running docker ps # View live logs docker logs -f my-api # Stop the container docker stop my-api
OUTPUT
CONTAINER ID NAME STATUS PORTS d7a3b891f2c1 my-api Up 3 seconds 0.0.0.0:8080->3000/tcp Server listening on port 3000 Connected to DB
WHY
-p 8080:3000 means "on my laptop, go to localhost:8080 — it forwards to port 3000 inside the container". The container stays isolated; you only open the ports you need.
03
Multi-Container App with Docker Compose
Run Node.js API + PostgreSQL together with one command
compose
FILE
./docker-compose.yml
version: '3.8' services: api: build: . # builds from your Dockerfile ports: - "8080:3000" environment: - DATABASE_URL=postgres://postgres:secret@db:5432/mydb depends_on: - db # wait for db to start first volumes: - .:/app # live-reload: sync code into container - /app/node_modules # but DON'T sync node_modules db: image: postgres:16-alpine environment: - POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret - POSTGRES_DB=mydb volumes: - pg_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data # persist DB data volumes: pg_data:
CMD
# Start everything docker compose up -d # See what's running docker compose ps # Tear down (keeps volumes) docker compose down # Tear down AND delete data volumes docker compose down -v
OUTPUT
✔ Container myapp-db-1 Started ✔ Container myapp-api-1 Started NAME SERVICE STATUS PORTS myapp-api-1 api running 0.0.0.0:8080->3000/tcp myapp-db-1 db running 5432/tcp
04
Push Image to Docker Hub (Registry)
Publish your image so any server or CI pipeline can pull it
push / pull
CMD
# 1. Login to Docker Hub docker login # → prompts for username + password/token # 2. Tag the image with your Docker Hub username # format: username/repo:tag docker tag myapp:1.0 ibrahiem17/myapp:1.0 docker tag myapp:1.0 ibrahiem17/myapp:latest # 3. Push both tags docker push ibrahiem17/myapp:1.0 docker push ibrahiem17/myapp:latest # 4. On any other machine — pull and run it docker pull ibrahiem17/myapp:1.0 docker run -p 8080:3000 ibrahiem17/myapp:1.0
OUTPUT
The push refers to repository [docker.io/ibrahiem17/myapp] 1.0: digest: sha256:a3f8...7e2d size: 1234 latest: digest: sha256:a3f8...7e2d size: 1234
WHY
Always push both a version tag (1.0) and latest. Kubernetes manifests can pin to 1.0 for stability. CI pipelines use latest for dev builds. Never use only latest in production — you can't roll back a tag that moves.
05
Multi-Stage Build — Shrink Production Image
Use a builder stage; copy only the compiled output into a tiny final image
multi-stage
FILE
./Dockerfile
# ── STAGE 1: Builder (has all dev tools + source) ────────── FROM node:20-alpine AS builder WORKDIR /app COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci # clean install (faster than npm install in CI) COPY . . RUN npm run build # e.g. compiles TypeScript → dist/ # ── STAGE 2: Production (only the dist/ output) ──────────── FROM node:20-alpine AS production WORKDIR /app COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci --omit=dev # no devDependencies in prod COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist EXPOSE 3000 CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]
CMD
docker build -t myapp:prod . docker images | grep myapp
OUTPUT
REPOSITORY TAG IMAGE ID SIZE myapp prod b2d9e44c8f1a 72MB ← production (tiny!) myapp 1.0 a3f8c91b7e2d 185MB ← dev (had all tools)
WHY
Builder stage has compilers, test runners, source code — none of which belongs in production. Multi-stage build keeps the final image lean (smaller attack surface, faster pulls, cheaper ECR storage).
06
Volumes — Persist Data Between Container Restarts
Without a volume, all data inside a container dies when it stops
volumes
CMD
# Create a named volume docker volume create pgdata # Run PostgreSQL mounting the volume to its data dir docker run -d --name mydb -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16-alpine # Stop and delete the container — data SURVIVES in the volume docker stop mydb && docker rm mydb # Start a NEW container, re-mount same volume — data is back! docker run -d --name mydb-v2 -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16 # Inspect where the volume lives on disk docker volume inspect pgdata
OUTPUT
[ { "Name": "pgdata", "Mountpoint": "/var/lib/docker/volumes/pgdata/_data", "Driver": "local" } ]
WHY
Containers are ephemeral by design — their filesystem is wiped on removal. Named volumes are managed by Docker and live outside the container lifecycle. Always use volumes for databases, uploads, and anything that must survive a restart.
☸️ Kubernetes — Practical Use Cases
01
Deploy an App — Deployment + Service
The two files every K8s app needs: a Deployment (runs pods) + Service (exposes them)
deploy
FILE
./k8s/deployment.yml
apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: myapp labels: app: myapp spec: replicas: 3 # run 3 pods selector: matchLabels: app: myapp template: metadata: labels: app: myapp spec: containers: - name: myapp image: ibrahiem17/myapp:1.0 ports: - containerPort: 3000 resources: requests: cpu: "100m" # 0.1 CPU core memory: "128Mi" limits: cpu: "500m" # max 0.5 CPU core memory: "256Mi"
FILE
./k8s/service.yml
apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: myapp-svc spec: selector: app: myapp # routes traffic to pods with this label ports: - port: 80 # service port targetPort: 3000 # pod port type: LoadBalancer # cloud gives you an external IP
CMD
kubectl apply -f k8s/ kubectl get deployments kubectl get pods kubectl get services
OUTPUT
NAME READY UP-TO-DATE AVAILABLE myapp 3/3 3 3 NAME READY STATUS myapp-79f8b9d5c-4pqx7 1/1 Running myapp-79f8b9d5c-k2nbt 1/1 Running myapp-79f8b9d5c-v9mzj 1/1 Running NAME TYPE EXTERNAL-IP myapp-svc LoadBalancer 52.14.8.201 ← visit this IP
02
Scale a Deployment Up & Down
Handle traffic spikes in one command — no downtime
scale
CMD
# Scale up to 10 replicas (traffic spike) kubectl scale deployment myapp --replicas=10 # Watch pods come up in real time kubectl get pods -w # Scale back down at night kubectl scale deployment myapp --replicas=2 # Or edit the YAML and reapply kubectl edit deployment myapp # opens vi — change replicas: 10
OUTPUT
deployment.apps/myapp scaled myapp-79f8b9d5c-4pqx7 1/1 Running myapp-79f8b9d5c-k2nbt 1/1 Running myapp-79f8b9d5c-abc12 0/1 ContainerCreating myapp-79f8b9d5c-def34 0/1 ContainerCreating myapp-79f8b9d5c-abc12 1/1 Running ← new pod ready
03
Rolling Update — Deploy New Version with Zero Downtime
K8s replaces pods one-by-one; users never see downtime
rolling update
CMD
# Update image to v2.0 — triggers rolling update kubectl set image deployment/myapp myapp=ibrahiem17/myapp:2.0 # Watch the rollout progress kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp # View rollout history kubectl rollout history deployment/myapp # Something wrong? Roll back to previous version instantly kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp
OUTPUT
Waiting for deployment "myapp" rollout to finish... 1 out of 3 new replicas have been updated... 2 out of 3 new replicas have been updated... deployment "myapp" successfully rolled out # After undo: deployment.apps/myapp rolled back
WHY
K8s won't terminate old pods until new ones are Ready. If the new pod fails health checks, the rollout pauses automatically — your old pods keep serving traffic. This is why you always define readinessProbe in production.
04
ConfigMap — Inject Config Without Rebuilding Image
Separate config from code; change settings without a new deploy
configmap
FILE
./k8s/configmap.yml
apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata: name: myapp-config data: NODE_ENV: production LOG_LEVEL: info MAX_CONNECTIONS: "100"
FILE
./k8s/deployment.yml (updated containers section)
containers: - name: myapp image: ibrahiem17/myapp:1.0 envFrom: - configMapRef: name: myapp-config # all keys become env vars
CMD
kubectl apply -f k8s/configmap.yml kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yml kubectl describe configmap myapp-config
OUTPUT
Name: myapp-config Data ==== LOG_LEVEL: info MAX_CONNECTIONS: 100 NODE_ENV: production
05
Exec into a Running Pod — Debug Live Issues
SSH-equivalent for Kubernetes — get a shell inside any running container
debug
CMD
# Get pod name kubectl get pods # Open a shell INSIDE the pod (like SSH) kubectl exec -it myapp-79f8b9d5c-4pqx7 -- sh # Inside the container now — debug freely: # ls /app check files # cat /app/.env check injected env file # curl localhost:3000/health test the API locally # env | grep NODE check env vars # exit leave the shell # Stream live logs from a specific pod kubectl logs -f myapp-79f8b9d5c-4pqx7 # Describe pod — see events, errors, resource usage kubectl describe pod myapp-79f8b9d5c-4pqx7
OUTPUT
/app # ← you are INSIDE the container now $ curl localhost:3000/health {"status":"ok","db":"connected"} $ env | grep NODE NODE_ENV=production
WHY
CrashLoopBackOff? exec won't work (container keeps dying). Use: kubectl logs myapp-xxx --previous to see logs from the previous crashed instance. Or override the command: kubectl debug pod/myapp-xxx -it --image=busybox
06
Secrets — Store Passwords & Tokens Safely
Like ConfigMap but base64-encoded; never hardcode secrets in your image
secrets
CMD
# Create secret from literal values (never commit this to git!) kubectl create secret generic db-secret --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=supersecret123 --from-literal=JWT_SECRET=myjwtsecret
FILE
./k8s/deployment.yml (add under containers)
envFrom: - configMapRef: name: myapp-config - secretRef: name: db-secret # DB_PASSWORD + JWT_SECRET injected as env vars
OUTPUT
secret/db-secret created # Verify (values are hidden): kubectl get secret db-secret NAME TYPE DATA AGE db-secret Opaque 2 5s
⚡ GitHub Actions — Practical Use Cases
01
Run Tests on Every Push & Pull Request
The most fundamental CI pipeline — catch broken code before it merges
CI
FILE
./.github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI on: push: branches: [main, develop] pull_request: branches: [main] jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Checkout code uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Setup Node.js uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: '20' cache: 'npm' # cache node_modules between runs - name: Install dependencies run: npm ci - name: Run linter run: npm run lint - name: Run tests run: npm test
OUTPUT
✓ Checkout code 2s ✓ Setup Node.js 8s ✓ Install dependencies 12s (cached) ✓ Run linter 3s ✓ Run tests 7s All checks passed ✓ ← green tick on your PR
02
Build & Push Docker Image on Merge to Main
Automatically publish a new versioned image after every successful merge
docker CI/CD
SETUP
Go to GitHub Repo → Settings → Secrets and Variables → Actions
Add: DOCKERHUB_USERNAME = your Docker Hub username
Add: DOCKERHUB_TOKEN = Docker Hub Access Token (not your password)
FILE
./.github/workflows/docker-push.yml
name: Build and Push Docker Image on: push: branches: [main] # only on merge to main jobs: build-push: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Login to Docker Hub uses: docker/login-action@v3 with: username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }} password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }} - name: Build and push uses: docker/build-push-action@v5 with: context: . push: true tags: | ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/myapp:latest ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/myapp:${{ github.sha }}
OUTPUT
✓ Login to Docker Hub ✓ Build and push ibrahiem17/myapp:latest ibrahiem17/myapp:3f8a9b2c... ← git SHA = immutable tag
WHY
Using github.sha as image tag means every commit gets a unique, traceable image. You can always roll back to the exact commit that caused an issue.
03
Deploy to a Server via SSH on Push to Main
SSH into your VPS/EC2 and run deploy commands automatically
CD / SSH
SETUP
In GitHub Secrets add:
SSH_PRIVATE_KEY = your private key content (cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa)
SERVER_HOST = your server IP or domain
SERVER_USER = ubuntu (or ec2-user)
FILE
./.github/workflows/deploy.yml
name: Deploy to Production on: push: branches: [main] jobs: deploy: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Deploy via SSH uses: appleboy/ssh-action@v1.0.3 with: host: ${{ secrets.SERVER_HOST }} username: ${{ secrets.SERVER_USER }} key: ${{ secrets.SSH_PRIVATE_KEY }} script: | cd /opt/myapp git pull origin main docker compose pull docker compose up -d --no-deps docker system prune -f
OUTPUT
✓ Deploy via SSH Connecting to 52.14.8.201... Already on 'main' Pulling ibrahiem17/myapp ... done Recreating myapp-api-1 ... done
04
Parallel Jobs — Run Lint, Test, Security Check Simultaneously
Split slow pipelines into parallel jobs; only proceed if ALL pass
parallel
FILE
./.github/workflows/ci-full.yml
name: Full CI on: [push, pull_request] jobs: lint: # runs in parallel with test + security runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: npm ci && npm run lint test: # runs in parallel with lint + security runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: npm ci && npm test security: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: npm audit --audit-level=high deploy: needs: [lint, test, security] # waits for ALL three if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - run: echo "All checks passed — deploying!"
OUTPUT
lint ────────────── ✓ 18s test ────────────── ✓ 22s ← all ran simultaneously security ───────── ✓ 9s ↓ deploy ──────────── ✓ All checks passed — deploying! Total: 24s ← vs 49s if run sequentially
05
Matrix Strategy — Test on Multiple Node.js Versions
Run the same job across multiple versions/OS in one config block
matrix
FILE
./.github/workflows/matrix.yml
name: Test Matrix on: [push] jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest strategy: matrix: node-version: [18, 20, 22] # spawns 3 parallel jobs steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Use Node ${{ matrix.node-version }} uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }} - run: npm ci && npm test
OUTPUT
test (18) ───── ✓ All tests passed test (20) ───── ✓ All tests passed test (22) ───── ✗ TypeError: Buffer() is deprecated ← caught!
🏗️ Terraform — Practical Use Cases
01
Create an S3 Bucket on AWS
Your first Terraform resource — the classic "Hello World" of IaC
S3 / AWS
FILE
./main.tf
# Tell Terraform to use the AWS provider terraform { required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = "~> 5.0" } } } provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1" } # Declare the S3 bucket resource resource "aws_s3_bucket" "my_bucket" { bucket = "ibrahiem-devops-practice-2024" # must be globally unique tags = { Name = "Practice Bucket" Environment = "Dev" } }
CMD
# 1. Initialize (downloads the AWS provider plugin) terraform init # 2. Preview what will be created — ALWAYS do this first terraform plan # 3. Create the actual resources terraform apply # → type "yes" to confirm # 4. See what Terraform is managing terraform state list
OUTPUT
Initializing provider plugins... Terraform has been successfully initialized! Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy. + aws_s3_bucket.my_bucket bucket: "ibrahiem-devops-practice-2024" tags: { Environment = "Dev", Name = "Practice Bucket" } Apply complete! Resources: 1 added.
02
Provision an EC2 Instance
Launch a virtual machine on AWS with key pair and security group
EC2 / compute
FILE
./ec2.tf
# Security group — allow SSH and HTTP resource "aws_security_group" "web_sg" { name = "web-sg" description = "Allow SSH and HTTP" ingress { from_port = 22 to_port = 22 protocol = "tcp" cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"] # ⚠️ restrict this in production! } ingress { from_port = 80 to_port = 80 protocol = "tcp" cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"] } egress { from_port = 0; to_port = 0; protocol = "-1" cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"] } } # The EC2 instance resource "aws_instance" "web" { ami = "ami-0c02fb55956c7d316" # Amazon Linux 2 (us-east-1) instance_type = "t2.micro" # free tier eligible key_name = "my-key-pair" vpc_security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.web_sg.id] tags = { Name = "WebServer" } } # Print the public IP after apply output "public_ip" { value = aws_instance.web.public_ip }
CMD
terraform plan terraform apply -auto-approve # skip the "yes" prompt # Destroy everything when done (saves cost!) terraform destroy
OUTPUT
Apply complete! Resources: 2 added. Outputs: public_ip = "54.211.48.132" # SSH into it: ssh -i my-key-pair.pem ec2-user@54.211.48.132
03
Variables — Make Your Config Reusable
Stop hardcoding values; use variables so the same code works for dev/staging/prod
variables
FILE
./variables.tf
variable "region" { description = "AWS region to deploy into" type = string default = "us-east-1" } variable "instance_type" { description = "EC2 instance size" type = string default = "t2.micro" } variable "env" { description = "Environment name: dev / staging / prod" type = string }
FILE
./terraform.tfvars (never commit to git if it has secrets!)
region = "eu-west-1" instance_type = "t3.small" env = "staging"
CMD
# Pass vars inline (useful in CI) terraform apply -var="env=prod" -var="instance_type=t3.medium"
OUTPUT
Plan: 1 to add. instance_type = "t3.medium" ← var override applied tags.env = "prod"
04
Remote State — Store tfstate in S3 (Team Setup)
By default state is local; for teams, store it in S3 so everyone shares the same state
remote state
FILE
./backend.tf
terraform { backend "s3" { bucket = "myteam-terraform-state" # must exist already key = "myapp/terraform.tfstate" region = "us-east-1" encrypt = true dynamodb_table = "terraform-locks" # prevents concurrent applies } }
CMD
# Re-initialize to migrate state to S3 terraform init -migrate-state
OUTPUT
Successfully configured the backend "s3"! Terraform will now store state in s3://myteam-terraform-state/myapp/terraform.tfstate
WHY
The DynamoDB table is used for state locking — only one terraform apply can run at a time. Without it, two engineers applying simultaneously could corrupt your state file.
05
Modules — Reuse Infrastructure Patterns
Wrap common patterns into a module so you don't repeat yourself across environments
modules
FILE
./modules/ec2/main.tf
variable "instance_type" {} variable "env" {} resource "aws_instance" "this" { ami = "ami-0c02fb55956c7d316" instance_type = var.instance_type tags = { Name = "${var.env}-server" } } output "ip" { value = aws_instance.this.public_ip }
FILE
./main.tf (using the module)
# Dev server module "dev" { source = "./modules/ec2" instance_type = "t2.micro" env = "dev" } # Prod server module "prod" { source = "./modules/ec2" instance_type = "t3.medium" env = "prod" }
OUTPUT
Plan: 2 to add. + module.dev.aws_instance.this (t2.micro, dev-server) + module.prod.aws_instance.this (t3.medium, prod-server)
🐧 Linux — Practical Use Cases
01
Find & Kill the Process Using a Port
"Port 3000 already in use" — here's how to fix it in 10 seconds
process
CMD
# Find what is using port 3000 lsof -i :3000 # Or with ss (faster on modern systems) ss -tlnp | grep :3000 # Kill the process by PID kill 18423 # If it doesn't die — force kill kill -9 18423 # One-liner: find and kill in one shot lsof -ti :3000 | xargs kill -9
OUTPUT
COMMAND PID TYPE NAME node 18423 IPv6 *:3000 (LISTEN) [18423 killed]
02
Monitor CPU, Memory & Disk in Real Time
The essential commands for understanding what a server is doing right now
monitoring
CMD
# Real-time process + CPU + memory (press q to quit) htop # Disk usage — how full are your drives? df -h # Disk usage — which folder is eating space? du -sh /var/log/* # sorted by size du -sh * | sort -rh | head -20 # Memory usage snapshot free -h # CPU + system overview top # then press M to sort by memory, P for CPU # Network — what ports are open? ss -tlnp
OUTPUT
Filesystem Size Used Avail Use% Mounted on /dev/xvda1 50G 12G 38G 24% / /dev/xvdb1 20G 19G 0.8G 96% /var ← nearly full! total used free Mem: 7.8G 5.1G 2.7G Swap: 2.0G 0.4G 1.6G
03
Set Up a Cron Job — Automate Recurring Tasks
Run scripts on a schedule: backups, cleanup, health checks
cron
FILE
./backup.sh
#!/bin/bash # Daily DB backup script DATE=$(date +%Y-%m-%d) BACKUP_DIR=/opt/backups mkdir -p $BACKUP_DIR # Dump PostgreSQL database pg_dump -U postgres mydb > $BACKUP_DIR/mydb-$DATE.sql # Compress it gzip $BACKUP_DIR/mydb-$DATE.sql # Delete backups older than 7 days find $BACKUP_DIR -name "*.gz" -mtime +7 -delete echo "Backup complete: $BACKUP_DIR/mydb-$DATE.sql.gz"
CMD
# Make the script executable chmod +x backup.sh # Open crontab editor crontab -e # Add this line (runs every day at 2 AM): # ┌─ minute (0-59) # │ ┌─ hour (0-23) # │ │ ┌─ day of month (1-31) # │ │ │ ┌─ month (1-12) # │ │ │ │ ┌─ day of week (0=Sun) 0 2 * * * /opt/backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1 # List all scheduled cron jobs crontab -l
OUTPUT
0 2 * * * /opt/backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1 # In /var/log/backup.log the next morning: Backup complete: /opt/backups/mydb-2024-01-15.sql.gz
04
File Permissions — chmod & chown Explained
Fix "Permission denied" errors and understand rwx in 3 minutes
permissions
CMD
# See current permissions ls -la myapp/ # -rw-r--r-- means: owner=rw, group=r, others=r # Make a script executable chmod +x deploy.sh # add execute for everyone chmod 755 deploy.sh # rwxr-xr-x (owner full, others read+exec) chmod 600 .env # rw------- (only owner can read — good for secrets!) chmod 700 ~/.ssh # rwx------ (your SSH dir — others cannot see it) # Change owner (run as root) chown ubuntu:ubuntu /opt/myapp # user:group chown -R ubuntu:ubuntu /opt/myapp # -R = recursive (all files inside)
OUTPUT
-rw------- 1 ubuntu ubuntu 512 Jan 15 .env -rwxr-xr-x 1 ubuntu ubuntu 1024 Jan 15 deploy.sh drwx------ 2 ubuntu ubuntu 4096 Jan 15 .ssh/
CHEATSHEET
400 = read-only (SSH key files) | 600 = rw owner only (.env, secrets) | 644 = web files (owner rw, others r) | 755 = scripts and dirs | 777 = everyone full access (⚠️ never use in prod)
05
grep, tail & pipe — Read Logs Like a Pro
Find errors in massive log files instantly; watch logs stream live
logs
CMD
# Follow a log file live (Ctrl+C to stop) tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log # Show last 100 lines tail -n 100 /var/log/myapp.log # Find all ERROR lines in a log grep "ERROR" /var/log/myapp.log # Case-insensitive search grep -i "error" app.log # Show 3 lines BEFORE and AFTER the match (context) grep -B3 -A3 "TypeError" app.log # Live errors only — follow AND filter tail -f app.log | grep "ERROR" # Count how many 500 errors happened grep "HTTP 500" access.log | wc -l # Show Docker container logs live docker logs -f myapp-api-1 | grep "error"
OUTPUT
2024-01-15 14:32:11 [ERROR] DB connection timeout after 5000ms 2024-01-15 14:32:12 [ERROR] DB connection timeout after 5000ms 2024-01-15 14:32:15 [WARN] Retrying connection (attempt 3/5) 2024-01-15 14:32:18 [INFO] DB connected successfully
🌿 Git — Practical Use Cases
01
Feature Branch Workflow — The Standard Way to Work
Never commit directly to main; always use a branch, then open a PR
workflow
CMD
# 1. Make sure you start from latest main git checkout main git pull origin main # 2. Create and switch to a new feature branch git checkout -b feature/add-auth # 3. Write your code... then commit git add . git commit -m "feat: add JWT authentication middleware" # 4. Push your branch to GitHub git push origin feature/add-auth # 5. Open a Pull Request on GitHub UI # → team reviews → CI runs → merge to main # 6. After merge, clean up your local branch git checkout main git pull origin main git branch -d feature/add-auth
OUTPUT
Switched to a new branch 'feature/add-auth' [feature/add-auth 3f8a9b2] feat: add JWT authentication middleware Branch 'feature/add-auth' set up to track origin/feature/add-auth.
02
Resolve a Merge Conflict
Two people edited the same file — here's how to resolve it without panic
conflict
CMD
# You are merging and hit a conflict git merge main # CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/config.js # Open the conflicting file — it will look like this:
CONFLICT
src/config.js (conflict markers added by Git)
<<<<<<< HEAD ← YOUR changes const PORT = 8080; ======= ← divider const PORT = 3000; >>>>>>> main ← THEIR changes (from main)
CMD
# EDIT the file — delete the markers, keep what you want: # const PORT = process.env.PORT || 3000; ← best of both # Stage the resolved file git add src/config.js # Complete the merge git commit -m "merge: resolve PORT conflict, use env var" # Check — no more conflicts git status
OUTPUT
Merge made by the 'recursive' strategy. src/config.js | 2 +- 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)
03
git stash — Save Work Without Committing
Mid-task and need to switch branches urgently? Stash it.
stash
CMD
# You are halfway through a feature when a hotfix comes in # Stash your current work (like a clipboard) git stash push -m "WIP: halfway through auth feature" # Now your working directory is clean — switch branches safely git checkout main git checkout -b hotfix/login-crash # ... fix the bug, commit, push, merge ... # Come back to your feature branch git checkout feature/add-auth # See what is stashed git stash list # Restore your stashed work git stash pop # applies latest stash AND removes it from stash list
OUTPUT
stash@{0}: On feature/add-auth: WIP: halfway through auth feature On branch feature/add-auth Changes not staged for commit: modified: src/auth/middleware.js Dropped stash@{0}
04
git rebase — Clean Up History Before a PR
Squash messy WIP commits into one clean commit before requesting review
rebase
CMD
# You have 4 messy commits on your feature branch: # abc123 WIP # def456 fix typo # ghi789 almost done # jkl012 finally works # Squash last 4 commits interactively git rebase -i HEAD~4 # Editor opens — change to: # pick abc123 WIP # squash def456 fix typo # squash ghi789 almost done # squash jkl012 finally works # → save → another editor opens for the combined commit message # Write: "feat: add JWT authentication" # Force push (you rewrote history) git push --force-with-lease origin feature/add-auth
OUTPUT
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feature/add-auth. git log --oneline f9c3a2b feat: add JWT authentication ← 4 commits became 1, clean! a81b3d1 feat: previous work
05
Undo Mistakes — reset, revert & restore
The right tool for every "oh no" moment — without losing work
undo
CMD
─── Scenario 1: Unstage a file (not yet committed) ─── git restore --staged src/secrets.js # remove from staging, keep changes ─── Scenario 2: Discard ALL local changes (dangerous!) ─── git restore . # reverts working directory to last commit ─── Scenario 3: Undo last commit but KEEP the changes ─── git reset HEAD~1 # unpacks last commit back to working dir ─── Scenario 4: Undo a commit that was ALREADY PUSHED ─── # NEVER force-push to shared branches! # Use revert — creates a new "undo" commit git revert abc123 # creates commit that reverses abc123 git push origin main # safe to push ─── Scenario 5: I committed to wrong branch! ─── git log --oneline -1 # copy the commit hash git reset HEAD~1 # undo the commit on wrong branch git checkout correct-branch git cherry-pick abc123 # apply that commit here
RULE
revert = safe for shared branches (adds new commit). reset = rewrites history, only use on your own local branches. --force-with-lease > --force (checks nobody else pushed first).

Same as a real office job
Every other tab in this cheatsheet teaches you one piece — a Docker command, a kubectl command, a YAML file. This tab is different: it's one single real task, followed all the way through, so you can see exactly how those pieces connect in an actual job. Nothing here is abstract — every file and command below is something a real DevOps engineer or backend dev would actually type or click, in this exact order.

The scenario: you're on a small team running a Node.js API. QA files a bug: "The /health endpoint always returns 200 OK, even when the database is completely disconnected — our monitoring never catches real outages." You're assigned the ticket. Here is everything that happens between you reading that sentence and the fix being live in production.
1️⃣ Ship a Code Change
2️⃣ Coming Soon

🎬 Example 1 of 5 — Shipping a Code Change to Production
Click any step below to open it — click again to close it.
01
Start from a clean main, create a branch
You never edit code directly on main — ever
git
CMD
# make sure you're starting from the latest, real main branch git checkout main git pull origin main # create + switch to a new branch for JUST this fix git checkout -b fix/health-check-db
WHY
This is the single most repeated habit in any real dev/DevOps job. A feature branch keeps your unfinished, unproven work completely isolated from the code everyone else is running. Nothing you do for the next several steps can break anything for anyone else.
↓ now you actually go find the bug
02
Open the real file and find the actual bug
This is the whole reason the ticket exists
before
FILE
routes/health.js — as it is right now
const express = require('express'); const router = express.Router(); router.get('/health', (req, res) => { res.status(200).json({ status: 'ok' }); // always "ok" — never checks anything! }); module.exports = router;
WHY
Found it in about ten seconds. The endpoint doesn't check anything at all — it's hardcoded to say "ok" no matter what. That's exactly why monitoring never noticed the database had gone down: the health check was lying the whole time.
↓ so you fix it
03
Make the fix — small and boring, on purpose
Most real fixes are a handful of lines, not a rewrite
after
FILE
routes/health.js — after your edit
const express = require('express'); const router = express.Router(); const db = require('../db'); router.get('/health', async (req, res) => { try { await db.query('SELECT 1'); // actually ping the real database res.status(200).json({ status: 'ok' }); } catch (err) { res.status(503).json({ status: 'db unreachable' }); // now it can actually fail } }); module.exports = router;
WHY
Four real lines changed. It now runs one tiny query against the database — if that fails, the endpoint honestly reports 503 instead of lying. This is what "fixing a bug" looks like 90% of the time in a real job: small, targeted, boring.
↓ before you tell anyone, you check it yourself
04
Run it locally — never push code you haven't tested
The cheapest place to catch a mistake is your own laptop
local
CMD
npm test
OUTPUT
Health endpoint ✓ returns 200 when db is reachable (42ms) ✓ returns 503 when db is down (38ms) 2 passing
WHY
This takes seconds and happens before a single other person or system is involved. Catching a mistake here costs you nothing. Catching it later — in CI, or worse, in production — costs everyone time.
↓ it works locally, so now it leaves your laptop
05
Commit and push the branch
Your change becomes visible to the team for the first time
git
CMD
git add routes/health.js git commit -m "fix: health check now verifies DB connection" git push origin fix/health-check-db
WHY
The commit message says what changed and why — the fix: prefix follows Conventional Commits (covered in the Git tab). Six months from now, someone reading history understands this instantly without asking you.
↓ this is where GitHub itself starts reacting to what you did
06
Open a Pull Request — the literal clicks
Not a diagram — this is exactly what's on your screen
GitHub UI
ON SCREEN
1. GitHub shows a yellow banner on the repo page: "fix/health-check-db had recent pushes — Compare & pull request" 2. You click [ Compare & pull request ] 3. Title field: "Fix: health check now verifies DB connection" 4. Description box: "QA reported /health always returns 200 even when the DB is down. This adds a real DB ping so monitoring can actually detect outages." 5. Reviewers panel, right side → you add your tech lead 6. You click [ Create pull request ]
WHY
The PR isn't optional busywork — it's the gate. From this point, nothing you wrote can reach main without going through everything below.
↓ you didn't click anything for this next part — it just happens
07
CI fires automatically on your PR
This YAML file already existed — you didn't write it today
GitHub Actions
FILE
.github/workflows/ci.yml — already sitting in the repo
name: CI on: pull_request: branches: [main] jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: 18 - run: npm install - run: npm test
ON YOUR PR PAGE
✓ CI / test (pull_request) — Successful in 34s
WHY
Someone on your team set this file up once, months ago. Since then it has run on every single pull request, automatically, forever — no one has to remember to run tests manually. This is the entire, literal meaning of "CI": a YAML file plus a trigger. If this check were red, GitHub would grey out the Merge button — broken code physically cannot merge.
↓ the robot approved it — now a human does
08
Code review — a real teammate reads your diff
The human safety net sitting right next to the automated one
review
ON SCREEN
Your teammate opens the PR → "Files changed" tab Reads the red/green diff of routes/health.js Leaves a comment: "LGTM, good catch 👍" Clicks [ Approve ]
WHY
LGTM = "looks good to me," probably the most-typed phrase in software. Tests catch things a human might miss; a human catches things tests can't — like "wait, should this actually be a 500, not a 503?"
↓ one click here is the trigger for literally everything after it
09
Merge — the click that starts the release
Nothing else needs to happen manually from here
GitHub UI
ON SCREEN
You click the big green [ Merge pull request ] button → then [ Confirm merge ] → GitHub shows: "Pull request successfully merged and closed" → your fix/health-check-db branch's code is now inside main
WHY
This single click is the cause of every remaining step below. You will not touch a keyboard again for the rest of this example — everything from here runs by itself.
↓ a SECOND, completely different pipeline wakes up — not the one from step 7
10
Build the Docker image and push it to the registry
A different trigger, a different job, running for a different reason
GitHub Actions
FILE
.github/workflows/deploy.yml — a separate file from ci.yml
name: Deploy on: push: branches: [main] # not pull_request — this fires on the MERGE itself jobs: build-and-push: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: docker/login-action@v3 with: username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USER }} password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }} - run: docker build -t mycompany/api:${{ github.sha }} . - run: docker push mycompany/api:${{ github.sha }}
WHY
Notice the trigger: on: push to main — different from ci.yml's on: pull_request. Two separate YAML files firing at two separate moments for two separate reasons. ${{ github.sha }} tags the image with the exact commit hash, so at any point later you can look at a running image and know precisely which code is inside it.
↓ the image exists in the registry now — but nothing is running it yet
11
Tell Kubernetes to actually run the new image
The moment your fix genuinely goes live
kubectl
FILE
.github/workflows/deploy.yml — one more step, same job
- name: Deploy to Kubernetes run: | kubectl set image deployment/api-deployment \ api=mycompany/api:${{ github.sha }} \ --record
OUTPUT
deployment.apps/api-deployment image updated
WHY
kubectl set image tells the existing Deployment (from the Kubernetes tab) "swap your containers for this new image." Kubernetes then does a rolling update on its own — old pods keep serving traffic until new ones are confirmed healthy, so no user of the API notices anything happened.
↓ "the pipeline finished" is not the same as "it actually works" — so you check
12
Verify it's actually live — the step beginners skip
A real engineer never trusts a green checkmark alone
verify
CMD
kubectl rollout status deployment/api-deployment curl https://api.mycompany.com/health kubectl logs -l app=api --tail=20
OUTPUT
deployment "api-deployment" successfully rolled out {"status":"ok"} 2024-01-15 api-7d9f8 Server listening on port 3000 2024-01-15 api-7d9f8 DB connection verified on /health check
WHY
This is the step most beginners forget. A finished pipeline just means "the steps ran" — it doesn't guarantee the fix behaves correctly against a real, running system. A real engineer always closes the loop by actually looking.
🔁
That's the whole thing, nothing skipped
Ticket → branch → code → local test → push → PR → automatic CI → human review → merge → automatic Docker build → automatic deploy → manual verify. Every tool from every other tab in this cheatsheet — Git, Docker, GitHub Actions YAML, Kubernetes — is just one link in this exact chain. That's genuinely all "DevOps" means at a real company: making this chain run itself, safely, every single day.
🐳 Example 2 of 5 — Running Your First App in Docker
Click any step below to open it — click again to close it.
This one is deliberately small. No Git branches, no Pull Request, no CI, no Kubernetes — just Docker, by itself, so the basic idea actually clicks before you touch anything more advanced. Every terminal output below is written to look exactly like what your real terminal will show — same layout, same wording — so when you try this yourself on a real computer, nothing looks unfamiliar or scary.

The goal: take a tiny app, put it inside a container, run that container, actually talk to it, read its logs, then clean up after yourself. That's it. That's the whole example — and it's also the exact foundation underneath everything Example 1 automated.
01
The app — as simple as it gets
One file, zero dependencies, nothing to install
index.js
FILE
index.js
const http = require('http'); // built into Node — nothing to npm install const server = http.createServer((req, res) => { res.end('Hello from inside a container! 🐳'); }); server.listen(3000, () => { console.log('Server running on port 3000'); });
WHY
That's genuinely the whole app. No framework, no package.json, no npm install step — on purpose. This example is about understanding Docker, not Node, so everything that isn't Docker has been stripped down to almost nothing.
↓ now you tell Docker how to package it
02
Write the Dockerfile — 4 lines, explained one at a time
A Dockerfile is just a short recipe, read top to bottom
Dockerfile
FILE
Dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine WORKDIR /app COPY index.js . CMD ["node", "index.js"]
WHY — line by line
FROM node:20-alpine — start from a tiny, ready-made Linux system that already has Node.js installed. You are not building an operating system — you're borrowing one that already exists.

WORKDIR /app — make a folder called /app inside that system, and treat it as the "current folder" for every line after this one.

COPY index.js . — copy your index.js from your own computer into that /app folder, inside the image.

CMD ["node", "index.js"] — the command that runs automatically the moment someone starts a container from this image.
↓ turn that recipe into an actual image
03
Build the image
This is exactly what your own terminal will print
docker build
CMD
docker build -t hello-app:1.0 .
OUTPUT
[+] Building 1.8s (9/9) FINISHED => [internal] load build definition from Dockerfile 0.0s => [internal] load .dockerignore 0.0s => [internal] load metadata for docker.io/library/node:20-alpine 1.2s => [1/3] FROM docker.io/library/node:20-alpine 0.0s => [internal] load build context 0.0s => [2/3] WORKDIR /app 0.1s => [3/3] COPY index.js . 0.1s => exporting to image 0.2s => => writing image sha256:9f8e7d6c5b4a3c2d1e0f9a8b7c6d5e4f => => naming to docker.io/library/hello-app:1.0
WHY
Each => line is one instruction from your Dockerfile being carried out. -t hello-app:1.0 just gives the result a name and a version tag so you can refer to it later instead of typing a long hash.
↓ check that it's actually sitting on your machine now
04
Confirm the image exists
It's a saved template now — nothing is running yet
docker images
CMD
docker images
OUTPUT
REPOSITORY TAG IMAGE ID CREATED SIZE hello-app 1.0 9f8e7d6c5b4a 3 seconds ago 134MB
WHY
This is the important mental split beginners usually miss: an image is just a saved, inert file sitting on disk — like a .zip you haven't extracted yet. Nothing is running. That only happens in the next step.
↓ now actually start it
05
Run it as a container
Every flag explained — nothing left as a mystery
docker run
CMD
docker run -d -p 3000:3000 --name hello-app hello-app:1.0
OUTPUT
9f8e7d6c5b4a3c2d1e0f9a8b7c6d5e4f3a2b1c0d9e8f7a6b5c4d3e2f1a0b9c8d
WHY — every flag
-d — "detached": run in the background and give me my terminal back immediately.

-p 3000:3000 — connect port 3000 on your real computer to port 3000 inside the container. Format is always host:container. Without this flag, the app runs, but nothing outside the container can ever reach it.

--name hello-app — give this specific running container a name you can refer to, instead of typing that long ID every time.

That long string printed back is just the full container ID — you'll rarely need the whole thing.
↓ double check it's really running
06
Confirm it's actually running
The command you'll type more than any other Docker command
docker ps
CMD
docker ps
OUTPUT
CONTAINER ID IMAGE COMMAND CREATED STATUS PORTS NAMES 9f8e7d6c5b4a hello-app:1.0 "node index.js" 8 seconds ago Up 8 seconds 0.0.0.0:3000->3000/tcp hello-app
WHY — the columns, quickly
CONTAINER ID / IMAGE — which image it came from. COMMAND — what's actually running inside. STATUS — "Up 8 seconds" means healthy and alive right now. PORTS — confirms the 3000→3000 connection from step 5 actually took effect. If this list is empty, your container isn't running — that's the very first thing to check when something feels broken.
↓ it's running — so actually talk to it
07
Actually talk to it
The entire point of everything above
curl / browser
CMD
curl http://localhost:3000
OUTPUT
Hello from inside a container! 🐳
WHY
You could type localhost:3000 into a browser instead and see the exact same text. Walk the round trip in your head: your request left your terminal → hit port 3000 on your real machine → Docker forwarded it through the tunnel from -p 3000:3000 → your Node server inside the container answered → the response came back out the same way. That tunnel is the entire reason the -p flag exists.
↓ see what the app itself has been saying
08
Check its logs
Usually the very first thing you look at when debugging
docker logs
CMD
docker logs hello-app
OUTPUT
Server running on port 3000
WHY
Anything your app prints with console.log ends up here — nowhere else. When something goes wrong later with a real app, this is the first command almost anyone reaches for.
↓ and finally, clean up after yourself
09
Stop it, then remove it
The image is untouched — you can start fresh anytime
cleanup
CMD
docker stop hello-app docker rm hello-app
OUTPUT
hello-app hello-app
WHY
Docker just echoes the name back — that's genuinely all it prints, which surprises a lot of beginners expecting more output. stop shuts the container down gracefully. rm actually deletes it. Your hello-app:1.0 image from step 3 is completely untouched — run docker run again any time and you get a brand-new container from the exact same image.
🧱
This is the foundation everything else stands on
Write code → describe it in a Dockerfile → build an image → run a container from it → talk to it → read its logs → clean up. Go back and look at Example 1's steps 10 and 11 — the automatic docker build and the automatic deploy. That's this exact sequence, just triggered by a robot instead of by you typing it. Once this feels boring and obvious, Example 1 stops looking like magic.
⚡ Example 3 of 5 — Your First Full CI/CD Pipeline
Click any step below to open it — click again to close it.
If YAML, GitHub Actions, "secrets," and "deployments" have ever felt intimidating, that feeling ends here. Every single thing below is something you already did with your own two hands in Example 2 — build an image, run it, check it, ship it. The only difference in this example is that a computer types those exact same commands for you, automatically, every time you push code, without getting tired or making a typo. That's genuinely the entire concept of "CI/CD." Nothing more mystical than that.

Every screen shown below is copied from what GitHub and Docker Hub actually show you — same labels, same layout, same wording — researched live for this exact page, so nothing surprises you the first time you open the real thing yourself.
01
The one new file — a GitHub Actions workflow
6 steps, each one you can already explain to yourself
.github/workflows/ci-cd.yml
FILE
.github/workflows/ci-cd.yml
name: CI/CD on: push: branches: [main] jobs: build-test-deploy: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Checkout code uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Set up Node uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: 20 - name: Run the test run: node test.js - name: Log in to Docker Hub uses: docker/login-action@v3 with: username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USER }} password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }} - name: Build and push image run: | docker build -t mycompany/hello-app:${{ github.sha }} . docker push mycompany/hello-app:${{ github.sha }} - name: Deploy run: kubectl set image deployment/hello-app hello-app=mycompany/hello-app:${{ github.sha }}
WHY — every named step, one sentence each
Checkout code — downloads your repo's code onto GitHub's temporary computer, so it has something to work with.

Set up Node — installs Node.js on that temporary computer. Same idea as installing it on your own laptop.

Run the test — runs the exact test.js file from the next step. If it fails, everything below never runs.

Log in to Docker Hub — logs into your Docker Hub account using two secret values saved once in Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions, so GitHub is allowed to push images on your behalf. You never type a password in the YAML itself.

Build and push image — the exact same docker build command from Example 2, plus docker push, now run automatically instead of by you.

Deploy — tells Kubernetes to swap in the freshly-pushed image, the same kubectl set image idea from Example 1's step 11.
↓ but "run the test" needs an actual test.js file to run
02
The test — no framework, no npm install, still real
Proof the app actually answers before anything ships
test.js
FILE
test.js
const http = require('http'); require('./index.js'); // this line alone starts the server on port 3000 setTimeout(() => { http.get('http://localhost:3000', (res) => { if (res.statusCode === 200) { console.log('✓ Server responded with 200 OK'); process.exit(0); } else { console.error('✗ Unexpected status:', res.statusCode); process.exit(1); } }).on('error', (err) => { console.error('✗ Request failed:', err.message); process.exit(1); }); }, 500);
WHY
No Jest, no test runner, nothing to install — just plain Node starting the server and checking it actually says "200 OK" before anything gets built or shipped. process.exit(1) is the one line that makes the whole pipeline stop dead if the app is broken. That's the entire mechanism behind "CI catches broken code" — an exit code, nothing more magical.
↓ both files exist — now the one action that starts everything
03
Push — the exact same git you already know
Identical to Example 2's git steps, plus two new files
git
CMD
git add . git commit -m "add CI/CD pipeline" git push origin main
WHY
Nothing new here at all — this is the identical git add / commit / push sequence from Example 2. You're just pushing two new files this time: the workflow YAML and test.js.
↓ you didn't click anything else — GitHub noticed the push on its own
04
Open the "Actions" tab and watch it appear
Real GitHub UI, verified live for this page
github.com
ON SCREEN — right after you push
Actions All workflows ● CI/CD add CI/CD pipeline CI/CD #1: Push #main by you In progress · main
A FEW SECONDS LATER
✓ CI/CD add CI/CD pipeline CI/CD #1: Push #main by you Success · 38s · main
WHY
A small yellow dot means it's currently running. A green checkmark means every step succeeded. A red ✕ would mean something failed — most commonly your test.js from step 2. This exact list, with this exact wording, is what every single GitHub repository's Actions tab looks like, whether it's a weekend hobby project or a company with 10,000 engineers.
↓ click the run's name to open it — this is what's inside
05
Open the run — watch every step tick past
This exact shape, forever, on every workflow ever
github.com
ON SCREEN
build-test-deploy succeeded in 38s ✓ Set up job ✓ Checkout code ✓ Set up Node ✓ Run the test ✓ Log in to Docker Hub ✓ Build and push image ✓ Deploy ✓ Complete job
WHY
Notice "Set up job" always appears first and "Complete job" always appears last — GitHub adds those automatically to every job that has ever run, on every repo. Everything between them is just your steps: list from the YAML, in the exact order you wrote them, each one clickable to see its own raw log if you're curious. Once you've seen this shape a single time, every future pipeline you ever open looks instantly familiar — that recognition is most of what "experience" with CI/CD actually is.
↓ scroll up on that same page — there's a small summary box too
06
The Summary box — the same one on every run
Also copied live from a real run, so it's exact
github.com
ON SCREEN
Summary Triggered via push main you commit a1b2c3d Status Success Total duration 38s Artifacts – ci-cd.yml on: push
WHY
Triggered via push, Status, Total duration, Artifacts — this exact box appears at the top of every workflow run on GitHub, for every repo that has ever existed. It never changes shape, only the numbers inside it change.
↓ the "build and push image" step actually did something real — go check
07
Confirm the image actually landed on Docker Hub
Real Docker Hub layout, checked live for this page
hub.docker.com
ON SCREEN — hub.docker.com/r/mycompany/hello-app
mycompany / hello-app Overview Tags Tags TAG LAST PUSHED a1b2c3d... a few seconds ago
WHY
Same tagging idea from Example 1's step 10 — ${{ github.sha }} means the tag is literally the exact commit that produced it. Open the Tags page on any real Docker Hub repository and this is precisely the layout you'll see: an Overview tab and a Tags tab, a list of tags, and when each was last pushed.
↓ the "deploy" step ran too — same as Example 1's step 11
08
It's already deployed — nothing left to click
The last YAML step already did this for you
kubectl
OUTPUT — inside the "Deploy" step's log
deployment.apps/hello-app image updated
WHY
You never typed this kubectl command yourself — GitHub's computer ran it, using the exact command written in step 1's YAML. Kubernetes then rolls the new version out on its own, the same self-healing rolling update from the Kubernetes tab.
↓ trust nothing until you've actually looked — same rule as always
09
Verify it, one more time, yourself
A green checkmark is a claim — this is proof
curl
CMD
curl https://hello-app.mycompany.com
OUTPUT
Hello from inside a container! 🐳
WHY
Same message from Example 2's step 7 — because underneath all of this automation, it's still the exact same tiny app, in the exact same kind of container, just shipped by a robot instead of by hand.
😌
That's genuinely the whole thing — nothing was hidden from you
One YAML file → git push → GitHub runs your test → builds the image → pushes it → deploys it → you verify it. Every scary word — pipeline, workflow, CI/CD, deployment — is just a name for this exact sequence you've now watched happen, start to finish, with real screens. Example 1 does this again with more realistic office detail (a bug ticket, a code review); this one was stripped down on purpose so the mechanism itself — not the office process around it — is what stuck.
🚨 Example 4 of 5 — When Something Breaks (The Most Common DevOps Day)
Click any step below to open it — click again to close it. Yellow glowing rings mark exactly what you'd click in real life.
Examples 1–3 were all about shipping new code. But the single most common thing a DevOps engineer actually does, day after day, isn't shipping something new — it's noticing something broke and calmly fixing it, using the exact same tools already covered. This example is that story, in the smallest steps possible.
Think of it like a toy that stopped working. You wouldn't take it apart blindly. You'd check what changed last — new batteries? — put the old batteries back if that's what worked before, and check if it works now. That's this entire example. Website instead of toy, that's the only difference.
01
Notice something is wrong
You can't fix a problem you don't know exists
Grafana
WHY — before anything else
Nobody sits and stares at a website hoping to catch it breaking. Instead, a dashboard watches it automatically, all day, every day — this is the Monitor phase from the Lifecycle tab, finally shown in action. The moment something looks wrong, it tells you before a single user has to complain.
1.1Normally, the dashboard just sits there calm and green
UI
📊 Grafana — hello-app / HTTP availability (SLO)
Critical alert OK
1.2Then, one afternoon — it flips to red
UI
📊 Grafana — hello-app / HTTP availability (SLO)
👆 THIS IS THE SIGNAL
Critical alert FIRING
Error rate
38.2%
Was, 10 min ago
0.4%
requests failing, last 30 min
1.3Grafana also pings the team automatically — nobody has to be staring at the screen
UI
# incidents
🔔
grafana-bot2:41 PM
🔴 Critical alert firing: HTTP availability for public requests
Error rate 38.2% (threshold: 5%) — view dashboard
↓ okay, something's wrong — now figure out why
02
Figure out what changed recently
Almost every "it broke" moment traces back to the last deploy
GitHub Actions
WHY — before touching anything
Apps don't randomly break on their own while sitting still. Almost always, something changed — and the most recent change is the very last thing that got deployed. Before guessing, go look at exactly what shipped last.
2.1Open the Actions tab — find the most recent run
UI
👆 CLICK THIS ROW
✓Fix null check on checkout totalSuccess · 41s · main
✓Bump minor dependencySuccess · 36s · main
2.2Click in — see exactly what code shipped
UI
Fix null check on checkout total #47 Triggered via push · main · you · 2:36 PM Status: Success · Total duration: 41s
WHY this is the important part
Notice it says ✓ Success. That's not a contradiction — the tests that existed all passed. It just means nobody had written a test for this exact situation yet. A green checkmark means "the bugs we thought to test for didn't happen," not "there are zero bugs." That's exactly why the Grafana dashboard from Step 1 still matters even after CI passes.
↓ a suspect isn't proof — go check the actual evidence
03
Confirm it with real evidence
Don't guess — look at what the running app is actually doing
kubectl
WHY — before rolling anything back
A suspicious commit is a theory, not proof. Kubernetes is what's actually running the app right now — so ask it directly what's happening, the same way you'd check a patient's vitals before deciding on treatment.
3.1Check the pods
CMD
kubectl get pods
OUTPUT
NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE hello-app-7d9f6b7c8-x2k9p 0/1 CrashLoopBackOff 6 8m
3.2Read what it's actually saying
CMD
kubectl logs hello-app-7d9f6b7c8-x2k9p
OUTPUT
Server running on port 3000 TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'total') at /app/checkout.js:14:22 Process exited with code 1
WHY
CrashLoopBackOff just means "it crashes, Kubernetes restarts it, it crashes again" — on repeat. The log confirms the theory from Step 2: the checkout fix broke on a real input it wasn't tested against. Now it's not a guess anymore.
↓ now — restore service first, investigate deeper later
04
Stop the bleeding — roll back immediately
Restore service first. Debugging deeply can wait a few minutes.
kubectl rollout undo
WHY this comes before "fixing" it properly
Real users are hitting errors right now. Sitting down to carefully write and test a proper fix takes time they don't have. The fastest safe move is going back to the exact version that was working ten minutes ago — Kubernetes already remembers it.
4.1Roll back to the previous version
CMD
kubectl rollout undo deployment/hello-app
OUTPUT
deployment.apps/hello-app rolled back
4.2Watch it come back up
CMD
kubectl rollout status deployment/hello-app
OUTPUT
Waiting for deployment "hello-app" rollout to finish... deployment "hello-app" successfully rolled out
4.3Double-check the pod is actually healthy
CMD
kubectl get pods
OUTPUT
NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE hello-app-5f8c9d6b4-m4t7q 1/1 Running 0 22s
↓ the app is safe again — but there's one more thing, or this happens again tomorrow
05
Fix it where it actually lives — the code
Rolling back the app isn't enough — the bug is still sitting in Git
git revert
WHY this step can't be skipped
Step 4 fixed the running app, not the source code. If nobody touches Git, the very next person who deploys — maybe next week, maybe by accident — will re-ship the exact same broken commit, and this whole thing happens all over again.
5.1Find the exact commit that broke it
CMD
git log --oneline -3
OUTPUT
a3f9c1e Fix null check on checkout total 7b2e0d4 Bump minor dependency c19a44f Add checkout summary page
5.2Undo that exact commit, and push it
CMD
git revert a3f9c1e git push origin main
OUTPUT
[main 9c4d21a] Revert "Fix null check on checkout total" 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 4 deletions(-) To github.com/you/hello-app.git a3f9c1e..9c4d21a main -> main
WHY
git revert doesn't erase history — it adds a new commit that undoes the old one, so there's an honest record of what happened. That git push is the exact same trigger from Example 3 — it automatically re-runs the whole CI/CD pipeline, tests it, builds it, and re-deploys it. Nobody has to remember any extra step.
↓ "should be fixed now" is a guess — go confirm it like a real user would
06
Verify it's actually fixed
"Looks fixed to me" isn't good enough — check it from the outside
curl + Grafana
WHY
It's tempting to assume "the pipeline went green, so it's fine." Confirm it the same way a real visitor would — actually hit the app — and then confirm the dashboard agrees over time, not just in the first second.
6.1Hit the live endpoint directly
CMD
curl https://hello-app.example.com/checkout
OUTPUT
HTTP/1.1 200 OK {"status":"ok","message":"Hello from inside a container! 🐳"}
6.2Watch the dashboard confirm it over the next few minutes
UI
📊 Grafana — hello-app / HTTP availability (SLO)
👆 BACK TO GREEN
Critical alert OK
↓ one last thing — fixing it quietly isn't the whole job
07
Tell the team what happened
So it doesn't quietly repeat next month

WHY this counts as part of the job
Fixing it silently helps for exactly one day. Writing three short sentences — what broke, what fixed it, what changes going forward — helps the whole team, forever. This is the "close the loop" step that feeds back into Plan, all the way back at the start of the Lifecycle tab.

This loop — not shipping new features — is most of the actual job
Ship (Examples 1–3) → Monitor (Step 1) → Investigate (Steps 2–3) → Stop the bleeding (Step 4) → Fix the source (Step 5) → Verify (Step 6) → Communicate (Step 7) → back to shipping again. Every tool used above is one you already met in an earlier example — nothing here was new, just used for a different reason.
